### <a id="fjs-d981"></a>2026-10-13 · `FJS-D981` — Q5 — How a machine proves it is the same member — An Ed25519 key pair: `signRequest({ privateKey })` and `verifyRequest({ publicKey })` sign the one canonical string, and the login mints an ordinary session.

Asked in [`IDEAS/haven.md`](IDEAS/haven.md) § Open questions. **A** was picked over **B** (no signature: the first run is answered a long-lived token, and the token is the identity).

The paper had planned a login signed with `signRequest()` and a session minted by `bearerClaim(...).mint()`. Neither works. `signRequest` is an HMAC, so it needs a secret both sides hold, and a stranger's server holds nothing; and a `bearerClaim` principal has no id (`FJS-D342`). The socket's `conn.user` comes only from `IAuth.verifySession`, so a bearer-only member joins no room and `@createdBy` has no id to stamp. A buys what B cannot: one key is one identity on every Haven server (2.3's `--api`), a session can expire because the key mints the next one, and the private key never travels. What it costs is the key-pair form in toolbelt. B's identity would be a token that can never expire, because losing it loses the nick.

**The key pair is a second form of the one scheme, not a second scheme.** It signs the same canonical string with the same freshness window and nonce. Only the last step differs, and the value's prefix names which: `v1-ed25519=` beside `v1-sha256=`. A side that verifies the other scheme answers by name (*signature is v1-sha256 and this side verifies v1-ed25519*) rather than *does not match*, for the reason the version prefix exists. Keys are base64url strings (raw public, PKCS#8 private), because a key is written to a file and sent in a JSON body.

**The login verifies with toolbelt directly, not through `createApp({ credentials })` (`FJS-D475`).** That door turns a signature into a principal, and an unknown key is no principal yet. The login's answer is a token. The session is a `Session` row with `@@trait(Grant)`, read back by Haven's own `IAuth`. `@frontierjs/auth` reads `sys.user` and an email, and a member has neither.

The nine (§ V), answered after the code (late, and named as such). **Origin:** one canonical string for both forms, and one key encoding, read and written only in `signature.js`. **Concept:** no new noun; *session*, *Grant* and *mint* already exist. **Complexity:** it is the problem's, since a stranger's server shares no secret with the machine. **Predictability:** the key pair rides the same headers, window and nonce as the HMAC. **Derived:** the member is derived from the key on every login. **Owner:** the verify is toolbelt's. The login's nonce memory is a second copy of `credentials.ts`'s private `remember()`; it moves into junction when a second caller wants one, and until then it is stated here. **Boundary:** the client sends a signed body and gets back a bearer token, so it needs to know nothing else. **Failure:** each refusal names its reason, and a taken nick is a 409. **Silence:** *a login the key did not sign makes nothing* is guarded by `login.test.ts`; four of its rows go red with the verify skipped (measured). *The scheme is named* is guarded by `signature.spec.js`. Adjudication: *paved road vs. the workaround*, resolved by extending the owner (toolbelt) rather than writing a verifier in the app. Tier: Register.

*Lives in:* `packages/toolbelt/src/signature/signature.js` (`generateSigningKeys`, the `privateKey`/`publicKey` forms) · `packages/haven/api/src/login.ts` · `packages/haven/api/src/auth.ts` · `packages/haven/db/schema.lite` (`Session`) · `packages/toolbelt/test/specs/signature.spec.js` · `packages/haven/api/test/login.test.ts`.

### <a id="fjs-d669"></a>2026-10-13 · `FJS-D669` — How does a picker learn which related rows a create policy will accept, and does `fli advise` name the case the schema cannot carry — Both: A for the one-hop `==` auth() shape the derivation can state, B's advise rule for every create conjunct it cannot (`||`, `in`, a computed claim).

Asked in [`IDEAS/owed-rulings.md`](IDEAS/owed-rulings.md) § Open questions. **C** was picked over **A** (extend the derivation: a top-level create conjunct of the shape `<relation>.<col> == auth().<claim>` emits `x-pick-where: { scheduleId: { hostId: 'auth().id' } }`, sierra's `options()` merges it into the related query as a filter with the claim filled from `session.user`, and the server still refuses (Invariant 6). One new schema keyword beside `x-determined`), **B** (no new keyword: the related model's own READ policy is the owner of "rows this caller may pick", and `fli advise` names the model pair where a create policy reaches through a relation the related model's read gate does not narrow, so the author narrows the read or writes a `where` on the field's `optionsQuery`).

The paper's recommendation, taken as written: A alone leaves every unpinnable policy silent, B alone makes every author hand-write what a `@@allow` already says; the derivable shape is derived (`FJS-D492`'s reasoning) and the rest is named rather than guessed.

### <a id="fjs-d960"></a>2026-10-13 · `FJS-D960` — Route or service for *linking* a second provider to a caller who is already signed — A service starts it: `connections.connect(provider)` records the caller on the `OauthFlow` row and returns the authorize URL, and the existing callback route finishes by attaching to that caller instead of issuing a session.

Asked in [`IDEAS/third-party-credentials.md`](IDEAS/third-party-credentials.md) § Open questions. **B** was picked over **A** (the route pair: `GET /auth/oauth/{provider}` attaches to the signed-in caller when a session cookie is present), **C** (no signed-in link: `FJS-D611`'s mailed invitation stays the only way to attach a provider).

The paper's recommendation, taken as written: `FJS-D20`'s line is whether a call can be refused for want of a session, and starting a link can; the callback must stay a route because the provider redirects a browser there, and it already exists. A makes a sign-in link's meaning depend on an ambient cookie, so a forged link attaches an attacker's provider account to a signed-in victim.

### <a id="fjs-d578"></a>2026-10-13 · `FJS-D578` — How does a field `@allow('write', auth().isStaff)` reach the generated form — Litestone carries the CALLER-ONLY subset as a fact beside the bit (`x-litestone-write-claims`, e.g. `{ isStaff: true }` or `['auth().isStaff']`), derived by one function next to `determinedColumns` in `policy.js`; sierra's control table disables the control when the session user fails it, and a predicate that reads the row stays a bare bit. Same shape as `x-determined` (`FJS-D492`): an affordance, the boundary enforces regardless (Invariant 6). Needs a defined subset (`auth().<claim>` truthiness, `==` a literal, `&&`) and unknown answers permissive.

Asked in [`IDEAS/owed-rulings.md`](IDEAS/owed-rulings.md) § Open questions. **A** was picked over **B** (carry the whole predicate expression as data and ship an evaluator to the browser. Answers row predicates too, but is a second reader of the policy language in the client, which the schema comment already refuses), **C** (keep the bit; the page hides the column by the session itself (what Transit does now) and `declinedFields` reports a refusal after the save. No new keyword, but every app copies the policy by hand).

The paper's recommendation, taken as written: it is the `x-determined` pattern applied to the write half, answers the case that caused the row without an evaluator in the browser, and a row-dependent predicate degrades to today's behavior.

### <a id="fjs-d670"></a>2026-10-13 · `FJS-D670` — How does Basecamp turn on OAuth when auth requires `cookieAuth` and the whole app is Bearer — A switch, as `example/api/src/app.ts` does with `SHOP_COOKIE_AUTH` (`COOKIE_AUTH` gates both `cookieAuth` and the `oauth` block, ~85/447/472): cookie mode and `oauth` turn on together exactly when at least one provider has its env vars set, and stay Bearer otherwise. The web client's `cookieAuth` twin (`FJS-787`) must follow the same switch, and the manifest carries no auth fact today, so either it gains one or the web build reads the same env. A fleet that wants SSO gets it; a fleet that sets a provider loses the desktop shell's login, as under A. Two modes to test.

Asked in [`IDEAS/owed-rulings.md`](IDEAS/owed-rulings.md) § Open questions. **B** was picked over **A** (move the whole app onto cookie sessions: `cookieAuth: true` plus the sierra twin, providers built from env (`GITHUB_*`, `GOOGLE_*`, `OIDC_*`), login screen draws one button per `GET /auth/oauth` entry. One mode. The server still ACCEPTS `Authorization: Bearer` and `x-api-key` under cookie mode (`http.ts` `setAuthCookie`), so API keys keep working; what changes is every LOGIN, whose token now goes into a cookie and leaves the body (`plugin.ts` ~697), so the desktop shell on `tauri://localhost` and any password-login script can no longer sign in, and every Basecamp drive re-tests under a different credential), **C** (wait for auth to build the short-lived-code exchange the `plugin.ts:117` comment names as the missing piece, so a Bearer app can finish a redirect flow; Basecamp then passes `oauth` with no mode change. Nothing ships until auth does).

The paper's recommendation, taken as written: `example/` already proves the switch (`verify:oauth`), it adds no noun, and a fleet with no provider configured keeps every login it has today; A breaks the shell's login for every fleet and C blocks a table-stakes feature on a larger build. C stays the real fix for the shell and is owed to auth either way.

### <a id="fjs-d847"></a>2026-10-13 · `FJS-D847` — Does a `@@sync` model whose policy walks a model the device does not sync get that model's schema emitted, or is it refused at build — Refuse at build a `@@sync` model whose policy names a model that is not `@@sync`, naming the model to add it to.

Asked in [`IDEAS/owed-rulings.md`](IDEAS/owed-rulings.md) § Open questions. **B** was picked over **A** (walk the policies when emitting the device schema and add each model they reach).

The paper's recommendation, taken as written: A puts a model's schema on the device without its rows, so the policy reads an empty table and answers wrong in silence; B fails loudly and is the refusal half every gap ships with.

### <a id="fjs-d923"></a>2026-10-12 · `FJS-D923` — A `@@softDelete` column is written by `remove()` and `restore()` and by no patch; every update-family verb naming `deletedAt` is refused by name, `asSystem()` included

`update({ data: { deletedAt } })` was `remove()` spelled as a patch and graded as one: at the UPDATE gate, with no cascade walked and no removal announced, so a caller the delete gate refused removed the row anyway (`FJS-2578`). `update`, `updateMany`, `upsert` and `upsertMany` (its `update:` list, or every key its rows carry when there is none) throw `SoftDeleteWriteError` — 400, because the verb is wrong rather than the caller, the shape `BulkTransitionError` already has. **`asSystem()` is refused too**: the cascade is integrity, not authority (`FJS-D502`), and `sys.<model>.remove()` already lifts the gate. **`create` may still state the column** — creating a row already deleted removes nothing, and it is the import shape. An omitted key (`undefined`) is not a write.

Picked by the owner in session as **B** over **A** (grade a non-null patch at the delete gate and a null one at the update gate — a second, weaker `remove()` that walks no cascade) and **C** (reroute the patch through `remove()`/`restore()` — a patch that silently cascades). Junction's override path (`softDelete:` on a service over a model declaring none) already refused the column with *use remove()*; this puts the same refusal at the Data boundary for every caller. Proved by `packages/litestone/test/restore-access.test.ts` § *a soft-delete column is written only by remove() and restore()* — every refusal paired with the verb that removes and a write of another column that lands; with the check removed, 2 of its 3 tests fail. Graded on § V after the build, named as late: *ergonomics vs. strictness* decides it — the patch was the convenient spelling and the destructive one.

### <a id="fjs-d916"></a>2026-10-12 · `FJS-D916` — A key's scopes are refused by junction, against a scope each service DECLARES; a method naming none refuses a scoped key, and mcp's tool list reads the same answer

An API key issued with scopes carried its issuer's whole standing everywhere but auth's own services (`FJS-2116`): no method could say what scope it needed, so nothing refused the rest. Three apps met it three ways — basecamp a 200-line hook and vocabulary, portal a plugin hooking auth's services, sstime a `bearerClaim` grant for a counterparty that is not a stranger. **The names stay the app's** (`FJS-D407`); **the refusal is junction's**, in `callService` beside the method policy, so one owner grades every wire caller (Invariant 4).

- **Declared on the service.** `scope: 'clock'` covers every method; `scope: { read, write }` splits on `isReadMethod`, the line idempotency and the announcement already draw. A `methods:` entry's `scope:` overrides, and `scope: false` admits any key — auth's `account.get`, so a key can still ask who holds it.
- **Fail closed.** A key with a non-empty `scopes` reaches a method only when the method names a scope it holds; one naming none is a 403. A key with no scopes is held to none, so a whole key is a key issued empty — basecamp's `admin` is the picker's word for that and is never stored.
- **Graded at the edge.** An `internal` call is the app's own code inside a call already admitted and is not graded again; `mcp`, `http` and `websocket` are.
- **mcp derives.** The tool list withholds what `scopeRefusal` would refuse, so a key is never offered a verb it would be refused. `narrow` stays for a rule the app holds beyond scopes (basecamp's `NOT_FOR_AGENTS`).
- **Read, not resolved.** `requiredScope(svc, method)` computes at call time, since a move method joins the table when the app serves its schema.

Folds in auth's scoped-key refusal at `people`/`account-recovery` (`FJS-1446`'s second half); `caller()`'s *a key never manages credentials* (`FJS-D615`) is a different rule and stays. Refused: a derived `<service>:<read|write>` vocabulary in junction (one app's names baked in, which `FJS-D407` refused for mcp), and fail-open for an undeclared method (today's hole with a smaller door). Not Invariant 6's ground: a scope grades the credential, not a row, and is declared where `gate:` and `claims:` on a method are (`FJS-D408`, `FJS-D514`) rather than in a hook. Graded on § V after the build, named as late: *paved road vs. the workaround* (three apps, one workaround) and *ergonomics vs. strictness* (a leaked key costs its issuer's whole standing) decide it; a scope declared too broad is the app's judgment and nothing reports it. Picked by the owner in session. Proved by `packages/junction/test/method-scopes.test.ts` and `packages/mcp/test/plugin.test.ts` § *a scoped key is offered what its scopes reach*.

### <a id="fjs-d915"></a>2026-10-11 · `FJS-D915` — Does an OAuth sign-in owe the TOTP code — Yes: OAuth is a first factor like a password and a magic link. `oauthResolve`'s three sign-in branches end at `firstFactorProven(user, { provider })`; on a challenge the callback sets the `login_challenge` cookie and redirects through `oauthFailure` with a new `OAUTH_ERRORS` code, `code_required`, and the page finishes through `completeSignIn`. One error code, no new route.

Asked in [`IDEAS/owed-rulings.md`](IDEAS/owed-rulings.md) § Open questions, on [`FJS-2541`](ISSUES.md#fjs-2541). **B** was picked over **A** (the provider counts as both factors; nothing to build, and a stolen provider account walks past a factor its owner turned on), **C** (a per-provider `secondFactor: 'ours' | 'theirs'` trusting the OIDC `amr` claim; GitHub sends none, so for most providers C is B plus an option).

The paper's recommendation, taken as written: turning on TOTP is the person saying *my account needs the code*, and `FJS-D888` already held the mailbox to it. Strictness follows what a mistake destroys (§ IV), here the account. A newly registered account has no factor, so `oauth.registered` is unchanged. **Amended at the ruling:** `code_required` is not a message. Sierra's `?oauth_error=` reader turns it into `session.awaitingCode`, the state a password challenge sets, so a page already wired for a password sign-in's code finishes an OAuth one unchanged through `submitCode()`. Read as an error it would put *enter your code* on a page with no box to type it in. `confirmOAuthLink`, the mailed link's way to a session, ends at `firstFactorProven` too: it is a fourth door to the same session. C can be added beside B if a provider's own MFA ever needs to count. **What fails when it stops holding:** an auth row asserting an OAuth sign-in on a `totp` account answers a challenge and no session, and a `verify:oauth` step that finishes one through the page. Both are owed by the build.

### <a id="fjs-d888"></a>2026-10-10 · `FJS-D888` — Magic-link sign-in: what a mailbox proves — It is a FIRST factor. An unknown address gets its account at the click, through `onRegister`; an account with a second factor owes its code after the click, as after a password; an account whose only way in is an OAuth provider is refused. The mail carries a link and a six-digit code, either one spends it.

Asked in chat on [`FJS-2537`](ISSUES.md#fjs-2537). Four questions, each answered with the recommended option except the last, where the owner chose to add the code over shipping the link alone.

- **Unknown address — create at the click** over refuse. It is `oauthResolve` § 3 (create only on a proven address), and the click is the proof. A row made at the request would squat the address (`FJS-D612`). A closed signup refuses in `onRegister`, so the flow needs no flag of its own.
- **Second factor — owed** over *the link is enough*. Password and link both end at one `firstFactorProven()` in `auth.ts`, so neither one gets around the other's code.
- **Provider-only account — refused**, at the request (no mail) and again at the click, for `FJS-987`'s reason: the mailbox never secured that account. The test is `confirmPasswordReset`'s, so an account with no credential at all (an invitation) is let in.
- **A six-digit code beside the link**, for a person reading the mail on another device. The code is compared against the row the ADDRESS names and never used to find a row. Misses count on `Verification.attempts` up to `loginChallengeAttempts`, at which the row is spent.

The flow exists only where `onMagicLinkRequested` is set; without it `auth.ts` defines neither method and the plugin mounts no route. Default TTL is 15 minutes, request is rate-limited like a reset, verify sits behind login's limiter.

### <a id="fjs-d880"></a>2026-10-10 · `FJS-D880` — Anonymize vs delete — Derive it from the gate: erasure deletes a row whose delete gate admits SYSTEM, anonymizes it (each `@pii` field nulled, or blanked where required) where only the update gate does, and refuses naming the model where neither does.

Asked in [`IDEAS/compliance-from-the-seed.md`](IDEAS/compliance-from-the-seed.md) § Open questions. **A** was picked over **B** (declare it per model, `@@erasure(delete | anonymize | refuse)`, with `refuse` the default for a model that declares nothing), **C** (no anonymize: erasure deletes what it can reach and refuses the whole request when any reached model is undeletable; anything subtler is a hook).

The paper's recommendation, taken as written: the gate already states what SYSTEM may do to a row, so a per-model word restates it and can disagree with it. Refuse-loudly survives as A's third branch, and the data map prints which branch each model takes, so a derivation the owner did not intend is visible in the artifact rather than in an audit.

### <a id="fjs-d685"></a>2026-10-10 · `FJS-D685` — Does a write fold the app's global filter and the plugins' read filters — Fold both scopes into `update`, `updateMany`, `remove`, `removeMany`, `delete` and `deleteMany` (move them from `WALKS` to `NOT_RESTORE`). The filter is then one predicate for every verb that reaches a row, matching "every path that reaches a row applies every rule that guards it". The six cells promote to `on`; an update/delete of a hidden row answers `null`/`count: 0` like an absent id. `asSystem()` still does not lift it, so a job that maintains rows the app filter hides must say so with a flag.

Asked in [`IDEAS/owed-rulings.md`](IDEAS/owed-rulings.md) § Open questions. **A** was picked over **B** (Keep writes unscoped and write it down: the filter is a READ view, access to writes is the policy and the gate (Invariant 6). The six cells become `-` with the reason; `docs/filtering.md` § Global filters says "reads" rather than "every query". The tenant function filter then needs a `@@allow` beside it to scope a write).

The paper's recommendation, taken as written: docs say "every query on a model, regardless of call site", a per-caller function filter is read by an author as scoping, and a write that ignores it is the silent hole Invariant 6 exists to refuse; B leaves the common tenant-filter case unsafe by default.

### <a id="fjs-d862"></a>2026-10-10 · `FJS-D862` — Are the factories handed to `setup()` / `phases().arrange()` bound to the system client — Yes: both hand out `env.factories` rebound to `env.system`. `env.factories` itself stays on the unscoped client.

Asked in [`ISSUES.md`](ISSUES.md) by the litestone docs audit. **A** was picked over **B** (stay unscoped, and the d.ts names `.asSystem()` as the move): a fixture is the world the test starts in, and a gate graded on one is graded at level 0, which grades nobody. An arrange a gate can refuse is an act, and the arrange/act split is the reason `phases()` exists. Measured before the ruling: `t.arrange(({ factories }) => factories.lead.createOne())` on a `@@gate("4.4.4.5")` model threw `"Lead.create" requires level 4, user has level 0`.

**Why not `env.factories` too.** Binding in `_buildEnv` would turn every bare `env.factories.x.createOne()` into a system write, and a test that relies on a gate refusing an unscoped factory would pass the write instead of failing it. Scoping it to the two arrange surfaces fixes the trap without moving anything else; `env.factories` widening is a separate question if one is ever asked.

The nine, answered after the code was green and named as late. Origin: none added — the arrange map is derived from `env.factories` through `Factory.usingDb`, never kept beside it. Concept: none; `factories` keeps its name and shape. Complexity: the problem's — arrange/act/assert is the field's own split. Predictability: up inside a phase (`system` and `factories` now agree), and one cost named: `factories` binds differently in `env` than in the tools, which the d.ts says on both. Derived: yes, memoized once per env. Owner: `usingDb` already owned rebinding a factory and propagates it through `_factoryFor`; nothing new rebinds. Boundary: `ArrangeTools` typed and tested. Failure: a fixture is no longer refused, and `env.factories` still is, loudly. Silence: arrange and setup factories write past a gate while `env.factories` stays graded — the test named below asserts both halves. Adjudication: *ergonomics vs. strictness* — strictness follows cost, and refusing a fixture protects no row. Tier: Register; the map is `docs/testing.md` and the d.ts.

*Lives in:* `packages/litestone/src/testing.js` (`arrangeTools`) · `testing.d.ts` (`ArrangeTools.factories`, `TestEnv.factories`, and the factory options on `TestEnvOptions`) · `docs/testing.md` · `test/litestone.test.ts` § *arrange and setup hand out system-bound factories*.

### <a id="fjs-d511"></a>2026-10-10 · `FJS-D511` — Should a named move's `@gate` be able to LOWER the model's update level, rather than only floor it — Keep the floor; *many may submit, few may edit* is a capability grant, not a gate. Everyone who makes the move sits at the update level, and `@@capabilities` (which covers moves by default, `FJS-D140`) grants `Timesheet.submit` to many roles and `Timesheet.update` to few. No new gate spelling, and the access stays in the schema.

Asked in [`IDEAS/owed-rulings.md`](IDEAS/owed-rulings.md) § Open questions. **D** was picked over **A** (A move's `@gate` REPLACES the update level for a write that is exactly that move (only the state column, or `transition(id, name)`); an ungated move keeps the update level. Any other field in the payload still needs update. `fli check` warns on a move gated below update, naming it as a deliberate drop box), **B** (Keep the floor; add an explicit move attribute (e.g. `@open` / `@gate(4) @replaces`) that opts one move out of the update level. Two spellings of gate, but the lowering is visible at the move), **C** (Keep the floor; the drop box is a custom method under `asSystem()`. No framework change; the access leaves the schema (strains Invariant 6)).

the owner's 2026-09-28 note held: the drop box is level-5 users told apart by capabilities, and capabilities now exist — FJS-D140 has @@capabilities cover moves by default, so the move and the edit are granted separately with no second meaning for @gate. A stays the answer if a gate-ladder app that has not opted into capabilities needs a below-update move.

### <a id="fjs-d855"></a>2026-10-10 · `FJS-D855` — **What stops text one principal wrote from steering tools another principal — A write the model proposes is shown to the person and runs only on their confirmation; reads run unasked. A custom method counts as a write unless it is declared read-only, the direction `mcp`'s `gradedNeed` already reads it in, so a wrong guess asks too often rather than too rarely. And the surface never auto-loads a URL out of the model's output, since an image link carrying a read value is a write to the attacker's server.

Asked in [`IDEAS/chat-surface.md`](IDEAS/chat-surface.md) § Open questions. **C** was picked over **A** (accept it as the caller's own authority: the model can do nothing the caller could not, and that is the bound), **B** (taint the turn: once a tool result or a retrieved row enters context, methods that write are withdrawn for the rest of the turn).

The paper's recommendation, taken as written: whether a method writes is already derived from its verb, so C needs no new concept and holds whatever the model read. B needs the turn to track which text came from where, which is a new concept. A treats the victim's authority as the bound, and the victim's authority is exactly what the attack uses.

### <a id="fjs-d845"></a>2026-10-09 · `FJS-D845` — Gates on the child — The child's gate is not checked: the parent's gate authorized the cause, and each child audit entry names the caller as actor and the parent write as the cause.

Asked in [`IDEAS/cascading-fields.md`](IDEAS/cascading-fields.md) § Open questions. **A** was picked over **B** (the caller needs update level on every child model, and the whole write is refused when it lacks one), **C** (children the caller cannot write are skipped).

The paper's recommendation, taken as written: a cascade is integrity, and `FJS-D502` already splits integrity from authority. B lets a child model's gate veto a parent write the caller is allowed to make, and C is the silent drift the feature exists to end.

### <a id="fjs-d619"></a>2026-10-09 · `FJS-D619` — Is a workspace roster meant for viewers, and if so what of a colleague's `User` row does it carry — Yes: the roster projects `User` to name, email and avatar.

Asked in [`IDEAS/owed-rulings.md`](IDEAS/owed-rulings.md) § Open questions. **A** was picked over **B** (no: the roster is graded at the `User` read policy).

The paper's recommendation, taken as written: colleagues see colleagues. The defect is that the whole row goes out.

### <a id="fjs-d616"></a>2026-10-09 · `FJS-D616` — Should `GET /auth/email/verify` change anything — The link stays a GET that lands on a page, and the page POSTs the token.

Asked in [`IDEAS/owed-rulings.md`](IDEAS/owed-rulings.md) § Open questions. **A** was picked over **B** (the GET keeps consuming the token, for mail ergonomics).

The paper's recommendation, taken as written: scanners already consume the token, and a GET that writes breaks HTTP's own contract.

### <a id="fjs-d615"></a>2026-10-09 · `FJS-D615` — Is an empty or blank scope list an unscoped key, and does an unscoped key reach the credential services at all — A, and the credential services refuse every API key, scoped or not: managing credentials takes a session.

Asked in [`IDEAS/owed-rulings.md`](IDEAS/owed-rulings.md) § Open questions. **C** was picked over **A** (a blank or non-string entry is refused at `create`. An unscoped key stays its owner at the credential services), **B** (a blank entry means unscoped, as today, and is documented).

The paper's recommendation, taken as written: the normalization fails open, and a key that can mint keys cannot be contained by revoking it.

### <a id="fjs-d835"></a>2026-10-09 · `FJS-D835` — `asSystem()` inside an episode — Allowed, as built: a service's `asSystem()` is the service's decision for every caller, the subject included, and the trail names the operator.

Asked in [`IDEAS/shipped/support-mode.md`](IDEAS/shipped/support-mode.md) § Open questions. **A** was picked over **B** (refused: litestone throws on `asSystem()` while the context carries an episode), **C** (allowed, and each `asSystem()` inside an episode writes a trail entry naming the call).

The paper's recommendation, taken as written: the episode's ceiling is the subject's, and the subject's own call through that service bypasses the same way, so B makes an operator unable to see what the subject sees. What an episode must not reach is already refused by name (`refuseDelegated`), and a narrower lift is `FJS-D575`'s `system: ['@@gate']`, which keeps the audit actor.

### <a id="fjs-d834"></a>2026-10-09 · `FJS-D834` — Reads — Inside an episode, every model with `@@trail` logs reads whatever its `reads` setting, decided in litestone's logger off the `episodeId` that `installLogContext` already hands it.

Asked in [`IDEAS/shipped/support-mode.md`](IDEAS/shipped/support-mode.md) § Open questions. **B** was picked over **A** (reads stay opt-in per model; an app that wants the DSAR answer declares `reads: true` where it matters), **C** (inside an episode, every model logs reads, `@@trail` or not, into the default trail).

The paper's recommendation, taken as written: the condition already reaches the logger, so the rule's home is the one read-logging check that exists, not a new seat. Under A an operator reading a record leaves nothing, and the DSAR answer is incomplete without anything saying so. C writes a trail for models the app never declared one for.

### <a id="fjs-d832"></a>2026-10-09 · `FJS-D832` — A request carrying a session AND a bearer grant is refused unless the grant states `session: 'merge'`; merged, the person is the trail's actor.

Asked in [`IDEAS/owed-rulings.md`](IDEAS/owed-rulings.md) § Open questions as `FJS-D664`. **C** was picked over **A** (refuse always: a live grant beside a session is a 400 and an app meaning both composes by hand) and **B** (keep the merge and have litestone grade a `@default(auth().x)` stamp on a session-holding principal as `FJS-D576`'s read).

The paper's recommendation, taken as written. `bearerClaim` merged a grant's claims onto whatever session the request also carried, so an org-A agent presenting an org-B widget token was one principal holding both standings, and `@default(auth().contactId)` stamped B's contact on a thread A's own rule admitted — a 201 where typing the same id is a 422 (`FJS-1987`). A merged principal is two standings under one name, which is the confused deputy, and the mistake it allows breaks tenant separation, so the default refuses (*ergonomics vs. strictness*). A junction-wide refusal breaks the other real lane: `example`'s store sends `x-cart-token` on every call, signed in or not, so under **A** every shopper who signs in mid-basket is a 400. *Paved road vs. the workaround* asks for a flag only where the road has two lanes, and chatwoot's and ela's hand-written refusals are the measurement that it does.

**The refusal runs BEFORE the grant is read**, so it says nothing about whether the token works — a dead token beside a session is the same 400 as a live one, and the shape of a request is not an oracle for which tokens exist (`FJS-D696`'s reason one step earlier). `describe()` carries `session`, and `junction principal` prints *Beside a session* for every bearer, so a `merge` is on the committed snapshot where a reviewer reads it (the silence question).

**Under `merge` the person is the actor.** `FJS-D342` made the grant row the actor because a bearer principal carries no id; a person holding a grant as well has one, and `actorType` already filed that row as `user` while `actorId` named the link. Litestone's precedence is now operator, then the principal's id, then the grant (`audit-log.js`), with the grant's subject kept as `subjectId`. Two grants on one request were settled by `FJS-D819` the same way: first in the app's stated order.

**Not changed:** `ctx.locals[BEARER]` and `bearerOf()` are set under `merge` exactly as for a guest, so a service reading the grant reads it either way. The stressor copies that refuse by hand (chatwoot `visitor.ts`, ela and sstime `principal.ts`) are retired on each app's re-drive, not here.

The nine, answered after the code (late, and named as such): one origin — the option, read by `describe()`, read by the snapshot; no new noun; the problem's own complexity, both lanes measured in the tree; one declared behavior for every bearer; not derivable, since whether a signed-in caller legitimately holds a grant is an app fact; owned inside `bearerClaim` and inside litestone's one `actorId` line; a 400 that names the shape; a refusal because the mistake breaks tenant separation; and the test below plus the committed snapshot row are what turn a silent merge red.

*Pinned:* `packages/junction/test/bearer-claim.test.ts` § a session beside a grant · `packages/litestone/test/actor-type.test.ts`.

### <a id="fjs-d830"></a>2026-10-09 · `FJS-D830` — Should `capabilities { }` also NARROW — No: the block carries labels only, and the grantable set narrows by derivation. A move marked `@system` or `@gate(8)` is already left out by `packages/litestone/src/core/capabilities.js`.

Asked in [`IDEAS/shipped/permission-sets.md`](IDEAS/shipped/permission-sets.md) § Open questions. **A** was picked over **B** (Yes, as an allow-list: `capabilities { }` names the grantable ones, everything unnamed is ungrantable, and a `fli check` rule beside `gate-unreachable` compares the block against the derived set), **C** (Yes, as an exclusion list: `capabilities { exclude: [...] }` names the ungrantable ones, with the same `fli check` rule. The list is shorter, and a forgotten entry stays grantable rather than unreachable).

The paper's recommendation, taken as written: The one narrowing the tree has needed so far, engine-only moves, is already derived from the schema, so nothing has to be restated. B fails silently when an entry is forgotten, which is the cost this paper refuses. If a role editor proves 153 too many, C is the next step, because its forgotten entry fails open to the grant and stays visible.

### <a id="fjs-d819"></a>2026-10-09 · `FJS-D819` — A `@guarded` column is written by naming it in `system:`, so a grant is minted by the caller's own policy-graded create; the Grant trait is imported and declares no gate; `bearerClaim` carries the mint and the `FJS-D340` redeem.

Decided while building `FJS-1450` and `FJS-1749` together, the two gaps most apps had rewritten (8 and 9 of 17 stressors). Four moves, one ruling.

**`system: ['col']` admits a `@guarded` column.** `@guarded` was *refused on writes outside `asSystem()`*, so a required digest made the grant model uncreatable below 8 and every app chose between `asSystem()` — dropping the create policy that says who may issue a link — and a nullable digest filled in a second write. `system:` already means *this call writes the column as the application* for `@system` and for the gate (`FJS-D575`); the write half of `@guarded` is the same statement, and the read half stays locked. `refuseSystemEntries` and `refuseGuardedWrite` in litestone's `client.js` are the one owner.

**The trait declares no `@@gate`.** A trait's attribute is the one in force and a host's second is refused, so a shipped `@@gate("8")` made the host's `@@allow('create', …)` unreachable. Who may mint is the host's to declare, on the host model. `references/*` is exported: a model reference is copied because it names a key the host wires; a trait is imported because a copy is only drift.

**The mint and the redeem live on `bearerClaim`'s answer**, because the resolver already holds the four facts both need — model, column, key, purpose — and a second declaration of them is the drift `FJS-1749` measured (`COOKIE_PURPOSE` named in two files so the minter agrees with the reader). A `cookie()` bearer's minted token is a LINK token under `<purpose>.link`; `redeem()` rotates it to the cookie's own, so a clicked link is dead (D340's *once*). `mintOnCreate()` runs in the `validated` stage, since a `@guarded` column is not in the client's schema and a digest added before validation is an unknown key; the token leaves in the answer and `ctx.dispatch` keeps it out of the broadcast.

**The list keeps every grant.** `ctx.locals[BEARER]` is the first grant in the app's stated order — the trail's actor — and `bearerOf(ctx, model)` reads any; two live grants on one request is `FJS-D664`'s sibling and is stated here, not ruled.

The nine (§ V): one origin — key, purpose, model and column stated once and read by the resolver, the mint and the redeem; no new noun — *mint* and *redeem* are the verbs nine apps and `FJS-D340` already use, `signature` the kind `FJS-D522` asked for; the complexity is the problem's (a clicked link must die); predictable — `system:` admits a third column kind by the rule the first two follow; derived — the cookie name from `from: cookie()`, the link purpose from the purpose; the owners already exist (litestone's write refusals, junction's resolver); typed and tested at both boundaries; a dead link is one sentence (`FJS-D696`) and a misnamed column is refused by name; silence — a token in a broadcast is asserted absent, and a stale `exports.snapshot.md` fails CI. Adjudication: *paved road vs. the workaround* — the same workaround in nine places is a measurement of the road. Tier: Register.

*Lives in:* `packages/litestone/src/core/client.js` (`refuseGuardedWrite`, `refuseSystemEntries`) · `packages/litestone/references/Grant.lite` · `packages/junction/src/core/litestone.ts` (`bearerClaim`, `bearerOf`, `checkPrincipalSetting`, `describedOf`) · `packages/junction/test/bearer-claim.test.ts` · `packages/junction/test/principal-list.test.ts` · `packages/litestone/test/references.test.ts`.
