(`@transient`), not this one stretched.

### <a id="fjs-d47"></a>2026-08-14 · `FJS-D47` — The identity ladder: `@@gate("8")` is for credential material, not for `User`. A model is bounded by three declarations, and a level is only the first.

`8` reads as *the safest number*, and it is not a stronger `5` — it means
*nothing outside `asSystem()` has anything to say to this model*. That is true
of a password hash, a session token and a reset token. It is false of the table
an app's own screens list: at `8` the member list, the admin zone and the user
picker all have to go through `asSystem()`, where **nothing is enforced at
all** — so raising the gate moves the whole surface into the bypass. `FJS-170`
moved auth's `User` to `"4.4.4.5"` for that reason.

What `FJS-177` then showed is that the level alone is not the ruling. A gate is
per MODEL, so update at USER(4) says *any signed-in caller may write any other
person's row*, and in basecamp that included `isSystemAdmin` — the column its
own resolver grades SYSADMIN(7) from. Measured, not inferred: a `developer`
promoted themselves.

**The rule.** Identity — and any model whose columns feed a level — is declared
with all three:

| | Question | On refusal |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `@@gate("4.4.4.5")` | what KIND of caller | throws, naming model and level |
| `@@allow('update', id == auth().id \|\| auth().isAdmin)` | WHOSE row | filters; the write matches nothing and answers |
| `@allow('write', auth().isAdmin)` on the graded columns | WHICH columns | drops the field, keeps the rest of the write |

Two consequences are the decision rather than the arithmetic.

**A column the caller can write is not a column a level can be graded from.**
Whatever the app's `getLevel` reads — `role`, `isAdmin`, a status, a membership
— must be out of that caller's reach, or the ladder grades a caller on a value
the caller chose. Where a level already covers it, that is enough:
basecamp's `WorkspaceMember.role` needs no field policy because writing the
membership is ADMINISTRATOR(5) and the caller being graded is USER(4).

**Write the policy against the same standing the level is graded from.**
`auth().isAdmin` is what `FrontierGateGetLevel` and `sessionGateLevel()` both
read for ADMINISTRATOR(5), so the level that deletes a person is the level that
sets their role — one idea, not two. This is why the scaffolds stopped grading
`role === 'admin'` in a resolver while the schema policy read a different field:
what `'admin'` MEANS is the app's decision, made once where the session is built
(`sessionFields`), and projected onto the standing everything else reads.

The cost, stated: a policy FILTERS where a gate REFUSES, so the write a policy
turns away returns normally. Nothing in a return value can tell you it was
refused — a test reads the row back through `asSystem()`.

### <a id="fjs-d48"></a>2026-08-10 · `FJS-D48` — Basecamp's gate ladder: a level is a fact about a caller IN A WORKSPACE, so it is resolved per request and carried on the principal.

The gap `FJS-007` recorded for ten phases was never the resolver. It was that
the shape Junction ships — `sessionGateLevel()`, standing that travels with the
row in `user` — cannot say *admin of THIS workspace*. The same person is `owner`
in one workspace and `viewer` in the next, so grading them from their user row
answers USER(4) everywhere, in every workspace, including the ones they are not
a member of.

So the level is resolved from the `WorkspaceMember` row for the workspace the
request is for:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| no session, or `suspended` | STRANGER (0) |
| authenticated, no membership in the workspace named | VISITOR (1) — reads `Workspace`, nothing else |
| `viewer` · `billing` | READER (2) |
| `developer` | USER (4) |
| `admin` | ADMINISTRATOR (5) |
| `owner` | OWNER (6) |
| `User.isSystemAdmin` | SYSADMIN (7), above any membership |

Three things about it are the decision rather than the arithmetic.

**The standing goes on the PRINCIPAL, not on the client.** Junction scopes the
Litestone client in an around hook installed by `createApp({ db })`, before any
hook knows which workspace is being addressed — and `getTable()` re-derives its
own scoped copy from `ctx.auth.user` on first use. A standing put only on
`ctx.locals.db` is therefore dropped the moment a service touches a model.
`applyStanding()` builds a fresh principal carrying `memberRole`, assigns it to
`ctx.auth.user`, and re-scopes from that. Fresh, never a mutation: over
WebSocket the session is resolved once at upgrade and shared by every frame on
that socket — and the internal-call path freezes it — so mutating would either
throw or leak one call's role into the next.

**It re-resolves when the workspace changes mid-request.** The workspaces
service addresses `ctx.id`, not the header, and an admin of the workspace they
are looking at must not carry level 5 into a patch of a different one.

**The hooks stay.** A gate refuses with a level; `requireWorkspaceRole` refuses
with the sentence a person can act on (*requires admin or owner in this
workspace — you have developer*). Two ladders over one membership row, so they
cannot disagree about who the caller is, only about what they say when refusing.
The gate is the boundary and covers what a hook cannot: an engine calling a
service in-process, a custom action nobody wired a hook onto, a where-clause
built by hand.

**What a gate deliberately does not do is scope rows.** It is per model:
*may this caller touch Server at all*, never *may they touch THAT server*.
Tenancy stays the `workspaceId` filter in every service read plus
`scopeToWorkspace` refusing a non-member. Expressing it as `@@allow` is the next
step and is not claimed by this ruling.

### <a id="fjs-d49"></a>2026-08-10 · `FJS-D49` — A tier above every tenant is a SEPARATE service, and the bit that grants it is a column named for the standing it grants.

Basecamp's four sysadmin screens read across every workspace. Nineteen of its
twenty services take `X-Workspace-Id` and refuse without it, so there were two
ways to answer them, and only one of them scales down to being wrong safely:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| Widen the existing services with `?scope=hub` | The tenancy decision moves into a **query string**, on nineteen services, each of which has to get it right. Nineteen chances to leak every tenant, and the one that forgets looks exactly like the eighteen that did not |
| One new service behind one hook | One place to be wrong. `requireSystemAdmin` is the whole guard, and `/hub` is greppable |

The second. What makes it hold is that the hub service takes **no workspace at
all** — there is nothing for a caller to widen. It reads through `asSystem()`,
not as a convenience but because `User` is the model auth's own fragment gates
at level 8, which even SYSADMIN(7) does not reach: no caller-scoped client can
read a user list, so writing those reads any other way would have meant
rewriting them when the gates landed. They landed the same day, and the hub
needed no change.

**The privileged bit is `User.isSystemAdmin Boolean`, and the name is
load-bearing.** Not auth's `role` — that column defaults to `"user"`, nothing in
the app reads it, and putting the grant there would give one column two owners.
Not an env allowlist, which cannot be granted or revoked by the people who need
to. The name is the one `sessionGateLevel()` already grades **SYSADMIN(7)** on
(`junction/src/core/litestone.ts`), so the column filling these screens today is
the column `@@gate` will read tomorrow. The cost, accepted: two fields beside
each other that both look like privilege, so the schema comment says which one
this app enforces on.

**Refusal is 404, not 403.** The hub is not a screen someone is being refused;
it is a surface they have no business knowing exists — the same reasoning the
workspaces service already uses for a workspace you are not a member of.

*Lives in:* `packages/basecamp/api/src/services/hub/hub.service.ts`,
`api/src/core/hooks.ts` (`requireSystemAdmin`); 4 data tests, 25 browser checks.

### <a id="fjs-d50"></a>2026-08-10 · `FJS-D50` — A status column that nothing reads is not a state, and suspension needs a door on each side.

`User.status` had been a free `String` since the schema was written, and
@frontierjs/auth — which owns the model — never looks at it. So "suspended" was
a word the app could store and nothing anywhere would honor: a Suspend button
would have reported success and revoked nothing. The same would have been true
of a new `Workspace.status`.

Three things together make it real, and none of them is sufficient alone:

1. **The vocabulary is an enum** (`UserStatus`, `WorkspaceStatus`), so the
   column carries a CHECK and the service's copy of the list is held against it
   by a test in both directions. A free string beside a service that invents
   values is the shape that let `AlertRule.severity` default to a value its own
   API refused.
2. **The front door refuses.** A suspended user cannot sign in — checked AFTER
   the password, so the refusal does not tell an unauthenticated caller which
   addresses are suspended accounts.
3. **The already-open door refuses.** A token issued before the suspension stops
   resolving, at an app-level `before: all` hook. Deleting the `Session` rows is
   not enough on its own: an API key is a `Credential` and survives that.

For a workspace the one door is `scopeToWorkspace`, the hook every scoped
service already runs — so suspension bites in nineteen places by being written
in one. And it is **not** deletion: `@@softDelete(cascade)` stamps every child,
a status change stamps nothing, and conflating them would make a reversible-
sounding action unrecoverable.

*Lives in:* `packages/basecamp/api/src/core/session-auth.ts`,
`api/src/core/hooks.ts`; pinned by db tests and by `verify.mjs` § 13f.

### <a id="fjs-d51"></a>2026-08-10 · `FJS-D51` — A machine account is created from an admin screen. A human is not.

The hub's Users screen creates `UserKind.bot` accounts and deliberately ships
without the mock's Invite button. The asymmetry is the whole point: creating a
bot hands nobody anything — it has no password credential, so there is no way
for it to sign in, and its only route in is an API key issued to it separately.
Creating a human from the same screen would be an administrator minting an
account with a password only they know, which is why the human path is
invite → accept and stays unbuilt (`FJS-032`).

Three rules fall out of it, each refused by name at the API:

- **A bot's address is at `bots.invalid`** — RFC 2606 reserves the TLD, so it
  resolves nowhere. `User.email` is required and unique and a bot has no inbox;
  a plausible-looking address would eventually be mailed.
- **A bot may not own a workspace.** An owner is the one member `removeMember`
  refuses to remove and the one role that can delete the tenant.
- **A bot may not hold the hub tier.** `isSystemAdmin` is a revocable human —
  the point of it is that somebody can be asked why they used it.

It also closes a gap `api-keys.service.ts` had recorded in its own comment since
Phase 6: a key was always minted for the caller, because nothing else existed to
own one, so CI's key was a person's key and revoking it when they left broke the
pipeline. A key may now name a bot — and only a bot, only in this workspace, and
only one that does not outrank you.

*Lives in:* `packages/basecamp/api/src/services/hub/hub.service.ts`
(`createBot`), `api/src/services/api-keys/api-keys.service.ts`
(`assertBotOwner`).

### <a id="fjs-d52"></a>2026-08-06 · `FJS-D52` — Raw SQL is available through `asSystem()` only, on any schema that declares access rules.

Fixes `FJS-005`.

`db.sql` goes straight to the read connection — no `@@gate`, no `@@allow`, no
`@guarded`, no `@scoped`, no `@@softDelete`, because all of those are enforced
above SQLite. For a deliberate escape hatch that is defensible. What was not is
that it was the **same function on every proxy**: `db.$setAuth(user).sql` closed
over the user and never read it, so a caller who had done everything right got
every row in the table, silently. Measured on one model with `@@allow` +
`@guarded` + `@@softDelete`:

```
$setAuth({id:1}).invoice.findMany()   → 1 row,  ssn absent
$setAuth({id:1}).sql`SELECT * …`      → 3 rows, ssn plaintext, another owner's
                                         row and a soft-deleted one included
```

**The unscoped client was the wider gap, not the narrower one.** An
unauthenticated `db.invoice.findMany()` returns **0** rows — the policy
evaluates with `auth() == null` and matches nothing — while `db.sql` returned
all 3. So the defect is not "the scoped proxy drops its scope"; it is that raw
SQL ignores the schema on every path and the ORM never does. That is why the
rule covers `db.sql` too, overturning `IDEAS/scoped-sql.md`'s "unchanged".

The rule:

| Surface | Schema declares access rules | It does not |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `db.sql` | **throws** | unchanged |
| `db.$setAuth(u).sql` | **throws** | unchanged |
| `db.asSystem().sql` | works — the documented bypass | works |

"Access rules" means `@@gate`, `@@allow`/`@@deny`, `@guarded`, `@encrypted`/
`@secret`, field-level `@allow`, `@scoped`. **Not** `@omit` or `@@softDelete`:
those shape what a read returns rather than who may read it, and refusing raw
SQL for a soft-delete column would fire on most schemas for a lifecycle rule.

**Coarse per schema, not per statement, on purpose.** Deciding per statement
means parsing the statement, and a hand-written SQL validator that is subtly
wrong grants a FALSE guarantee — worse than an honest raw hatch, because people
trust it. The escape routes are numerous and all real in SQLite (`main.` and
`temp.` qualification, `ATTACH` — which litestone exposes on the proxy —
`PRAGMA`, views created mid-statement, comment and string-literal tricks).
SQLite's own authorizer would be the right mechanism and **`bun:sqlite` does not
expose it** (verified: `Database` has no `setAuthorizer`).

The refusal names both ways forward: `asSystem().sql` to bypass deliberately, or
`where: { $raw: sql`…` }` to stay on the ORM — verified to keep every policy
(1 row, `@guarded` column still withheld).

**Scoped raw SQL as a capability — a per-identity view set — is NOT built.**
`IDEAS/scoped-sql.md` designs it; it is a feature where this is a defect, and
the consumer that made it urgent (the AI agent surface) does not exist. Revisit
with it. *Amended 2026-09-10:* that surface was called `herald` when this was
written and is `@frontierjs/mcp` since `FJS-D258`.

*Lives in:* `packages/litestone/src/core/client.js`
(`schemaDeclaresAccessRules`, `rawSqlRefusal`, `_runRawSql`); 9 tests in
`test/litestone.test.ts` § "raw SQL and the access rules it cannot enforce",
5 of which fail if the refusal is removed.

### <a id="fjs-d53"></a>2026-08-01 · `FJS-D53` — Gates enforce by default when declared; undeclared imposes nothing.
Any model with `@@gate` is enforced from the first request via the shipped
`FrontierGateGetLevel` resolver (null user → STRANGER) even with no GatePlugin
installed. A user-supplied `GatePlugin({ getLevel })` replaces the resolver
entirely. Models without `@@gate` are completely open. `asSystem()` bypasses
(except LOCKED). Rationale: a declared gate that silently does nothing is a
fail-open security default — verified live before the fix.
*Lives in:* `packages/litestone/src/core/client.js` (default plugin injection);
tests in `test/elegance-fixes.test.ts`.

## Query & write semantics (Litestone)

### <a id="fjs-d885"></a>2026-10-17 · `FJS-D885` — How does a String column state a human sort order: a `@collate(nocase)` field word written into the DDL, or human order as the default for a `@label` / valueset `order` column — A field word `@collate(nocase)` (or `@collate(binary|nocase|rtrim)`, SQLite's three), emitted as `COLLATE NOCASE` on the column so ORDER BY, comparisons and an index all agree. The author states it per column; the DDL differ, `litestone introspect` (which already meets `COLLATE NOCASE` on adopted databases) and `explain` learn one word. NOCASE folds ASCII only, so `Émile` still sorts after `Zed` — a partial answer to "as a person reads them".

Asked in [`IDEAS/owed-rulings.md`](IDEAS/owed-rulings.md) § Open questions. **A** was picked over **B** (human order as the default for a `@label` / valueset `order` column: the compiler adds a case-insensitive collation to ORDER BY on those columns only, no new word. Nothing for the author to state, but the same column sorts differently by which clause names it, an index on the column stops serving the ORDER BY, and the rule lives in the query compiler rather than the schema (Invariant 6's direction runs the other way)).

The paper's recommendation, taken as written: the order is a property of the column, so it belongs in the schema where the DDL and an index can serve it, and it matches what introspect already round-trips; a valueset or `@label` column that wants it states it once.

### <a id="fjs-d1043"></a>2026-10-17 · `FJS-D1043` — Can a currency-named price carry places finer than its minor unit, or is a sub-minor rate never money — `@money(USD, places: n)`: the currency still decides the point, `places` adds n digits past the minor unit (scale = minor + n, so `@money(USD, places: 6)` is 8 places), refused past the 9-place cap and with `@scale`/`@big` as today. One declaration names currency and exactness; `formatMoney`, `x-money`, `MoneyInput` and the raw-money check read the same attribute and only learn that the scale is not the currency's own.

Asked in [`IDEAS/owed-rulings.md`](IDEAS/owed-rulings.md) § Open questions. **A** was picked over **B** (a rate is never money: keep `@scale(n)` bare and add a currency-naming sibling, `@scale(9) @currency(USD)` (or `@scale(9, currency: USD)`), so the field-held form is `@currency(field: code)`. `@money` stays whole minor units; the new word is the one a rate reads, at the cost of a second currency-carrying attribute beside `@money`), **C** (refuse and document: a sub-minor rate is stored as an exact integer in a named unit (e.g. micro-dollars, `@unit`-style) and priced in the app; no schema spelling carries the currency. Zero new surface, but the spend-cap reconcile in serpgrid and lago's fee columns stay currency-blind).

The paper's recommendation, taken as written: the currency already decides where the point is, and a rate is that same decision n digits further, so one attribute with one extra argument keeps a single owner for "what currency is this number" where B grows a second.

### <a id="fjs-d975"></a>2026-10-17 · `FJS-D975` — What word says a `@@transitions` move stamps a time column in the same write — A per-move attribute beside `@gate`/`@system`/`@seals`: `send: draft -> sent @stamps(sentAt)`. `transition()` (and `update()` landing that move) puts the clock in the named `DateTime` columns in the one UPDATE, the way `@updatedAt` stamps; the column is engine-owned (a payload naming it is refused like `@system`). Move-keyed, so two moves into one state can stamp different columns, and it extends an attribute list that already exists.

Asked in [`IDEAS/owed-rulings.md`](IDEAS/owed-rulings.md) § Open questions. **A** was picked over **B** (a field attribute naming the state it records: `sentAt DateTime? @enteredAt(status.sent)`. The column declares itself, so every write that lands `status` in `sent` stamps it, `transition()` or a form's `update()` alike, and the row says where its time came from. A new noun on the field, and a state reached by two moves stamps once per entry unless it says otherwise), **C** (neither: let `transition(id, name, { data })` carry extra columns written with the move. No new schema word, but the caller supplies the time (forgeable, restated per call site) and the stamp stays optional, so a direct `transition()` still leaves `sentAt` null).

The paper's recommendation, taken as written: the move is already the unit that carries `@gate`, `@system` and `@seals`, so the stamp belongs on it and the engine writes it, which is what makes a direct `transition()` unable to leave it null.

### <a id="fjs-d1145"></a>2026-10-17 · `FJS-D1145` — How does allocating an `@@extensible` slot avoid a whole-tenant scan when the slot is not the slot index's leading column — The allocator records each slot it hands out, per (model, tenant, scope), in a table Litestone owns, never on the app's declaring model, which would gain rows the app never wrote. A slot that is neither in that record nor in the `taken` set the allocator already reads has never held a value, so it needs no clear. A slot in the record clears, and takes the scan, exactly as today. A tenant's first fill of its pool (every Posthog declaration) costs nothing. Reuse pays one scan per reuse. The record is written by the one path that allocates, not by the delete, so a declaration deleted outside the client still leaves its slot recorded and clearing on reuse. A slot STATED on a raw insert skips the allocator, so it goes unrecorded unless it is still taken. Invariant 1 holds.

Asked in [`IDEAS/owed-rulings.md`](IDEAS/owed-rulings.md) § Open questions. **A** was picked over **B** (move the clear off the declaration: the delete marks the slot dirty and clears it in rowid-chunked transactions outside the declaring write. The allocator skips a dirty slot until its clear finishes. The writer is never held, even on reuse, but Litestone owns no job runner (Caravan sits above it, Invariant 1). So the chunking is a new resumable loop inside Litestone, and a crash mid-clear needs the dirty mark to survive and resume), **C** (one index per slot, `(tenant, scope, tN)`, so every slot leads one and the clear seeks as `t1`'s does today (0 ms). No new record or state, but each extensible write maintains one index per slot (10 in Posthog's pool, not 1). It also drops the composite index's one-term reach that `allocateExtSlot`'s "in INDEX order" comment is built on).

The paper's recommendation, taken as written: the measured cost is all first-fill, where a slot provably never held a value, and A makes exactly that case free with one record written by the owner that already exists (`allocateExtSlot`). B pays for a job loop to fix reuse, which nothing measured yet. C taxes every write to fix allocation, which is rare. A's guard is that a reused slot still never carries the old key's values: `FJS-1752`'s reuse test keeps it red-capable, and `FJS-3134`'s EXPLAIN test extends to assert that a first fill issues no clear.

### <a id="fjs-d1063"></a>2026-10-17 · `FJS-D1063` — A numeric bound (`@lte`/`@gte`/`@lt`/`@gt`) on a `@scale`/`@money` column: is its number read in declared units, or is the ambiguous bound refused at parse — Keep minor units and refuse the bound that is ambiguous: a numeric bound on a `@scale`/`@money` column is a parse error that names the stored figure (`@lte(100) on rate bounds 100 minor units = 0.01 at 4 places; write @lte(1000000) for 100`), and the message at the boundary says `minor units`. Nothing converts, so every copy of the number stays honest; cost is that the author writes `@lte(1000000)`, which is what the caller sends anyway.

Asked in [`IDEAS/owed-rulings.md`](IDEAS/owed-rulings.md) § Open questions. **B** was picked over **A** (the bound is in declared units: `@lte(100)` on `@scale(4)` means 100.0000, stored 1000000. One conversion (`bound × 10^places`) at the owner that reads `attr.value` for a scaled field, reached by validate, JSON Schema, the CHECK and the generator; the message prints the declared figure (`must be at most 100`). `@money(GBP)` reads the same (`@lte(50)` is £50). Cost: the bound and the value a caller SENDS (`1299`, minor units, `FJS-D142`) are in different units on one line, and a fractional bound (`@lte(0.5)`) becomes legal and must round-trip exactly).

The paper's recommendation, taken as written: `FJS-D142` already ruled that a scaled column's unit of exchange is the whole minor-unit number, so a bound that quietly speaks a second unit makes the line unpredictable; a parse refusal that names the stored figure is the boundary-owner answer and touches no copy of the number.

### <a id="fjs-d875"></a>2026-10-17 · `FJS-D875` — Does a `File` ref keep the public origin it was uploaded against, or does a read derive it from the storage config's current `publicBase` plus the key — Derive at read, stop storing: `serialize` no longer writes `publicBase`; `resolve` joins the plugin's current `publicBase` to `key` for a ref on the plugin's own provider, and falls back to the ref's own `endpoint` + `bucket` for a ref whose `provider` differs (the object genuinely served elsewhere). `useStorage(config).url(ref)` passes its config; the bare `fileUrl(ref)` keeps endpoint + bucket + key and returns null without an endpoint, as it does for a local ref today. `publicBase` leaves `FileRef` and the JSON Schema (`jsonschema.js:288`, `index.d.ts:255`).

Asked in [`IDEAS/owed-rulings.md`](IDEAS/owed-rulings.md) § Open questions. **A** was picked over **B** (keep writing it, flip precedence: `resolve` prefers the config's current `publicBase` and reads the stored one only when the config has none. Smallest diff; every ref still carries a stale copy of something the config knows, and a bare `fileUrl(ref)` still answers the old host), **C** (like A, but `fileUrl(ref, { publicBase })` takes the base as an explicit second argument so the pure helper can derive too. One more parameter on a public helper; callers outside the plugin must thread config through).

The paper's recommendation, taken as written: the stored copy is a second owner of a fact the config already holds (§ V.5), per-row `provider`/`endpoint` already cover the object served from somewhere else, and nothing has shipped so dropping the field costs no migration; B leaves the orphaning in `fileUrl`, C widens the helper for a caller that can use `useStorage`.

### <a id="fjs-d887"></a>2026-10-17 · `FJS-D887` — Does a lone `Int @id` emit `AUTOINCREMENT` always, only under `@default(autoincrement())`, or never — Every lone `Int @id` (and `BigInt @id`) emits `INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT`. One rule, no new word, a permalink never changes meaning, and a Prisma port keeps what it had. Cost: `sqlite_sequence` now exists (gotchas page flips, introspect must skip it), a small per-insert write, and an existing table needs the rebuild path to gain the keyword (pre-alpha, so a delete-and-recreate).

Asked in [`IDEAS/owed-rulings.md`](IDEAS/owed-rulings.md) § Open questions. **A** was picked over **B** (only `@default(autoincrement())` emits `AUTOINCREMENT`; a bare `Int @id` stays a plain rowid alias. The word finally means what Prisma and SQL authors read it as, and the cheap rowid stays available for a table that never exposes its id. Cost: two spellings for one-looking column, and the safe one is the one an author must remember to write (the permalink hazard remains for a bare `Int @id`)), **C** (never; keep reuse and point at `String @id @default(uuid())` or `@sequence(scope:)` for a stable id, leaving `gotchas.md` as the answer. Zero DDL change, and the Prisma port still loses its guarantee silently).

The paper's recommendation, taken as written: the unsafe default is the one nobody reports (§ V.9), and `Int @id` with `autoincrement()` already reads as "never reuse" to every author who types it; B keeps that same silent trap for the bare form, and the overhead SQLite documents is small against a permalink resolving to another row.

**Amended 2026-10-16, by 0.4: the feed is not the whole sync.** The feed's type catalog names no `project.*` type and, for no noun, a trash, archive, delete or uncomplete. So *the feed is what its sync reads* holds for `Todo`, `Message` and `Comment` only as the fast path. `Project` is kept by a re-walk of `projects.json`, and a scheduled walk of each claimed scope is the floor for the rest (`IDEAS/conduit-37signals.md` 6.2). ### <a id="fjs-d1180"></a>2026-10-16 · `FJS-D1180` — Does `@@mirror` take `absent:`, the drop-out rule `FJS-D843` held back for a second caller — No, withdrawn. Which rows are absent is decided by a COMPLETE read of a scope, and the scope is the sync's code; litestone keeps `missingSince` as the column a sync stamps and no word declares when.

Asked in [`IDEAS/mirror-apps.md`](IDEAS/mirror-apps.md) step 4.2, through the question tool. The step was planned on Mattermost's history cap as the second shape, and there is none: Team Edition self-hosted states no cap (read off the System Console in 0.2), the 10k cap is Cloud Free's, and chat's 200-post window is the app's own first-backfill size, which nothing drops out of. The two callers in the tree that do infer absence share no parameter a schema could hold: ELA reads one day's board and stamps each job of that day not on it, only when the board did not move mid-read (`sync-jobs.ts`, `complete`); chat reads one person's memberships and deletes each one not in it, aborted on any failed page (`FJS-D1155`). Neither declares it in a schema.

The nine, answered LATE (written with the ruling, after the owner's pick): 1 origin — the drop-out rule stays in one place, the sync that knows its scope · 2 concept — one word fewer than `FJS-D843` promised · 3 complexity — the problem's, and the field names it *deletion detection*: only the reader knows what it read in full · 4 predictability — `missingSince` means what it meant, stamped by the sync · 5 nothing restated; the scope was never written in the schema · 6 owner — the connector's sync · 7 a caller learns one column · 8 failure — a partial read stamping rows is the sync's to refuse, as both callers already do · 9 must stay true: no row is stamped or deleted off a partial read. What fails when it stops: ELA's `job-mirror.test.ts` for the day board; chat's removal rows in the 3.3 probe, a scratch run and not a drive — **`none`** for chat until a drive grades it. § IV: *doctrine vs. discovery* — `FJS-D843` promised the word on a premise the probe disproved, so the ruling is amended in writing rather than the word built to keep it. Tier: Register.

### <a id="fjs-d1162"></a>2026-10-16 · `FJS-D1162` — How a claimed mirror's forward grades the caller's write before it sends — `db.$checkWrite(accessor, op, row, changes?)` → `{ ok, message?, rule? }`, a litestone verdict beside `$readAs` over the one `policyVerdict`: the gate, the `@@capabilities` grid, then `create` on the payload at its literal defaults, `update` on the stored row and `post-update` on it with the changes over it, `delete` on the stored row. The nine, answered before the build:

2. Concept: one name in the `$check*` family.
3. Complexity: the problem's own, since Ash, ZenStack, Zero and Kubernetes all name it.
4. Predictability: one shape for three verbs, the JS verdict `$readAs` already grades with.
5. Derived: from the schema.
6. Owner: `policyVerdict`, inside litestone; junction asks.
7. Boundary: typed in `index.d.ts` and the junction client type.
8. Failure: a 403 before the send, and an undecidable policy throws.
9. Silence: conduit `junction-integration.test.ts` *grades the app's own write policies before it sends* and *a model declaring @@transitions*, each failing with its change undone.

No adjudication in tension.

### <a id="fjs-d1155"></a>2026-10-16 · `FJS-D1155` — A mirrored row the Provider drops: stamped or deleted — Deleted when its loss is a loss of ACCESS (`ChannelMember`, a per-person `Thread`); a content row (`Post`, `Channel`) keeps the Provider's own `deletedAt` tombstone and takes `missingSince` when a whole read stops listing it. `missingSince` is for content, never for a grant.

The nine, answered after the build (late, named here): origin, the broker's believed handshake, which already existed; concept, one optional field on a type that existed; predictability, every held socket gets it; derived, from the handshake's own answer; owner, conduit's broker transport (`FJS-D1127`); boundary, typed; failure, logged, never blocks frames; silence, the two cases and the connector drive's `socket.openedOnEveryConnection`. No adjudication in tension.

### <a id="fjs-d1153"></a>2026-10-16 · `FJS-D1153` — Whose socket a mirror app listens on — Each linked person's own, on their own token, and their backfill spends the same token: rule 3 gains *a sync READS as the person whose view it is*. The Provider sends a channel's events to that channel's members only, and no admin or bot role widens it, so a private or direct channel reaches the app through a member or not at all.

Asked in [`IDEAS/mirror-apps.md`](IDEAS/mirror-apps.md) step 3.3. The owner stopped the first hearing to ask for prior art; three research passes read the Mattermost server (`ShouldSendEvent` in `web_conn.go`: channel events to channel members, no bypass), matterbridge, the Matrix bridges, Mattermost's own webapp and mobile clients, and the sync platforms (Merge, Paragon, Nango, Beeper, mautrix). Bridges hold one service socket joined to the channels they bridge and never see a DM; Mattermost's own clients, and the platforms that sync for an end user, hold one per person. A mirror app is a client its people read through, not a bridge of chosen channels, so the client shape fits. Picked over **one service socket, the bot joined to every mirrored channel** (rule 3 as written; DMs never mirror and the bot shows in every private member list) and **a hybrid of the two** (two code paths for one kind of row; nothing read does it). The same post arrives on every member's socket and lands once by its key. Lives in `fjs-prototypes/chat/api/src/providers/chat/` (`listen`, `unlisten`, the `chat-sync` plugin's `work`) and the connector's `mattermostSocketTarget({ id, ref })`; drive row `socket.perPersonSeesWhatOnlyTheyMay`.

The nine, answered after the build (late, named here): origin, the Provider's delivery rule; concept, none — a broker target per person, the kind `FJS-D1127` named; predictability, what a person sees in the Provider is what their socket carries; derived, the person from the account's link; owner, the app's provider folder; boundary, a ref per person (`CHAT_SOCKET:<user id>`), since a dial runs outside any call; failure, **a person's refused token makes the whole app read not ready** — filed as `FJS-3150`; silence, the drive row and the probe. Adjudication: *paved road vs. the workaround* — the bridge shape is the ecosystem's road for a bridge, and a mirror app is not one; the road here is Mattermost's own client.

### <a id="fjs-d1152"></a>2026-10-16 · `FJS-D1152` — What a connector's claim calls the Provider's person — `Profile`, never `User`: `User` is the `@@auth` model of every app `fli new --auth` scaffolds, so a claim keyed `User` collides with it out of the box. Mattermost's claim keys its user `Profile`, and a row naming one holds it as `profileExternalId`; an app's account links to its Profile through `User.profileExternalId @system`.

Asked in [`IDEAS/mirror-apps.md`](IDEAS/mirror-apps.md) step 3.1, through the question tool, where the owner asked which answer is right whatever it touches. Picked over **auth resolving its model through `@@auth`** so the app could rename its own account to free `User` (right on its own merits and filed as `FJS-3146`, but here it would let the Provider's noun choose the app's, which is rule 2 inverted), **the app re-keying the claim at bind** (a claim is plain data, but every auth app would have to, so the default would be broken), and **auth's models as files the app owns** (reverses `FJS-D16`, whose evidence is basecamp's copy storing OAuth tokens in plain text with its suite green, and it frees no name, since auth reads `sys.user` 48 times). Merging the two is refused by construction: auth creates its `User` with no Provider key, and a mirror key is required. Lives in `../conduit-connectors/packages/conduit-mattermost/src/mirror.ts`.

The nine, answered after the build (late, named here): origin one, the claim's keys; concept none new, a model name is the app's; predictability, every scaffolded app binds the claim unchanged; derived, nothing to derive; owner, the connector; boundary, the app binds as-is; failure, a claim keyed onto a model that is not `@@mirror` is refused at boot by name (`FJS-D1125`), so the clash was loud, not silent; silence, the drive's `mirror.claimShape` row names `Profile`. *Familiarity vs. precision*: the vendor's habit says `User`, and the app's noun wins.

### <a id="fjs-d1151"></a>2026-10-16 · `FJS-D1151` — Does a `@@mirror` relation carry a foreign key — No: a relation on a `@@mirror` model whose foreign key is a Provider column emits no FOREIGN KEY, derived as `@system` is. A dangling reference reads as no related row, and as a refusal under `check()`; `onDelete`/`onUpdate` on such a relation is refused by name, since with no constraint it would act on nothing. A `@local` key is the app's and keeps its constraint, as does an app-owned model's relation to a mirror (`User.profileExternalId`).

Asked in [`IDEAS/mirror-apps.md`](IDEAS/mirror-apps.md) step 3.1, through the question tool with the three shapes as code. Picked over **a per-relation `enforce: false`** (twelve hand-written copies of one fact in one schema, the copy `FJS-D843` refused) and **keep the constraint and order the sync** (every sync fetches each missing parent first, recursively, and a reply past a cap can never land without its root nulled, which changes the Provider's data). Prisma's `relationMode = "prisma"` is the field's precedent. Cost, owed to Phase 4: the exit adds the constraints back, and an orphan must be settled then. Lives in `expandMirror` (`packages/litestone/src/core/parser.js`) and the FK loop of `src/core/ddl.js`; `test/system-column.test.ts` § *a @@mirror model* (the child-before-parent case fails with the DDL skip removed).

The nine, answered after the build (late, named here): origin one, `@@mirror`; concept none new, the tag is internal; complexity the problem's, two systems and the Provider's order; predictability, the same tier as the derived `@system` and `missingSince`; derived from `@@mirror`, which is why **B** lost; owner, the parser's expansion and the DDL emitter that already owned the constraint; boundary, the generated types already read an included relation as `T | null`; failure, a dangling reference is not destructive and reads as absent, while a declared `onDelete` that would do nothing is refused by name; silence, a mirror child lands before its parent and a dangling key under `check()` refuses, and the same test case fails when either stops. *Ergonomics vs. strictness*: the strictness is not dropped but held where the truth is, the Provider.

### <a id="fjs-d1144"></a>2026-10-16 · `FJS-D1144` — The key of a `@@mirror` model: is its `@unique` derived or required — Derived, unless a `@@unique` already names the key: a key unique per account (ELA's `@@unique([accountId, externalId])`) stays as written, and `FJS-D843`'s derivation replaces 2.4's *mark it @unique* refusal. ### <a id="fjs-d1142"></a>2026-10-16 · `FJS-D1142` — How a `@@mirror` model says which of its columns are the app's own — A field word, `@local`: every stored column of a `@@mirror` model but the `@id` and a `@local` one is derived `@system`, so a caller's write to the Provider's data is refused by name instead of overwritten by the next sync, and `missingSince DateTime? @system` is derived for the sync to stamp. `@local` is refused off a `@@mirror` model, on the key, on the `@id`, on a relation, and beside `@system`. ### <a id="fjs-d989"></a>2026-10-15 · `FJS-D989` — How does `@@exclude` grade a member's range read through a to-one relation, and regrade the children's keys when the parent's range moves — Admit a to-one `@from(rel, column)` field (`FJS-D911`, built by `FJS-1305`, still open) as a range end: `startsAt DateTime @from(shift, startLocal)`, `range: [startsAt, endsAt]`. `gradeKey` reads the member's range through the relation's join, and the ledger gains a reverse edge: a write naming a column some member's range `@from`s notes every key the parent's children hold. `@from` stays the one owner of crossing a relation; waits on `FJS-1305`.

Asked in [`IDEAS/owed-rulings.md`](IDEAS/owed-rulings.md) § Open questions. **A** was picked over **B** (a one-hop dotted path inside `range:`: `range: [shift.startLocal, shift.endLocal]`, the path resolved as a policy's `relation.column` path is, with the same reverse edge. The spelling the author reaches for first, but it is the second way to cross a relation — the shape `FJS-D911` refused for `@derived` (its option C)), **C** (keep the copy and close the hole at the parent: a parse refusal naming the path rather than a token error, plus a documented hazard that a copied range goes stale on the parent's write. Smallest; the roster keeps a hand-kept copy that is silently wrong after a Shift moves).

The paper's recommendation, taken as written: `FJS-D911` already ruled `@from` the owner of bringing a parent's column onto a row, so the range is derived rather than copied and the only new mechanism is the reverse edge, which every option except C needs anyway.

### <a id="fjs-d970"></a>2026-10-13 · `FJS-D970` — Does search span models — Yes, over ONE shared index: `db.$search(q, { models, limit, offset, prefix })` reads `_search`, graded per model inside the query, ranked on one bm25 scale.

Asked in [`IDEAS/shipped/cross-model-search.md`](IDEAS/shipped/cross-model-search.md). **E** was picked over **A** (each app composes N per-model `search()` calls and groups by kind — linear's `search.service.ts`), **B** (`@@searchable(title, subtitle, link)`), **C** (a junction route fanning out N per-model calls) and **D** (a sierra function making N graded `find({ $search })` calls and grouping).

linear's Q4 measured that bm25 is not comparable across indexes (−0.981 as an issue title, −3.287 as a comment body for the same text) and that both shorter spellings leak or starve. Both findings held, and both were about PER-MODEL indexes. The paper's gate rebuilt the same rows into one `_search(model UNINDEXED, rid UNINDEXED, title, body)` and the pair scored −6.925 and −6.925: one vocabulary, one scale. So the premise moved and the finding is kept — the policy still goes INSIDE the query, before the limit — which is why the owner is litestone and not sierra: each model's branch is the `visibleWhere` + correlated `EXISTS` its own `search()` already builds (`FJS-262`, `FJS-1692`), composed with `OR` under one `MATCH`. `FJS-D333` stands: `search()` keeps its verb because FTS5 is another engine on another table, and `_search` is one more of those. The four fixed by this ruling, so a second builder cannot re-derive them:

- **Membership and title are derived, never declared.** A model is in `_search` because it declares `@@fts`; its `title` is the column `@@label` names, its `body` the `@@fts` columns joined. A `@@fts` model with no `@@label` is refused at parse with the fix in the message. B was refused for restating both and for `-able` (`FJS-D249`).
- **`models` names accessors (`['issue', 'comment']`) and the default is every `@@fts` model.** Which models a palette holds is the call site's — junction's `search` service names them at its mount — so *should ELA's mail be in ⌘K* is answered where the app is, with no schema word. A hit is `{ model, id, title, sub, _rank, _snippet }`, `model` the accessor, `sub` from `x-identify`.
- **`_search` is `trigram` whatever the models' own tokenizers, and the title weight is 10**, placed by column index — `bm25()` weights are positional over every declared column, `UNINDEXED` included, so `bm25(_search, 3, 1)` weights `model` and changes nothing; the gate's first run did exactly that. The gate's small corpus ranked the same under `trigram` and `unicode61` at 3; the spanning test's fixture (40 rows sharing one word) did not — under `trigram` a bare body edged a title carrying four other words (−2.046 against −2.036) while `unicode61` held, and 5 and 10 both hold under both. 10 is the margin the paper measured, so it is the weight (amended 2026-10-13, the same day, from the test's measurement). `trigram` is chosen because a short word is then a match rather than `FJS-2332`'s scan, except below three characters where the scan fallback is still owed.
- **A model whose gate or capability refuses the caller holds no hit for them, and a caller refused every model named is refused by the first refusal's name.** maid.tech's Roles read different models (a Closer holds `Contact.read` alone), and one refused branch had made the whole call a 403, hiding the models the caller may read. Dropping the branch matches a row its policy hides; refusing when nothing is left keeps *may read nothing* from reading as *found nothing* (amended 2026-10-14 by the owner, over dropping always and over keeping the 403 for the app to narrow). `search-spanning.test.ts` § a model the caller may not read.

Costs taken knowingly: text is indexed twice while the per-model `_fts` tables stay (step 4.3 prices reading them from `_search`), and the differ learns a table no model owns. Lives in `packages/litestone/src/core/ddl.js` (the table and triggers), `client.js` (`$search`), junction's `search` service and sierra's `paletteSource`; the plan is the paper's § Plan.

### <a id="fjs-d950"></a>2026-10-13 · `FJS-D950` — Is a ratio between two counts a refusal, or a state the data may be in — A flag the row carries: `underRatio Boolean @derived(adults * eventRatioAttendees < eventEnrolled * eventRatioAdults)` on Shift, the event's three values brought on by `FJS-D911`'s to-one `@from`. Every read says it, `where: { underRatio: true }` lists the rooms to fix, and SRC's badge is that field. No new word, once the three rows above close; it refuses nothing, and *answering for the room on the day* (a `@@commitment` at the shift's start, or a report) is a later question. **Owes its artefact, because B is wrong in silence exactly as `FJS-2778` measured** (a `@derived` over a `@from` reads one answer and filters another): `ratio.test.ts` flips to read `underRatio` off every shift and through `where: { underRatio: true }`, and asserts both agree with SRC's `ratioInfo`.

Asked in [`IDEAS/owed-rulings.md`](IDEAS/owed-rulings.md) § Open questions. **B** was picked over **A** (refuse on both writes: `@minItems` takes an expression over the parent's columns (`assignments Assignment[] @minItems(ceil(event.enrolled * event.ratioAdults / event.ratioAttendees))`), graded at the outermost commit as `FJS-D347` grades a literal, and an Enrollment write re-grades every Shift of its Event. The price: SRC's sample cannot be loaded, a roster cannot be built one write at a time, and D347's *only parents a write touched* grows a second hop), **C** (a validation warn: the write lands and the result carries a warning. Litestone has no warning channel on a write result, so this is a new mechanism, and it reaches whoever made the write rather than whoever answers for the room, and is gone by the next read).

The paper's recommendation, taken as written: strictness follows what a mistake destroys (`PHILOSOPHY.md` § IV): a plan under ratio harms nobody until the day, and refusing it at plan time makes a plan impossible to write — SRC's own sample is the evidence. B adds no word, closes three filed gaps that other apps already want (ELA's totals, linear's state category), and puts the rule where every surface reads it. If the owner wants a refusal, it belongs at the moment the shift starts, which is a commitment, not a commit.

### <a id="fjs-d571"></a>2026-10-13 · `FJS-D571` — Does a CSV extract neutralize a text cell that starts with `= + - @`, tab or CR, at the cost of what a re-import reads back — Always guard, one owner: a `csvCell` in `@frontierjs/toolbelt/cells` beside `parseCell`, which prefixes `'` to a TEXT cell whose first character is `= + - @`, tab or CR unless the whole string reads as a number by `parseCell`'s own number rule, not a second regex (`-12.50` is left alone). `export.js`, Studio's dump and Transit call it and their copies are deleted, and the export manifest records that the guard ran. CSV becomes the format a person opens, and `ndjson` stays the round-trip format, already exact.

Asked in [`IDEAS/owed-rulings.md`](IDEAS/owed-rulings.md) § Open questions. **A** was picked over **B** (guard on request: `@@export(csv, guard: formulas)` or a run option, default off. It keeps CSV byte-exact by default, so the unsafe extract is the one nobody asked for, and it adds an option), **C** (no guard: document that a CSV extract is data, not a spreadsheet, and point a spreadsheet reader at a sanitizing import. No code changes, and every app that hands staff the file must remember).

The paper's recommendation, taken as written: a CSV extract is opened in a spreadsheet far more often than it is parsed back, a reader that needs fidelity already has `ndjson`, and one writer in toolbelt removes three copies of the rule instead of adding a fourth. *Ergonomics vs. strictness*: an evaluated formula is destructive and a stray `'` is cosmetic, so the guard is the default. *Paved road vs. the workaround*: Transit's copy measures the road, and B is the flag that widens the shoulder. Artefact: the red test above plus a toolbelt test over `= + - @`, tab, CR and numeric text; a fourth hand-rolled writer stays silent (`none`). Tier: Register (a `DECISIONS.md` ruling).

### <a id="fjs-d588"></a>2026-10-13 · `FJS-D588` — Does a copy derived from other rows (an inherited tree grant) get a write hook that hears every write with its rows inside the transaction, does the framework own the tree grant so no copy exists, or does the writing service keep the copy — Complete the hooks: `createMany`/`updateMany` fire `onAfterWrite` once per row (rows by `RETURNING *` only when a plugin listens, the `deleteMany` prefetch precedent), and nothing more yet: the in-transaction timing is not built, and it and B (the framework owns the tree grant) are decided after notion Q1's B is measured.

Asked in [`IDEAS/owed-rulings.md`](IDEAS/owed-rulings.md) § Open questions. **A** was picked over **B** (the framework owns the tree grant (notion PLAN Q1 spelling B, a `@@tree` closure table it maintains, or C, a recursive policy, or D, a materialized path). No copy exists, so nothing goes stale. B–D are not measured yet; Q1 parked them), **C** (neither: the copy is a convention the writing service keeps (what the stressor's passing run did), documented in the litestone hazards. No code, and every writer that forgets it fails open silently.).

The paper's recommendation, A's first half: a bulk write that no hook hears is a predictability defect whatever Q1 answers (its siblings are heard), and fixing it coins no noun. The in-transaction timing is a new concept that B would make unnecessary here, so it waits for B's numbers. `FJS-D581` ruled A (the proxy), so the option's `$guardWrites` clause no longer applies.

### <a id="fjs-d665"></a>2026-10-13 · `FJS-D665` — **FJS-D665 — After a restore, may the outbox relay send a row the backup recorded — Litestone stamps a restored database with the time its backup was taken, a generic fact on the client. The relay holds every undelivered row created before that time until an operator releases or drops it, and B's `--dry-run` list stays as the read surface. Restoring after a disaster, with the live files gone, is safe under this option.

Asked in [`IDEAS/time-travel.md`](IDEAS/time-travel.md) § Open questions. **A** was picked over **B** (the paper's B and nothing more: the list is printed, the relay resends, and handlers stay idempotent (the `deliverOutbox` contract already says so)), **C** (restore carries the live database's `deliveredAt` marks forward into the restored copy, through a schema attribute that names the table to keep at present. It has nothing to carry when the live file is the thing that was lost).

The paper's recommendation, taken as written: a duplicate mail, webhook or charge cannot be undone, so *strictness follows cost* calls for a hold rather than a warning. A is also the one option that still holds when no live file survives, which is when most restores happen.

### <a id="fjs-d512"></a>2026-10-13 · `FJS-D512` — What does the zone binding spell when the wall clock's zone lives on another model, and is the zone column refused by a new `@zone` validator — `@zone` beside `@date`/`@datetime`/`@time` on the zone column (IANA set via `Intl.supportedValuesOf`), and `@zoned(path)` on `@time`/`@date` columns taking a one-hop relation path (`site.timeZone`), the `FJS-499` one-hop precedent; litestone only refuses and describes (`x-zoned` in JSON Schema), and an instant pair stays the app's `@system` columns.

A closes the `"banana"` hole and makes the pairing declared rather than remembered at the cost of one validator and one path argument; B's recompute-on-write is the real fix for the Azores case, but it is a derived-column mechanism the language does not yet have, and deserves its own ruling. - **The commitment half (`FJS-2170`)** — `readBy(kind, by, timeZone)` in `litestone/src/core/commitment.js` reads a day-kind `by` in one zone per `due()` call, so lago's `on: periodEnd + graceDays` fires 9 h late for Tokyo and 7 h early for Los Angeles from one sweep. Under A the `@zoned(path)` on the `@date` is what `dueSql` reads per row, with `due()` grouping by zone; the alternative is a `zone:` argument on `@@commitment` itself, a second place to say the same binding. Red assertion owed: `due({ by: '2026-10-03T15:00Z' })` holds the Tokyo invoice and not the Los Angeles one.

### <a id="fjs-d908"></a>2026-10-13 · `FJS-D908` — How does a per-row zone (a column, possibly two relations away) reach a `where` — A zone-aware operator the client lowers: the caller states the wall-clock rule and the zone field (`{ startsAt: { localTime: { atOrBefore: '08:00', zone: 'inviteeTimeZone' } } }`); litestone selects the distinct zones present (`SELECT DISTINCT zone`, bounded and indexable), computes each zone's instant bound with `fromWall`/`partsIn`, and lowers to `(zone = ? AND startsAt <= ?) OR …`. SQL stays instant-only, so `FJS-D143` stands and the cost is one DISTINCT plus an index range per zone. The zone must be a column of the same row; a zone two relations away (`Shift → Employee → User`) needs a join the lowering does not do today, so that case stays open or is solved by A + a denormalized zone column. Adds an operator to `where`, `$checkWhere` and the directive table.

Asked in [`IDEAS/owed-rulings.md`](IDEAS/owed-rulings.md) § Open questions. **A** was picked over **B** (a materialized instant: a stored column the app or a hook keeps current (`remindAt`), plain `where remindAt <= now`, fully indexable, any relation depth because the app writes it. No litestone change at all and `@generated` stays deterministic and same-row (`parser.js` ~973); the cost is that the rule lives in app code beside the write, goes stale when the zone or the rule changes, and `tooLate` (shifts starting before 08:00 local) is still the app's to define), **C** (a framework-bound window per zone, not per row: litestone exposes the *per-zone bound* as a helper (`db.booking.zonedBounds({ zone: 'inviteeTimeZone', wall: '08:00' })` returning `[{ zone, instant }]`) and the app composes the OR itself. Smallest surface and no operator, but every app re-writes the same OR and `$checkWhere` cannot see it, so it is Invariant 4's *beside the owner* by another route. - **Recommend A, same-row zone only** — it is the only choice that makes the database do the narrowing from a declaration, it keeps `FJS-D143`'s *SQL never evaluates a zone* intact (the zones are enumerated, then every comparison is an instant), and `FJS-1214` asks for the same word in declaration so the spelling is shared; B is the workaround an app can already use today and the row's two-relation case should be answered by it (or by a later join-lowering), not by widening A).

the only choice that makes the database do the narrowing from a declaration while SQL never evaluates a zone (FJS-D143): zones are enumerated, every comparison is an instant. Same-row zone only; a zone two relations away is a materialized instant (B), which an app can already write.

### <a id="fjs-d911"></a>2026-10-13 · `FJS-D911` — How does a parent's column reach a child's `@derived` or `@from` — Ship the to-one `@from(rel, column)` form: when the first argument names a to-one relation field on this model and the second a column on its target, `parseFrom` returns a `{ rel, column }` op and the client compiles it with the correlated scalar subquery a policy's `relation.column` path already builds. `@from` stays the one owner of "bring a value onto this row", the refusal's promise becomes true, and the `.some` refusal keeps its `exists: true` cure.

Smallest change, but the capability stays missing and the Linear schema keeps a copied `category` that goes stale when a state is re-categorised), **C** (let `@derived` itself accept a one-hop path (`@derived(state.category)`), routing `case 'path'` to the same subquery. The spelling the author reaches for first, but it is the second way to cross a relation that the `policy.js` comment says this language exists to avoid, and `@derived` stops being same-row).

The paper's recommendation, taken as written: `@from` is already the declared owner of crossing a relation onto a row and the refusal already promises it; B adds the missing to-one direction on existing machinery with no second origin.

### <a id="fjs-d922"></a>2026-10-13 · `FJS-D922` — Does a declared extensible key with no slot get filtered by a scan, as `extensible-columns.md` § The thirteenth field says, or refused, as `rewriteExtensibleWhere` does — and if refused, how does a filter UI learn which keys it may offer — Honor the doc: a slotless key compiles to `json_extract(<blob>, ?)` with the key bound as a path parameter (Invariant 8), ANDed with the scope the query already carries. Nothing slow can be asked for, but a tenant past the pool size cannot filter on a key they declared, and the Q6 measurement (most realistic declarations hold no slot) says that is most keys), **C** (A: scan for a slotless key, plus `$declaredFields()` marks `indexed` per key so a UI can warn rather than hide. ### <a id="fjs-d935"></a>2026-10-13 · `FJS-D935` — Q1 — Is a balance a column trait the engine keeps at write, or does `@from` stay the only aggregate — `@balance(Model, sum: field | count: true)`: stored, kept by triggers, refused below any constraint the column declares, and the source derived append-only.

Asked in [`IDEAS/ledger.md`](IDEAS/ledger.md) § Open questions. **A** was picked over **B** (no new word. Document the `move()` shape as the pattern and add a `litestone advise` rule that finds a column written beside an append-only child and suggests the reconciliation), **C** (`@from(…, stored: true)`: the same machinery as A behind an option on the existing word).

The paper's recommendation, taken as written: B leaves the promise in a comment, where `asSystem()`, a seed and `fli tinker` already break it without a sound. C puts two different answers to *can this refuse* behind one word, so reading `@from` would no longer tell a developer whether a write can fail. - **Evidence, 2026-10-09 — the Lago stressor, a second domain (prepaid credit).** `fjs-prototypes/lago` § Q2 graded a hand-kept `Account.balance` under `@@check("kind <> 'prepaid' OR balance <= 0")` against Σ `Posting.amount` read at the spend, two $7 spends of $10, in one process and in two (`api/test/journal.test.ts`). The kept column refused the second spend in every arrangement, `asSystem()` included. The sum refused it only when read inside the spending transaction (`$transaction`'s FIFO lock and `BEGIN IMMEDIATE` serialize it, across processes too); read before the transaction, both guards passed and only the column's CHECK stopped $14 leaving $10. The sum costs 230 µs at 1k postings, 3.3 ms at 10k and 37 ms at 100k on one account, inside the write lock, against 15–35 µs for the column. And a direct write moved the column with no posting, the drift A's triggers would close. Two things A's spelling must answer that inventory did not ask. **The floor is per row, not per column:** a receivable goes either way and a prepaid account may not, so `@balance(Posting, sum: amount) @gte(0)` on `Account` floors every kind; Lago's own wallet validates `balance_cents >= 0` only `if: :traceable?`. **The sign:** debit-positive postings put credit-normal accounts (prepaid, payable, revenue) below zero, so the floor is `<= 0` or a negation. TigerBeetle ships two flags, `debits_must_not_exceed_credits` and `credits_must_not_exceed_debits`, for this reason. Lago itself keeps `wallets.balance_cents` at write under a per-customer advisory lock and `lock_version` (`credits/applied_prepaid_credits_service.rb:23-42`), which is spelling (a) plus a lock.

### <a id="fjs-d917"></a>2026-10-12 · `FJS-D917` — What `search()`'s text means — the words a person typed, every one required; FTS5's own syntax is `raw: true`, and a box searched as it is typed says `prefix: true`

`search(text)` handed `text` to FTS5's `MATCH` unchanged, so the ordinary text of a search box was query language (`FJS-1440`): `mini-redis` a column filter, `c++`, `(512) 555-1234`, `.net` and an email address syntax errors, each a 500 over `$search` whose message named a word of the search. Four apps wrote the same quoting by hand to get past it (portal, remnant, linear, ela), which is *paved road vs. the workaround* measuring the road, so the road changes.

- **Words by default.** Each word becomes a quoted phrase, FTS5's literal, and all are required. A `"phrase"` the person typed stays one; a quote left open only separates. A text with no word left answers `[]` rather than FTS5's syntax error. This is `contains` a second time: its operand is text, not a LIKE pattern, with `$raw` for a pattern (`likePattern` and `ftsWords` sit together in `query.js`).
- **`raw: true` is the engine's language**, for text the code writes (ela's `{phone phoneDigits} : …` column filters). No directive reaches it. `$search` over HTTP and sierra's offline `local-db` pass through the default, so the person's text is words wherever it is searched.
- **`prefix: true` widens the last word**, which is what linear's palette and remnant's lemma lookup wrote as `toMatch(q) + '*'`. A last word ending in punctuation stays whole, because `"c++"*` tokenizes to `c*`, every c-word. It is an option and not the default because a submitted search (portal, remnant's verses) would widen `love` to `lovely`; under `tokenize: trigram` it changes nothing. `raw` with `prefix` is refused by name.

Refused: quoting in junction's `$search` alone. The owner of the translation is the one place that hands text to `MATCH` (Invariant 4); quoting at the transport would leave every server-side `search()` caller with its own copy, which is where the four copies came from. A short term under trigram (`FJS-2332`) is not answered here. Pinned by `packages/litestone/test/search-words.test.ts` (the measured corpus under all three tokenizers, each term asserted to FIND its row) and `packages/junction/test/real-litestone-client.test.ts` § *what a person types is words over HTTP*, which answers 500 with the default reverted.

### <a id="fjs-d568"></a>2026-10-10 · `FJS-D568` — How does a sealing model freeze a column from a LATER move than the seal — a move-scoped argument on `@immutable`, a second attribute, or no language change — `@immutable(after: <move>)`: the existing word with a scope. The column is writable until the named move's target, frozen from there and from every state reachable from it (`sealedStates`' own closure, generalized in `core/seal.js` to take a move name). Bare `@immutable` keeps its two meanings (create on a plain model, the seal on a sealing one). No new noun; one more argument form for the same word, and `db:explain @immutable` (FJS-1482) must describe all three.

Asked in [`IDEAS/owed-rulings.md`](IDEAS/owed-rulings.md) § Open questions. **A** was picked over **B** (a new attribute `@sealedBy(<move>)` (or `@frozenAt`): a second word for the same guard, so `@immutable` stays exactly "create or the seal" and the later freeze is greppable on its own. A new noun beside one that already means "frozen"), **C** (no language change; document the shipped recipe (`@@check("(status = 'accepted') = (signedName IS NOT NULL)")` plus `@allow('write', status == 'sent')` on the field). It leaves the silent 200 no-op on a later rewrite and `asSystem()` can still overwrite the signature).

The paper's recommendation, taken as written: the freeze guard, its error (`SealedDocumentError`) and its closure already exist in `seal.js` and the write guards in `client.js`; the argument only changes which move the closure starts from, so nothing is restated and the move name is checked at parse like `@seals`' own.

### <a id="fjs-d666"></a>2026-10-10 · `FJS-D666` — How does a JSON or /mcp caller supply a File column — An inline value: a data URL (RFC 2397, `data:<mime>;base64,…`) or `{ name, type, data }` with base64 `data`, which `readValue` decodes into bytes like a Buffer, `@accept` sniffing the bytes and not trusting the claimed type. The input schema for a File column is derived to describe that value rather than `FileRef`. The bound is junction's `http.maxBodySize`, the one a browser's multipart upload already meets, so it is not a new option. Its default is 256KB and base64 adds a third, so about 190KB of file gets through untouched: a phone photo (2–5MB) is refused until the app raises that setting, which is the same raise a form upload of that photo already needs. Today the 413 reads *Request body exceeds 262144 bytes* and names nothing to raise, so it names `http.maxBodySize`. One call, and the server stays the only author of a ref.

Asked in [`IDEAS/owed-rulings.md`](IDEAS/owed-rulings.md) § Open questions. **A** was picked over **B** (an upload route that takes the bytes and hands back a ref the create then accepts as an object. That needs the ref signed or checked against what the route issued: a ref the caller made up and naming another row's key would have that file deleted when this row's old refs are cleaned up. It is two steps per transport, and it is the PUT presign FJS-D260 already says comes later for direct-to-bucket upload), **C** (both, A now and B when direct-to-bucket lands).

The paper's recommendation, taken as written: it is the problem's own complexity (JSON has no multipart), it uses an existing name, its owner is the `readValue` already there, and B's forged-ref failure is destructive and silent unless it brings a signing scheme that is out of scale for this row. When B arrives, it arrives as FJS-D260's presign and does not depend on this.

### <a id="fjs-d852"></a>2026-10-10 · `FJS-D852` — Does this open the door to triggers generally — The grammar is the boundary: `@@cascade` takes a source field, a relation field path and a mode, so a computed value, a condition or a side effect has no spelling.

### <a id="fjs-d846"></a>2026-10-09 · `FJS-D846` — How many hops — One hop per declaration, chained: a child that declares its own `@@cascade` on the received field carries it a hop further, with a cycle guard.

Asked in [`IDEAS/cascading-fields.md`](IDEAS/cascading-fields.md) § Open questions. **C** was picked over **A** (one hop: the declaring model's direct children), **B** (the breadth-first walk with a cycle guard, as `@@softDelete(cascade)` does).

The paper's recommendation, taken as written: every hop is written on the model it leaves, so the walk can reach no model that did not say so and each error names one hop. `@@softDelete(cascade)` then desugars into one declaration per model on the walk, generated rather than inferred at runtime.

### <a id="fjs-d844"></a>2026-10-09 · `FJS-D844` — Does `updateMany` cascade — Cascade on `updateMany`: take the matched parent ids by `RETURNING`, as a bulk write on a logged model already does, and run the child statement over them.

### <a id="fjs-d843"></a>2026-10-09 · `FJS-D843` — Is a MIRRORED model a declaration — A model attribute, `@@mirror(key: externalId)`, `absent: 30d` added once a second caller shows the drop-out rule's shape: the model is declared a mirror, the key is named once, the three per-column attributes and gate 8 are DERIVED from it, `missingSince` is a derived `@system` column the sync maintains, a caller's write to a mirrored column is refused by construction, and `advise` stops asking a mirror for a machine.

**Amended 2026-10-16.** *`absent:` waits for a second caller* is withdrawn by [`FJS-D1180`](#fjs-d1180): there is no drop-out word; the sync that knows its scope stamps `missingSince`.

### <a id="fjs-d592"></a>2026-10-09 · `FJS-D592` — Q1 — does `@@extensible` take `FJS-D365`'s `scope:`, so a declaration is keyed per PARENT ROW as well as per tenant? (`FJS-D592`) — `@@extensible(column, declaredBy: Model, scope: field)`, `field` a foreign key on the extended model whose twin is on the declarer.
