A mod's words now reach a model with no tools, as `FJS-D1017` had it; what drives the machine is the loop, which already runs under `auto` with its own ladder, budget, pre-brief and close-out, so a task is held to a row in the register like every other fix. The model answers a plan and never a flag: an id must be a ready row of `fli next`, a package a bench, a severity `S1`–`S4`, and anything else is refused in a line with nothing started. A free-text task that matches no row is filed first, so the work traces back. *Unenforced:* the agent reads the loop's log for the row it is on and its outcome, and a change to that line's shape is reported by nothing. *Lives in:* `planOf`/`checkPlan` in `packages/haven/agents/agents.js`, `startLoop`/`fileRow`/`loopReport` in `packages/haven/web/src/taskmaster.js`; `agents/test/agents.test.js` asserts the loop's argv against a stub loop.

### <a id="fjs-d1019"></a>2026-10-15 · `FJS-D1019` — A mod's task runs a whole Claude Code session under `auto` — An agent handed `<nick> task: …` by a mod runs `claude -p --permission-mode auto` in the owner's checkout, with tools, the project's hooks and a $5 budget; `acceptEdits` and `bypassPermissions` were the other two.

The gate is the same one: the runner's `HAVEN_MODS`, never the server's, so a task is a nick the owner named driving the owner's machine, and a stranger's `task:` starts nothing. **`acceptEdits`** would deny every Bash call the project settings do not allowlist, since a print session cannot ask, and most tasks would stop short; **`bypassPermissions`** would make a mod's line a shell. `auto` lets Claude Code's classifier judge each tool call. Overrides § V's *failure mode proportional to the cost of being wrong* at the owner's choice: a wrong task can edit or run anything `auto` admits in the shared tree. *Lives in:* `WORK_PERMISSION` and `WORK_BUDGET_USD`, `packages/haven/agents/agents.js`; `agents/test/agents.test.js` asserts the mode and that a non-mod's task starts nothing.

### <a id="fjs-d1015"></a>2026-10-14 · `FJS-D1015` — A member's scene is mounted as a tree, never built as data — A Room row's placements are mounted by one generic `<Placements>` component that renders the same `<Piece>` and `<Door>` an owner's `.mesa` scene does, so the mounted tree still calls `stamp()` and `FJS-D997` stands unamended. The placement format exists only in the row; what the server and tests read is derived from the tree by `bun run frames`, as `.frame.txt` is.

Ruled by the owner over **B** (the tree compiles to placement data and `createStage` is built from that, amending `FJS-D997` to make the tree authoring only) and **C** (a scene is a placements JSON file, overturning `FJS-D997`). Answers the check `IDEAS/haven.md` 12.1 asked first.

**Why.** All three differ in who calls `stamp()`, a mounted tree or a loop over data. B's one gain is a stage the server builds without Mesa. For an owner's scene, 12.2's generated `world.json` already gives that. For a member's row, the API derives the same shape by mounting `<Placements>` headlessly when the row is saved, through the loader `web/test/stage.mjs` already uses, and never takes a world the caller sends. B would add a second way to build a stage for nothing. C undoes 5.5–5.8 a day after they were ruled. A row can name a piece only by key, so a piece a member may place lives in `pieces/index.js`; an owner's scene may still define one inline. A key the registry lacks, or two pieces on one cell, is refused by name when the row is saved, not when a screen draws it.

*Lives in:* `Placements.mesa` (new, 12.1, under `packages/haven/web/src/`), `web/src/pieces/index.js`; the plan is `IDEAS/haven.md` 12.1.

### <a id="fjs-d998"></a>2026-10-14 · `FJS-D998` — A Haven mod is a nick the server lists — `HAVEN_MODS`, read at every login both ways; the standing is `Member.role = 'mod'`, `@guarded`, and what a mod may do is two predicates in the schema, never a method or a hook.

`IDEAS/haven.md` 3.2 asked for a mod standing a ban is exercised through. The
standing is a column the login writes from the list and nothing below the
system touches: `role` is `@guarded`, so a member cannot appoint themselves,
and the ladder reads a role's presence (`FJS-D197`), so a mod grades USER(4)
and a member CREATOR(3) — the session carries no `role` any more, which is what
Haven's `CLAUDE.md` said all along. What a mod may do is said where the
Data boundary reads it (Invariant 6): `@@allow('update', id == auth().id ||
auth().role == 'mod')` for whose row, `@allow('write', auth().role == 'mod')` on
`bannedAt` for which column, and the read policy admits a mod to the banned
rows so a ban is lifted by naming the member. The ban is therefore an ordinary
`members.patch`, and the client's `/ban <nick>` and `/unban <nick>` send one.
A member sending the same patch is not refused: the row is filtered to nothing
and the column is dropped (`FJS-D22`), so the client reads the answered row and
says *only a mod bans*.

Over **B**, public keys in the list: unforgeable, but an operator has to find a
key in `~/.fli/haven/key.json` to type it, and a nick is what they see on the
screen. The window B closes is a stranger taking the owner's nick before the
owner's own first login on a server the owner just deployed, which is theirs to
walk through first; a nick held is `@unique`, so it cannot be taken after. Over
**C**, a `members.ban` method with a declared gate: that puts the standing in a
service declaration, one more place than the schema, for no row the schema
cannot say. The list is read when the app is built, as the session key is, so a
change to it is a restart; a nick struck from it is a member again on their
next login, not at once — a mod's session outlives their standing by one run.

### <a id="fjs-d997"></a>2026-10-14 · `FJS-D997` — A Haven scene is a component tree, and its picture is a generated file — A scene is a `.mesa` file: `<Scene>` provides `$context.scene` and every piece, door and pacer is a child component that stamps its cells and claims its footprint through it, the shape Threlte gives a Three.js scene in Svelte. The art is no longer typed: `src/scenes/<Name>.frame.txt` is rendered from the tree, committed beside it and pinned by `scenes.test.js`, so a scene is still read as a picture in a diff. Recognition (`compose()`) leaves the runtime and stays only as the editor's paste-art importer.

Ruled by the owner, over the hybrid (art stays the source, only live things become components) and over leaving it. Amends `IDEAS/haven.md` Phase 5's goal and Done-when, the 2026-10-13 *doors stay text* ruling inside 5.3 (a door is now `<Door x y to>` or a house's `door=`, placed; it REPLACES the wall cell under it, the one overlap a stage allows), and `FJS-D995` (a member's scene row holds placements and a palette, never a stranger's glyphs).

**Why.** Art as source held only what sits still: the cat was a `pacers` array, fire a palette flag, and every next ask — a window lit at night, a sign showing the count, a door that swings — was another config array beside the text. Recognition was a glyph fight that grew with the vocabulary (`_` roof against `_` wall, `|` table against `|` wall, a house in eleven parts because no two are one width), and both scenes were in the end stamped by a script rather than typed, so the text had already lost authoring and kept only reading. Reading is a print, and a committed frame is that print. Conversion is cheap both ways: the tree renders to the frame, and `compose().matches` is the importer.

**The nine**, answered before the first edit: one origin (the tree; the frame is generated and graded); no new noun (Scene, Piece, Door, stamp all exist); the complexity removed was ours; a scene now composes like every other Mesa UI; walkability, doors and the picture are derived; `Scene.mesa` owns the context, `#paint` the buffer, `#cell` `at()`, and `look()` and `compose()` as painters are deleted rather than paralleled; a piece knows `stamp` and `claim` and nothing else; two pieces on one cell refuse at mount naming the cell; the frame test fails when the render drifts. *Doctrine vs. discovery* was the hearing: the text editor works, and solves the thing being dropped. Register.

*Lives in:* `packages/haven/web/src/components/Scene.mesa`, `web/src/stage.js`, `web/src/scenes/*.mesa` and `*.frame.txt`, `web/test/scenes.test.js`; the plan is `IDEAS/haven.md` 5.5–5.8.

### <a id="fjs-d988"></a>2026-10-14 · `FJS-D988` — How a site-kit upgrade is proved, where site-kit lives, and who owns the import from an existing site — The bump is proved on a local registry before anything reaches npm; site-kit is `packages/site-kit`; `fli ksite:*` is deleted, and its `fetch` is `site-kit fetch`.

Asked in [`IDEAS/site-kit-plan.md`](IDEAS/site-kit-plan.md) Phase 5, four forks, each answered with the recommendation:

- **The proof is a local registry** over **a real npm publish now** and **versioned tarballs**. Verdaccio serves `@frontierjs/*` and `@kobami/*` from its own storage with no uplink, so npm's copies, behind the workspace, never answer; everything else proxies to npm. A registry is what a client upgrades from, and a tarball path is not: a peer's metadata is fetched from the registry (the reason ksite could not declare site-kit until now), and a caret range only means something there. The proof is `fjs-prototypes/ksite/baseline/upgrade.mjs`. The real publish is its own step, behind the owner's go.
- **site-kit moves to `packages/` now** over **at the real publish**. It is a framework package that will be published, and `fli ws:pub`, the Packages table and the `snapshots` phase read `packages/*`. The `website/packages/*` workspace glob is gone with it; the website is a consumer.
- **`@kobami/ksite`'s registry is picked at the real publish.** The local proof needs none, and the `@kobami` npm scope's owner is not established.
- **`fetch` (a page or sitemap to Markdown) is site-kit's**, over deleting it with the group or moving it to `@kobami/ksite`. By `FJS-D604`'s test, a site that is not a cleaning company would use it unchanged. `make:fetch-config` goes with it: its template is the config documented in site-kit's README. The legacy-to-site-kit converter reads ksite's legacy dialect, so it is `@kobami/ksite`'s bin (`ksite port`). The `theme.scss` import becomes `@ksite/themes/` by that codemod, and no `@/` alias is added (*preservation vs. evolution*: every legacy client goes through the converter anyway).

- **Owner.** Publishing stays `fli ws:pub`'s. The import is site-kit's and the legacy conversion is the preset's, so `fli` keeps neither, and `core/peer.js`, which existed only for `ksite:fetch`, is deleted.
- **Silence.** "A bump reaches a client with no copy" is `upgrade.mjs`: a client builds from `content/` and two dependencies, the files it builds match its linked build, N+1 carries both packages' changes, and the update touches only `package.json` and `bun.lock`. The proof found [`FJS-2842`](ISSUES.md#fjs-2842) on its first run.

Asked in [`IDEAS/haven.md`](IDEAS/haven.md) § Open questions. **A** was picked over **B** (a second surface, `site/` or `browser/`, holding its own routes that import the shared `Scene.mesa` and scenes. Invariant 3 unchanged).

The paper's recommendation, taken as written: B's routes are three one-line files that re-export the first's, a copy whose only job is to satisfy a reading of a layout rule; and the per-target attach is the mechanism `FJS-D978` already chose for placing a figure, so A adds a resolver where B adds a directory.

### <a id="fjs-d982"></a>2026-10-14 · `FJS-D982` — Q6 — How a machine with no checkout gets the client, and how it stays the server's version — Publish `@frontierjs/haven`. The server states the version it runs at `GET /haven/client` (`{ package, version }`, read from its own `package.json`). `fli haven` installs exactly that version into `~/.fli/haven/<version>/` on first sight, then imports its `web/src/sign-in.js` as it does now. A checkout's sibling Haven still wins, the way `dev:tui` runs the app in front of it. There is no floor: the client is always the server's. A version npm does not have is refused by name.

Asked in [`IDEAS/haven.md`](IDEAS/haven.md) § Open questions. **A** was picked over **B** (publish `@frontierjs/haven`. `fli haven` installs `latest`, sends its version on `POST /haven/login`, and the server refuses a client below a declared floor by name), **C** (the server serves its own client source, and `fli haven` downloads and runs it).

The paper's recommendation, taken as written: it keeps junction's direction (the server states, the client acts), derives the version from the deployed package instead of keeping a floor by hand, and closes the version gap rather than refusing it. B adds a floor someone has to remember to raise. C runs code from whatever `--api` names, which gives a private server's operator code execution on every visitor's machine. A's trust is npm's, the same as `bunx fli` itself.

### <a id="fjs-d984"></a>2026-10-13 · `FJS-D984` — Invariant 13 governs styling, not content: a terminal scene's palette is its pixels, and hex is how it says them.

A Haven scene is an art grid plus a `paint` grid naming `palette` entries (`packages/haven/web/src/scenes/`), drawn into an OpenTUI frame buffer by `web/src/paint.js`. A hearth needs four oranges and a fountain three blues, and the tone set has one of each, so tones would narrow the drawing to the vocabulary built for UI chrome. ### <a id="fjs-d983"></a>2026-10-13 · `FJS-D983` — Global fli tooling has no environment, so it takes a 5 where the env digit goes: 5500–5509.

7/8/9 is the test/dev/prod of a PROJECT. A tool run from `~/` (`fli gui`, studio, devtools, the proxy fallback, Haven) has no project and so no environment to be in, and filing it as dev/tooling/project 0 (8500–8509) put it in a dev space that does not exist when no app is open. The block keeps its tooling digit and slots: 5500 gui · 5501 pmap · 5502 studio · 5503 devtools · 5504 proxy · 5505 Haven. No project port in any env can reach it, so the guard that refused dev/tooling/project 0 is gone and 8500 is an ordinary slot again. `decode()` reads the leading 5 as env `global`. **`fli gui` run IN a project is that project's GUI**, so it takes the project's tooling row for the env — 8500 dev, 7500 `--test`, 9500 `--production` for project 0, plus a scaffolded app's `fli dev` slot as the service digit so the app on 8001 has its GUI on 8501 (`guiPort()`); 5500 is the GUI only where there is no project. 5500 is VS Code Live Server's default; `strictPort` makes that collision loud. ### <a id="fjs-d971"></a>2026-10-13 · `FJS-D971` — Does a static app's `document` reach the dev shell, and who applies it — Sierra applies `document` to `index.html` for `target: 'static'`, in dev and in the build (`build/document-shell.js`), through the serializer `wrapDocument()` uses (`documentParts()` in `prerender.js`). An attribute stated on `index.html` and in `document` both is refused, naming both. The wider rule is ruled with it — **Vite dev runs what the static build ships** — and only `document` is built: `_redirects` and host functions in dev wait until a site needs one there.

Asked in [`IDEAS/site-kit-plan.md`](IDEAS/site-kit-plan.md) Phase 3 step 5. **A** was picked over **B** (site-kit's shell applies it, for site-kit sites only) and **C** (leave the restatement). The probe found three apps stating it twice, not one: ksite (`<body id="app">` and its lead loader in `src/main.js`), `example/site` (`<body class="app theme-default">`), and the scaffold `fli make:site` writes into every new site surface. B fixes the first only. Sierra already owns turning `document` into HTML (Invariant 4), so the dev shell reuses the same serializer rather than adding a second one.

Why refuse rather than merge: a merge rule (shell wins, or `document` wins) is a second answer to which copy is true, and the build already gives one, since a prerendered page has only `document`. Why the build too: a static app whose home route is not prerendered publishes the shell as `dist/index.html`, and that page must match the others. Why the plugin is limited to `static`: an SPA has no `document`, and its `index.html` is the whole of its page. Re-running ksite's lead loader after each client navigation stays ksite's. `src/main.js` now reads the loader list from the page (the `bodyEnd` scripts) instead of restating the URL. Proved by `packages/sierra/test/document-shell.test.js`: a real dev server's `transformIndexHtml`, a real build's `dist/index.html`, head tags byte-identical to a prerendered page's, and the refusal.

### <a id="fjs-d962"></a>2026-10-13 · `FJS-D962` — Who owns the pre-ship site check, and how a preset adds to it — `site-kit check <dir>` is the check every site-kit site has, and a preset's `./preset` export returns a fourth key, `rules`, a list of `{ id, group, stage, run }`; a preset rule whose id a kit rule has replaces it.

Asked in `IDEAS/site-kit-plan.md` Phase 3 step 5(b). **A** was picked over **B** (the whole check stays in `@kobami/ksite`, and a second preset or the website copies it) and **C** (a second `check` key holding `{ rules, launched }`, so the launch mode is a preset hook of its own).

The check's two halves were already named in the plan, and the test is `FJS-D604`'s: a site that is not a cleaning company runs every built-stage rule (sitemap, canonical, titles, descriptions, headings, social, links, images, JSON-LD against schema.org) and every source-stage rule but the template leftovers unchanged, so they are site-kit's, and `@kobami/ksite`'s `config/names.js`, which restated site-kit's layout order for the components rule, goes with them. The nine, answered before the move:

- **Origin.** It removes one: `names.js` restated what `siteKit()` composes, and the check now reads the resolved site (`resolveSite()`), the same object the build is made from. The check's own rules read `dist/`, which the build wrote.
- **Concept.** One key, `rules`, in a noun the check already used (`rules/*.js`, "Adding a rule" in its README) and `fli check` uses for the same shape. No *Check* noun: a preset's rule is a Rule.
- **Complexity.** Lint, pre-commit and `fli check` all name the same shape — a list of rules each with an id, a group and a run; nothing here is new to the field.
- **Predictability.** A later rule wins a name, which is how `markdownLayouts` and a preset's `public/` already behave: the preset's `schema` rule replaces the kit's, so ksite keeps its per-setting fix hints without a second rule beside the kit's. A preset's rules sort after the kit's groups, so a report reads kit then preset.
- **Derived.** The component and layout directories, `siteUrl` and `description` are read from the resolved Sierra config, never restated. The template leftovers (`mycompany.com`, the 555 phone, the MaidTech pid, `launch_date`, `buildoutOnly`) are ksite's and stay in its rules, which read `ctx.settings` and `ctx.opts` for them; site-kit has no launch mode and no tool-page notion, because no second site has those words.
- **Owner.** site-kit's `check/` is the one runner, and the bin is the one `site-kit` already has (`FJS-D605`'s one command). `ksite-check` is deleted. C would have made the launch mode a second seam when a rule reading `ctx.settings.launch_date` already states it.
- **Boundary.** `loadPreset` refuses a key it does not read, a `rules` that is not an array, and a rule without `id`, `group`, `stage` and `run`, each by the preset's name; `runCheck(opts)` is `@frontierjs/site-kit/check`, and the finding shape is `finding.js`.
- **Failure.** The check itself exits 1 on an error and 0 otherwise, as before; a preset rule that throws is one `check-crashed` error naming the rule, never a run that dies.
- **Silence.** A kit rule that stops firing is caught by `test/check.mjs`, which builds a fixture site and asserts each group's findings; a preset's replacement rule is caught by ksite's `check:site` reading the same 9 errors as before the move. The one thing nothing grades is a preset rule that returns nothing on a site where it should fire — that is the preset's own test to write, and ksite's `checks.test.js` is it for the schema rule.

Adjudication: *batteries vs. smallness* — the check is a battery of site-kit and stays severable from Sierra, which has no site check and gains none here (`FJS-D608`: a Sierra owner is earned by a second consumer that is not a site-kit site). Tier: Map — `site-kit/README.md` and its `CLAUDE.md` state the key and the command; this ruling is the why.

### <a id="fjs-d961"></a>2026-10-13 · `FJS-D961` — Where a site's hand-written redirects live, and who reads them — Sierra merges the app's own `_redirects` (what reaches the output from its public directory, or from a site-kit site's `content/settings/_redirects`) with every route's `redirect:`, the routes' rules first; one path sent two places stops the build.

Asked in conversation, from [`FJS-2813`](ISSUES.md#fjs-2813). **A** was picked over **B** (route frontmatter only: every short link becomes a route file and a conversion rewrites each client's file) and **C** (a `redirects:` key in `site.md`).

Every legacy ksite client keeps its redirects in `content/settings/_redirects`, and maid.tech's are live campaign links with query strings (`/cbf-live/ /?utm_source=cbf`): short links, not moved pages, so B's route file per link is the wrong home and takes two hops for the no-slash form. A keeps the client's file as it is and keeps Sierra the one writer of `dist/_redirects` (`FJS-D920`). The routes' rules go first because a host takes the first match and an SPA's `/* /index.html 200` would otherwise swallow them. Sierra's merge is lenient about the app's lines, splats included, because only the host has to answer them; serveSite still refuses at start what it cannot answer. site-kit refuses `content/public/_redirects`, since Vite would copy it to the path the settings file is emitted to, and a preset's `public/_redirects` or `_headers`.

### <a id="fjs-d909"></a>2026-10-13 · `FJS-D909` — Where does the one doc-fence reader live and how does a package supply the prelude its examples run under — One reader in `@frontierjs/toolbelt` (a `docfences` kit: fences with `lang`, `words`, `line`, nearest preceding schema). Litestone's runner, `runnableFences` and `doc-audit` all import it; each package keeps its own `test/doc-examples.test.*` supplying its prelude, and `doc-examples-run` keeps grading the wiring. Toolbelt is below the graph (`FJS-D26`) so any package may import it; the cost is that `FJS-D860`'s "moves to `fli check`" is amended to "moves to toolbelt".

Asked in [`IDEAS/owed-rulings.md`](IDEAS/owed-rulings.md) § Open questions. **A** was picked over **B** (`fli check` owns the reader AND the run: a package declares `test/doc-prelude.{js,ts}` (default export `(block) => { imports, head }`), `fli check` writes each unmarked fence as a module under that prelude and runs it. One runner for 20 packages, no per-package test file; the cost is a new file convention plus a process fleet inside `fli check`, and the prelude for a drive-needing package (mesa served page, sierra build) is not a head string), **C** (Reader in `packages/cli/core`, package runners import it by relative path from the workspace, the way `@frontierjs/ui` reads mesa's CDP harness. No new package surface, but it makes every package's suite depend on cli, a reverse edge).

The paper's recommendation, taken as written: it is the only choice with one reader and no reverse edge, it keeps `FJS-D860`'s "the package owns its words" (the prelude), and the 19 runners then each become a small test over a shared reader instead of 19 copies of litestone's 226 lines.

### <a id="fjs-d931"></a>2026-10-12 · `FJS-D931` — Q5 — Pin the installs — Also pin a major for Docker and Caddy with an apt preference, keep every version beside `BUN_VERSION`, and report the installed versions in the heartbeat.

The versions belong in `enrollment.ts`, where the install script is and where the two pinned today already live, not in the Outpost's `config.js`. C makes every security patch a code change.

### <a id="fjs-d928"></a>2026-10-12 · `FJS-D928` — Q1 — Host firewall: nftables directly, or ufw — Nftables directly: one ruleset written by `installScript()`, read by the Outpost as `nft -j list ruleset`.

### <a id="fjs-d927"></a>2026-10-12 · `FJS-D927` — A plan is Phases of Steps: phases count from 0, a step is cited `2.3` and never reissued, and the next step is the first open box.

Picked by the owner in session. Plans spelled one sequence six ways: *Phase*
in most, then *Tier*, *Part*, *Wave*, *Step* and *Slice*. Phases started at 0
in some plans and 1 in others, and steps were `1.`, `- [ ]`, `3b` and `Step 5`.
Memory cited the same kind of position as "Phase 3 step 5", "slices 1-30" and
"waves 1-5", so a citation could not be read without opening the plan it came
from.

**A plan phase is a third qualified use under `FJS-D395`**: *a named step of
an ordered list something runs*, where a person or an agent does the running.
Inside its own plan the heading qualifies it. Anywhere else it is *plan phase*
or names the plan (`darkroom Phase 2`). *Step* is ordinary English. *Tier*
keeps its meaning of priority and *Wave* keeps its meaning of a parallel batch,
because neither says what comes next. *Slice*, *Part* and *Stage* are no longer
used for order.

**The position is derived, never written.** I proposed a `Next:` line at the
top of each plan. The fifth question of § V cut it: the first open box already
says the same thing, and a line that restates it is a second origin that
drifts.
Frontmatter `status:` carries § VII's lifecycle word.

§ IV's *preservation vs. evolution* is answered with evolution. No plan is
converted in bulk: each one converts when it is next worked on, and
`darkroom/PLAN.md` is the worked example. Enforced by: none. A `fli check` rule over plan
headings is held back until drift comes back.
*Lives in:* `.claude/skills/doc-hygiene/SKILL.md` § A plan's shape.

C gives the control plane's own container root on its host to read a config file.

### <a id="fjs-d920"></a>2026-10-12 · `FJS-D920` — Who owns the host files and the adapters — Sierra owns `_redirects`, `_headers`, the function bundle and each adapter; site-kit is a pass-through that presets the static-site defaults, layered site-kit, then preset, then site, as `config/vite.js` does.

### <a id="fjs-d860"></a>2026-10-10 · `FJS-D860` — What grades an example in a package's hand-written docs — The package's own suite runs every fence: a ```lite block is parsed and built, a ```js/```ts block runs as a module under the nearest preceding ```lite of its file, and three words on the info string are the whole contract — `fragment` (runs nothing), `throws` (passes only by throwing), `failing` (pinned to a filed defect, `test.failing`'s way). The `prisma` fence is gone: litestone's language is fenced ```lite.

The 2026-10-09 litestone docs audit read ~1300 claims and found 165 wrong, 17 of them examples that fail as written, and every one had lived because the only grader over a hand-written page was a link check (`catalog.test.ts`) and a byte comparison of the generated ones. Invariant 16 says a runnable example is verified; `packages/litestone/test/doc-examples.test.ts` is the first place that is true of prose.

The nine, answered after the runner was drafted and named as late. Origin: none — the docs are the origin and the runner reads them; a block's status is a word on its own fence, beside the code. Concept: two info words added and one fence name removed; `failing` is bun's own word. Complexity: the problem's — an example either runs or is a sliver, and only its author can say which, so the sliver is marked where the next reader sees it. Predictability: up — an unmarked block runs, the way an unmarked `*.test.*` is collected. Derived: the verdict is derived by running; nothing is restated. Owner: the package's suite, beside `catalog.test.ts`; when a second package wants one the extraction moves to `fli check` and the package stays the owner of its words (`FJS-2331`). Boundary: the three words, typed on the info string, tested by the runner. Failure: a wrong example is a red test — proportional, since the audit measured a wrong one at a session. Silence: a block marked `fragment` runs nothing and nothing says so, which is why the runner holds a ceiling on the count that ratchets down only (Invariant 14's shape).

**Why the nearest preceding schema and not a hidden default.** A page's examples follow the schema they talk about, so the reading a person makes is the one the runner makes; a page with none gets one block near its top, introduced by a sentence, which is also the page saying what its examples are about. A default schema in the test file would be a second origin the page never shows.

**Why `prisma` goes.** Familiarity vs. precision (§ IV): the ecosystem fence buys GitHub highlighting and says the language is Prisma's, which it is not, and the runner keying on `lite` is the loud failure the row asks for — a `prisma` block is an unverified one.

*Lives in:* `packages/litestone/test/doc-examples.test.ts` · the fences under `packages/litestone/docs/` and its root `README.md`, `AGENTS.md`, `CLAUDE.md`.

### <a id="fjs-d859"></a>2026-10-10 · `FJS-D859` — Does `fli check` flag a port literal in a test dir — Yes, `error`, landing after the 52 files move, so `structure` fails the next one.

Asked in [`IDEAS/workbench-branches.md`](IDEAS/workbench-branches.md) § Open questions. **A** was picked over **B** (yes, `warn`), **C** (no rule; FJS-2277 closes when the 52 have moved).

The paper's recommendation, taken as written: the failure is silent (a drive passing against the parent's server), and § V 9 asks for the artefact that turns it red; a warn is read only by whoever already knows. C leaves the 53rd file to whoever writes it. The pattern is text, so a fixture string (`memory: 8192`) can trip it — the rule's own test carries those as the negatives.

### <a id="fjs-d858"></a>2026-10-10 · `FJS-D858` — A test runs in a linked worktree the lock holds no branch number for — The helper claims it, through `claimSession` — the number `fli dev` would take, under the same lock, released by Archive as now.

Asked in [`IDEAS/workbench-branches.md`](IDEAS/workbench-branches.md) § Open questions. **A** was picked over **B** (the helper refuses, naming the worktree and saying to run `fli dev` there once), **C** (offset 0).

The paper's recommendation, taken as written: one claim path means a test and a dev server in one branch cannot disagree about the number. B makes every hand-made `git worktree add` a chore that teaches nothing, and C is the parent's ports, the silent wrong answer.

### <a id="fjs-d857"></a>2026-10-10 · `FJS-D857` — Who owns the port a test asks for — `ports.js`: one more export, a port by surface or by `{ category, service }` with the branch offset applied, imported as `@frontierjs/cli/core/ports.js`. example and basecamp already depend on `@frontierjs/cli`.

Asked in [`IDEAS/workbench-branches.md`](IDEAS/workbench-branches.md) § Open questions. **A** was picked over **B** (`@frontierjs/toolbelt/ports`: the formula moves there and cli imports it. The branch number is lock-file and git state, which a zero-dependency pure kit cannot read, so it would reach the test as an env var — and inherit D's gap), **C** (`@frontierjs/testing`: it would import cli's `ports.js` (a new edge from the Testing realm into tooling) or copy the formula, and example's drives are plain `.mjs` that import nothing from it today), **D** (no helper: every command fli runs sets `FLI_PORT_OFFSET`, and a test adds `Number(process.env.FLI_PORT_OFFSET ?? 0)` to its literal).

The paper's recommendation, taken as written: `ports.js` already owns the formula, the lock and the branch numbers, so A adds a reader to the owner (Invariant 4) where B and C add a second origin of the formula. D is the silent case this issue exists to close: `bun run test` in a branch, outside fli, gets an offset of 0 and drives the parent.

### <a id="fjs-d842"></a>2026-10-09 · `FJS-D842` — Config sprawl is the default outcome — Each config file has a closed key table, and its loader refuses an unknown key by name, pointing at the bucket it belongs in (`.lite`, env, or the other config file).

Asked in [`IDEAS/app-manifest.md`](IDEAS/app-manifest.md) § Open questions. **B** was picked over **A** (the three-bucket test as prose, as today; nothing refuses an unknown key in `frontier.config.js` or `junction.config.js`), **C** (B, plus a `fli check` rule that flags a config key whose value a schema read could produce (a model list, a plural)).

The paper's recommendation, taken as written: the closed table is the teeth: a key nothing reads is a typo or a restated fact, and both are silent today. C is a heuristic over values and would grade on guesses, so it waits until a real restated key shows up.

### <a id="fjs-d841"></a>2026-10-09 · `FJS-D841` — A linked worktree of an app takes N×10000 on every port, N the lowest free of 1–5 among its repo's linked worktrees: branch 1's 8120 is 18120 and its 7122 is 17122.

Asked in [`IDEAS/workbench-branches.md`](IDEAS/workbench-branches.md) § 6, for a Workbench branch, but it holds for any second checkout of an app. Picked over the scaffold's answer, a free SERVICE digit, because a fixed project already spends that digit on its own servers (basecamp's 8121 mail sink, 8122 DigitalOcean stand-in), so a slot would land a branch's API on its parent's sink. Also refused: the 7xxx block (it is `test`, and the parent's drives run there), a trailing zero (8120 becomes 80120, past 65535), and the Workbench handing out ports itself (a second owner beside `claimSession`).

Every digit of the schema keeps its meaning inside a branch, so a port reads as its parent's with the leading digit dropped. `claimSession` (`packages/cli/core/ports.js`) owns it, keeps N in the lock like a slot, and detects a linked worktree by `git rev-parse --git-common-dir` differing from `--git-dir`. Five is the ceiling (a sixth puts 8120 at 68120); 3–5 sit in Linux's ephemeral range and can find a port held by an outgoing socket, which `strictPort` refuses loudly, and lowest-free reaches them only when 1 and 2 are taken.

The nine (§ V): origin — `claimSession` alone; concept — none, *linked worktree* is git's word; complexity — the problem's, two checkouts of one app wanting one port; predictability — the parent's port plus a leading digit; derived — N is assigned once and kept, like a slot, so it does not move when another worktree goes; owner — `claimSession`, which already owns the slot; boundary — `FLI_PORT_*`, as today, graded by cli's ports tests; failure — a sixth worktree is refused naming the five holders, an ephemeral collision is `strictPort`'s refusal; silence — **a port written as a literal ignores the offset and reaches the parent's server**, with nothing to say so until `FJS-2277` closes. No § IV adjudication is in tension. Tier: Register.

### <a id="fjs-d840"></a>2026-10-09 · `FJS-D840` — Executable config cannot be audited — JS, but the default export must be a plain object literal — no imports, no computation, no `process.env` reads — enforced by a `fli check` rule. The loader resolves a relative path against the config file, so a file needs no `fileURLToPath` of its own, and an env override with a fallback (`process.env.JOBS_DB ?? …`) is refused like any other env read.

Asked in [`IDEAS/app-manifest.md`](IDEAS/app-manifest.md) § Open questions. **B** was picked over **A** (arbitrary JS, as built: `loadFrontierConfig` (`packages/cli/core/utils.js`) `import()`s `frontier.config.js` and `junction.config.js` is loaded the same way), **C** (`frontier.config.json` (or `.toml`), parsed rather than run).

The paper's recommendation, taken as written: it makes the file readable without running it and keeps the comments that carry basecamp's `frontier.config.js`, which JSON would strip. A value that needs computing is a secret (env) or derivable (`.lite`), which is the three-bucket test doing its job.

### <a id="fjs-d828"></a>2026-10-09 · `FJS-D828` — How does a tile know a port is *its* — Ask who holds the port (`pidsOnPort` in `core/ports.js`) and match the holder to the tile: inside the GUI child's process group, else a working directory under the row's `dir`.

### <a id="fjs-d579"></a>2026-10-09 · `FJS-D579` — From a framework checkout, does `fli new` default `--source local`, refuse npm when a template needs a newer feature than the published package, or keep npm — Default `local` when `fliRoot` sits in a framework checkout (`<root>/packages/junction/package.json` beside the cli), npm otherwise. Asked in [`IDEAS/owed-rulings.md`](IDEAS/owed-rulings.md) § Open questions. **A** was picked over **B** (keep the npm default and refuse it when the template needs a newer feature: a `requires` stamp per template feature checked against the registry's latest. Names the real cause, but is a second list that must be updated with every plugin-protocol change, and "newer than published" is a network lookup in a scaffold), **C** (keep npm and publish before the template changes. No code, and a red scaffold from the tree is the normal state between publishes; the next unpublished feature does it again).

The paper's recommendation, taken as written: the failure only exists from a checkout, where the cli and the packages are one version of one tree, so choosing the tree removes the gap instead of detecting it. The comment's reason for npm (a starting point for somebody else) is a published cli's case, and A leaves it untouched.

**The probe is a checkout marker, not a sibling.** In an npm install `fliRoot/..` is `node_modules/@frontierjs/`, where `junction/package.json` is present whenever junction is installed beside the cli, so *junction beside the cli* reads an install as a checkout. A checkout is: the cli's parent directory is `packages/`, the directory above it holds a `package.json` declaring `workspaces`, and the resolved `fliRoot` passes through no `node_modules`. `fliRoot` is the cli's real path (`import.meta.url`), so a `bun link`ed global `fli` resolves to the checkout and a registry install does not. The test that proves it covers the npm layout with junction installed beside the cli.

### <a id="fjs-d803"></a>2026-10-09 · `FJS-D803` — Do the `.lite` and `.mesa` diagnostics that exist in the VS Code extension belong in a terminal — Yes, through `fli check`: the `.mesa` errors already arrive there as `mesa-compiles`, and the `.lite` parser's errors and warnings join as a rule of the same shape, Mesa's warnings with them.

Asked in [`IDEAS/tooling-decisions.md`](IDEAS/tooling-decisions.md) § Open questions. **A** was picked over **B** (one terminal command per language (`litestone check`, `mesa check`)), **C** (editor only; the build already stops on an error).

The paper's recommendation, taken as written: `FJS-D133` makes `fli check` the one registry for *what is wrong with this app*, and the half for `.mesa` is built. The compiler stays the one owner of each diagnostic and the rule only relays it, so the editor and the terminal show the same list. C leaves every warning silent for anyone not in VS Code, including CI.

### <a id="fjs-d740"></a>2026-10-09 · `FJS-D740` — What it does about drift it cannot explain — Split it by Release id: a process reporting a different Release from the one the journal says is serving means the machine moved (stale image, half swap). ### <a id="fjs-d739"></a>2026-10-09 · `FJS-D739` — Whether a verdict is a metric — Yes, as a `gauge` of 1 or 0 per check through `registerMetricsSource`, with no new `MetricType` member.

The paper's recommendation, taken as written: a 0/1 gauge is how Prometheus has always reported `up`, so retention and alerting come with no new type. *When did it stop* is answered within the metrics retention window. C is owed only if somebody needs a verdict older than that window.

### <a id="fjs-d718"></a>2026-10-09 · `FJS-D718` — What is the honest false-positive budget — Zero by construction: a claim the resolver cannot decide is `undecidable`, reported and never failed, and a class that fires wrong is narrowed rather than tuned.

### <a id="fjs-d717"></a>2026-10-09 · `FJS-D717` — Does a claim need a stable id — No id: a claim is located by its file and its authority (the path, symbol or `exit:` command it names), and the ratchet is a count per check class, which is the shape `check-baseline.json` already has.

### <a id="fjs-d716"></a>2026-10-09 · `FJS-D716` — What is the relationship to `fli app:atlas` — None: two tools that share an instinct and no code.

### <a id="fjs-d715"></a>2026-10-09 · `FJS-D715` — Is this a product or a phase of `fli check` — A phase of `fli check`, which is where the in-repo half already runs: `packages/cli/core/doc-audit.js`, called from `checks.js`.

### <a id="fjs-d714"></a>2026-10-09 · `FJS-D714` — `ISSUES.md` (2 MB) and `DECISIONS.md` (1 MB) — A separate pass, after the `CHANGES.md` extraction proves the method.

### <a id="fjs-d711"></a>2026-10-09 · `FJS-D711` — What `fli done` asks instead — Nothing; the diff is the record.

### <a id="fjs-d710"></a>2026-10-09 · `FJS-D710` — Overlap with `atlas` and `project:map --json` — The lock is the four committed `*.snapshot.md` registers; `fli app:atlas` and `fli project:map` render them from one boot and commit nothing.

### <a id="fjs-d708"></a>2026-10-09 · `FJS-D708` — Directory or segment, not both as truth — As built: both are required (the junction loader globs `services/**/*.service.ts`, caravan `jobs/*.job.ts`), and `fli check` refuses a loaded segment outside its kind's folder by name.

Asked in [`IDEAS/app-manifest.md`](IDEAS/app-manifest.md) § Open questions. **C** was picked over **A** (segment authoritative: a `*.service.ts` anywhere under `src/` loads), **B** (directory authoritative: every file in `services/` loads; the segment is decorative).

### <a id="fjs-d707"></a>2026-10-09 · `FJS-D707` — Lowercase always — The segment is always lowercase and the stem takes the case of the name it registers: PascalCase for a type (`OrderPaid.notification.ts`, `Lead.mesa` per Invariant 19), kebab for a routed name (`user-profiles.service.ts`, `send-email.job.ts`); a `fli check` rule refuses two files that differ only in case.

The paper's recommendation, taken as written: the tree already does B and two rules depend on it (notifications stamp the type from the stem; Invariant 19 names a resource file for its model). The real hazard is the case collision, and the check names it directly.

### <a id="fjs-d706"></a>2026-10-09 · `FJS-D706` — Do not repurpose borrowed segments — A closed segment list, derived from the loaders (`.service.ts`, `.job.ts`, `.notification.ts`, …); a segment not on it means nothing to `fli`.

The paper's recommendation, taken as written: the list of loaders is the allow-list, so a borrowed segment can only be repurposed by adding a loader for it, which is a reviewed change. A deny-list is a second list that goes stale the day the ecosystem coins a segment.

### <a id="fjs-d705"></a>2026-10-09 · `FJS-D705` — Lock merge conflicts — Regenerate on conflict, as the committed `*.snapshot.md` registers work today: the header names the generator and its flags, and the `snapshots` CI phase fails a stale one.

The paper's recommendation, taken as written: the lock this paper describes already exists as `surface`/`jobs`/`notifications`/`principal.snapshot.md`, sorted and regenerated, and CI already refuses a hand-merged one. A merge driver is per-clone setup that a fresh clone silently lacks.

### <a id="fjs-d704"></a>2026-10-09 · `FJS-D704` — Deploy config and shareability are enemies — As built: `frontier.config.js` IS the deploy file (`deploy.server`, `deploy.web.domain` inline, basecamp's copy), the app's own config is `junction.config.js`, and the shareable unit is `db/schema.lite` plus `junction.config.js`, never `frontier.config.js`.

Asked in [`IDEAS/app-manifest.md`](IDEAS/app-manifest.md) § Open questions. **A** was picked over **B** (split `frontier.config.js` into an intent half (shareable) and a deploy file it references by path), **C** (keep `frontier.config.js` but move `server` and `domain` out to env or the per-run `--server` alias, so the file holds no infrastructure).

The paper's recommendation, taken as written: the name already went to deploy, and most of the intent block this paper wanted is derivable or already lives in `junction.config.js` (`FJS-D158`'s split). Calling the deploy file unshareable costs nothing; B builds a third config file for keys that have no home yet.

### <a id="fjs-d691"></a>2026-10-09 · `FJS-D691` — `mobile/` is a surface, and Invariant 3 names it. It wraps `web/` the way `desktop/` does.

Asked in the FJS Mobile report (artifact `5a2362a8`) § *Risks and rulings owed* 3, which tied it to ruling 1; `FJS-D689` answered that one by staging mobile. **It is not a target of `desktop/`**, even though one Tauri 2 project can build both. ### <a id="fjs-d689"></a>2026-10-09 · `FJS-D689` — Mobile work starts now. It does not wait for core to leave alpha.

### <a id="fjs-d675"></a>2026-10-08 · `FJS-D675` — `CHANGES.md` is retired. History is git; a lesson goes where it is read. Three markdown files at a package root are the standard, and `fli done` no longer asks for a change-log heading.

Asked in [`IDEAS/changes-retirement.md`](IDEAS/changes-retirement.md) § Open questions; **A** on all four. The paper's case, measured 2026-09-26: 23 files, 3.4 MB, grown 20–70 entries a day by the `changes-entry` gate, and each entry a copy of the diff, a test count, an `ISSUES.md` narrative and a `DECISIONS.md` argument. Only the lessons had no other home.

**Archived, not deleted.** The 24 files moved to `docs/changes-archive/<package>.md`. They are history-tier, like `docs/handoff-archive/`: they are never cited as behavior, `doc-audit` leaves their dead names alone, and nothing new is written there. This departs from the paper's *delete in the same commit as the extraction*. The archive is how the extraction runs package by package without a half-mined file sitting at a package root. A package's archive file is deleted once its lessons are filed.

- **Q1** — `fli done` asks nothing in its place. The diff is the record.
- **Q2** — a cli, toolbelt or config lesson goes in that package's own `CLAUDE.md`. A css lesson goes in `ui-hazards`.
- **Q3** — the developer half of release notes is git plus `fli changelog`.
- **Q4** — the long narratives on closed rows in `ISSUES.md` and `DECISIONS.md` get their own later pass.

**Amends** Invariant 17 (three files at a package root, `AGENTS.md` a permitted fourth), `PHILOSOPHY.md` § VII (the Register tier is `DECISIONS.md` and `ISSUES.md`, and history is git) and [`FJS-D163`](#fjs-d163)'s count. `frontierjs-vscode/CHANGELOG.md` is for the marketplace and stays.

**Silence.** A `CHANGES.md` that comes back at a package root is a `package-root-md` warning, because it is no longer in `STANDARD`. A live lesson dropped during extraction has no guard (`none`). The only guard is the per-entry pass, which reads the current source before it files anything.

*Lives in:* `packages/cli/core/done.js`, `packages/cli/core/checks.js` (`package-root-md`), `packages/cli/core/doc-audit.js` (`HISTORY`), `docs/changes-archive/`.

### <a id="fjs-d658"></a>2026-10-08 · `FJS-D658` — How `analytics:` reaches a static page — The build writes the vendor's own tag into every prerendered page's `<head>`, and the island entry resolves the provider so `track()` reaches it. A custom provider object is refused on that target.

Asked in chat while closing `FJS-2058`, which found `FJS-D608`'s *wire `sierra/analytics` into site-kit* had nothing to land on: a static page never loads `virtual:sierra`, the only place `initAnalytics` runs. **A** was picked over **B** (a small analytics module on every static page — `track()` everywhere, but a page with no island stops shipping zero JavaScript), **C** (refuse `analytics:` on `static` until `FJS-1539` gives the head a mechanism) and **D** (site-kit writes the tag, a second owner beside `sierra/analytics`, which `FJS-D608` ruled against).

**It is the edge test's second allow row.** `postbuild/inject-analytics.js` imports `analytics/tag.js`: `analytics:` is a battery key, and on this target the build is the only thing that runs. `tag.js` is the one description of what Plausible and GTM load; the runtime's `init` and the build's HTML both read it, which is how GTM's `gtm.js` start event, missing from the runtime before, reached both at once. Each prerendered page is a full load, so the vendor counts its own pageview and the router stays off the page. *Batteries vs. smallness* is the adjudication: the battery stays in sierra and costs a zero-JS page nothing.

### <a id="fjs-d653"></a>2026-10-08 · `FJS-D653` — What owns *is this file inside the root* — Keep both copies, with one vector set of URLs and verdicts that both packages' tests read (`FJS-D631`'s *vectors*).

### <a id="fjs-d648"></a>2026-10-08 · `FJS-D648` — What is the `content/settings/site.js` key that names `@kobami/ksite`, and what is the noun for what it names — `preset: '@kobami/ksite'`, and the noun is *Preset*: a package that contributes blocks, layouts, stylesheets and build plugins to a site-kit site.

### <a id="fjs-d627"></a>2026-10-07 · `FJS-D627` — Which surface owns a file two surfaces run — The side that runs it. The other surface gets its output through a service and never imports it by relative path.

### <a id="fjs-d626"></a>2026-10-07 · `FJS-D626` — Where does a Route live — `api/src/routes/`, and a file's path there is the URL it answers. Junction loads the folder the way it loads `*.service.ts`.

Asked in the app layout audit ([Where Code Lives](https://claude.ai/artifact/3dvt1QFJo4LCqXpfyYRsjP), row 4); the owner accepted the recommendation. Route is blessed (`FJS-D391`), but no folder was named for it, and five route groups in three apps used three spellings: calendly `api/src/routes/calendar-hook.ts`, transit `reports/routes.ts` and two siblings registered as plugins, and portal `core/search-stream.ts`. Each is a URL an outsider fixes, such as a vendor's webhook setting, a link in someone's inbox or an `EventSource` URL (`FJS-D13`), so reading the URL off the path suits them. *Paved road vs. the workaround*: three spellings in three apps is a measurement of a missing road.

**Path = URL keeps `routes/` one meaning.** `web/src/routes/` and `cli/src/routes/` already mean *the path is the address*. A folder where each file exports `register(app)` was the cheaper option, and it was rejected because it gives `routes/` a third meaning. A plugin that only mounts raw routes moves here.

README § Project Structure gains `routes/` when the loader is built (`FJS-1889`), not before, the way `FJS-D397` treated `cli/`. A warning for `app.get` or `app.post` outside `routes/` is in `app-layout` (`FJS-1888`).

### <a id="fjs-d625"></a>2026-10-07 · `FJS-D625` — How is an app's `src/` laid out — Kind first, area second. A file goes in the folder named for its kind, and an area is a subfolder inside that kind's folder: `domain/<area>/`, `components/<area>/`, `lib/<area>/`. There is no feature folder.

Asked in the app layout audit ([Where Code Lives](https://claude.ai/artifact/3dvt1QFJo4LCqXpfyYRsjP), rows 1, 2, 3, 7, 9 and 10); the owner accepted every row. Across eleven prototype apps and Basecamp, fifteen folders no document named had appeared under `api/` and `web/`, and about 35 modules sat loose in `web/src/`. README § Project Structure is the layout and this ruling is why.

- **No feature folder.** Loaders and checks find a file by its kind (`*.service.ts`, `*.job.ts`, `routes/`), so a route inside `share/` is invisible to a route check. A folder that cuts across kinds on purpose is a Slice, deferred by `FJS-D06` § 7, and an app-level one would settle that question by accident. Transit's `reports/`, `sends/`, `share/` and `sources/` split by kind.
- **`api/src/core/` sets up what the framework ships**: env, db, auth, gate, channels, mailer, conduit targets and the claim resolver. A plugin the app wrote goes in `api/src/plugins/` and is not autoloaded, because order matters and `app.ts` installs each one. Domain logic moves to `domain/`.
- **A helper in a loader's folder is private.** In `services/`, `jobs/` or `notifications/`, a file without the loaded suffix belongs to the files beside it. Once another folder imports it, it is domain logic and moves to `domain/`.
- **`web/src/lib/` holds every module that is not a route, resource or component.** The ecosystem's word for that spot; no framework word competes for it.
- **`web/src/stores/` holds state only the browser has**, a `watchProxy` that a component watches. A cache of server reads is not a store: it belongs to the Resource, and where the Resource cannot express it, that is a gap (`FJS-1891`). A split by kind (`state/`, `logic/`, `registrations/`) was rejected as five folders for about ten files. `stores/` is the one exception because the ecosystem names the folder and its test has two clear halves. It does not make *store* a framework noun: screen-local state stays unnamed (`FJS-D390`).
- **Every `.mesa` file that is not a route or resource goes in `components/`** (`FJS-D382`).

*Familiarity vs. precision*: `lib/` and `stores/` take the ecosystem's shape and words where the words fit. `app-layout` grades each folder rule as a warning (`FJS-1888`).

### <a id="fjs-d608"></a>2026-10-06 · `FJS-D608` — Which tooling gaps in `site-kit-parity.md` § 4 become framework owners — Wire every gap Sierra already owns (`defer-js`, `speculation`, `sierra/analytics`); fix the two filed as Sierra's (FJS-1539 head, FJS-1540 host function) in Sierra; start every gap with no owner (images, per-page JSON-LD, the lead fallback, animations) as site-kit code, and move one to Sierra when a consumer that is not a site-kit site needs it.

The paper's recommendation, taken as written: *batteries vs. smallness*: site-kit is the battery and stays severable, and a Sierra owner is earned by a second consumer, as *paved road vs. the workaround* measures a road. FJS-1539 and 1540 are already Sierra's rows, so C would build a second owner beside a filed one (Invariant 4).

The key's name, and the noun for what it names, go through `decision-rules` before code.

Every block stays in `@kobami/ksite` until a second engine wants it), **C** (site-kit is ksite renamed: the whole engine moves and ksite is content only).

### <a id="fjs-d601"></a>2026-10-06 · `FJS-D601` — Where does the model call live — The catalog, the ladder's checks and the emitter to `.lite` are one module with no model in it, and whatever runs the model calls that module — a skill for a developer, the prompt-to-app builder for anyone else. `fli` never holds a key.

### <a id="fjs-d593"></a>2026-10-06 · `FJS-D593` — What runtime is `fli` — `fli` runs under bun; `Bun.$` is the shell. The three shebangs flip, a missing bun is refused by name, and `create-frontier` (reached through `npm create`, so still node) spawns `bun` rather than `process.execPath`.

### <a id="fjs-d598"></a>2026-10-05 · `FJS-D598` — `fli deploy`'s edge is Caddy, the same host service a fleet machine runs (`FJS-D564`), with routes written into Outpost's `ingress` server through the admin API. nginx is gone from ring 0. The deploy target is an ssh destination, and an alias in `~/.ssh/config` is a whole one.

Asked by the owner while planning how to put Basecamp on a remote server from a laptop: keep `_steps-setup/05-nginx`, or swap it for Caddy to match the fleet. **Caddy all the way** was picked. **The reason is a collision, not tidiness.** Ring 0 put nginx on :80/:443, and enrollment puts Caddy there. So the box Basecamp is installed on could never also be enrolled as a fleet machine.

**What it is.** `deploy:setup` installs Caddy as the `caddy-api` unit (`--resume`, no Caddyfile), with the install line `enrollment.ts` uses. `05-caddy` reads Caddy's whole config and merges this app's routes in (`core/edge.js` § `applyEdge`). It writes the result back with `If-Match`, so a write Outpost made in between is a 412 and a re-read, not a lost route. Route ids start `fli-` and never meet Outpost's `fjs-`. A hostname another route names is refused, as `ingress.js` already refuses one. Certificates are Caddy's, so `deploy.<side>.ssl` is refused by name and `06-ssl` is deleted. A web release is the symlink swap alone, because Caddy reads the root per request. The pause guard is the first handler of every route: a `file` matcher on `.fli/paused`, serving the page with `status_code: 503`, and found by its `@id`. Each route writes its own access log, which Caddy rolls. Because the redirect is Caddy's own and precedes every route, a plain-http caller of a paused app gets a 301 and then the 503.

**The second half, the same day.** `--server` is a namespace-wide flag on `deploy:`. It takes an alias or `user@host` and replaces every server and user the block names, per target and per side (`_module.md` § `deployConfFor`, the one reader). `user` has no default. With none stated, ssh is handed the bare name, so the alias's User, Port, IdentityFile and ProxyJump apply. Before this, `deploy@` was prefixed and silently overrode the alias's User. The scaffold's `your-server.com` is refused, because it is a real domain.

**Adjudication**: *preservation vs. evolution*. nginx goes, with no alias and no flag to keep it. **§ V's ninth question**: *fli's routes load in a real Caddy beside Outpost's, a stale write is refused, and a paused app answers 503 while the Outpost app beside it answers 200* — `pauseEdgeCycle` in CI's `deploy` phase. Measured: dropping `status_code` reds it at *a paused app answers 200*. **Not enforced**: the two copies of the Caddy install line (`01-check-deps.md`, `providers/compute/enrollment.ts`) agree only by a pointer comment. **Late**: the nine were answered after the code was written, and say so.

### <a id="fjs-d589"></a>2026-10-05 · `FJS-D589` — The committed workspace pages hold the structure only. The three registers and the file counts are on `fli ws:atlas --live`, which is never committed.

Asked while reading a red `snapshots` phase in `fli gui`. **Structure only** was picked over **keeping both pages as they were** and over **committing the report and building the deck on demand**. The two pages are one model read two ways (`FJS-D223`), so a stale model staled both, and what staled it was nearly always a register: filing one row in `ISSUES.md` moved the open count, a severity table and the plate heat, and a new file anywhere moved a tracked-file count. Both pages were red on every branch, and the change `--check` exists to surface (a new command, drive, CI phase, snapshot or package) arrived under a diff of counts nobody read. Committing one page would halve that noise and keep its cause.

**`structureOf(model)` in `core/repo-map.js` is the line.** It returns the model with `issues`, `decisions` and `ideas` set to null and every package's `files` and subsystem counts set to null. `fli ws:atlas` renders it for both committed pages. `collect()` stays the one reader and still reads all of it, so `--json` carries the whole model and `--live` renders it. The renderers already omitted an absent source, so the deck's hub, plate heat, ⌘K rows and dossier issue lists appear on the live deck and nowhere committed. **The report drops its register section outright** rather than gaining a live edition. It is the runbook (*what do I run and where*), the registers are not runbook material, and a live report would need a second header path to avoid naming a generator.

No adjudication beyond § IV *preservation vs. evolution*: nobody reads a committed page for register state, since `fli next`, the GUI and the files themselves answer it, and nothing here has shipped.

*Decision rules.* Origin: fewer — the pages stop restating three registers. Concept: none added; `--live` already meant *varies between commits, never committed*. Complexity: the design's — a byte-compared page restating append-only files. Predictability: raised — these pages now move when their structure does, as `ddl` moves when the schema does. Derived: the projection is a function of the one model. Owner: `structureOf`, beside `collect()`. Boundary: exported and tested. Failure: a reader who wants the registers runs `--live`; nothing is lost. Silence: *a register edit or a new file leaves both committed pages byte-identical* — `test/repo-map.test.js`, which also asserts the model did change, so it cannot pass with nothing collected.

### <a id="fjs-d567"></a>2026-09-30 · `FJS-D567` — An App running on no online machine KEEPS its ingress record, pointing where it last ran, and the drift read names it red. The DNS is never emptied to follow a fleet that went down.

Asked in `FJS-1614`, the push that follows a machine leaving `online`. **Keep** was picked over **delete the record**. Deleting turns *the machine is down* into *the name does not exist*, which resolvers cache as a negative answer, so the hostname stays dark after the machine returns, until a push runs and the negative TTL lapses. Keeping costs nothing, since traffic to a dead machine fails either way, and the hostname answers again the moment the machine does. This is Route 53's rule: when every health-checked record fails, it answers them all rather than none.

No adjudication in tension: keeping dominates. A record naming a dead machine is already the outage, and an absent record is the outage plus a slower recovery. **§ V's ninth question**: *an App with no online machine is red on `/dns/` and its record is still there.* `edge.test.ts` asserts both: the push refuses as not-yet and writes nothing, and `records` answers the App in `stale` with `down: true`. **Enforced.** Where it lives: `push` and `records` in `packages/basecamp/api/src/services/edge/edge.service.ts`.

### <a id="fjs-d565"></a>2026-09-30 · `FJS-D565` — Once Caddy fronts a machine, a container's published port binds to `127.0.0.1`. That change goes in with the first route push and not before it.

Asked in [`IDEAS/fleet-ingress.md`](IDEAS/fleet-ingress.md) D7. **A loopback bind** was picked over **leaving `-p port:containerPort` on every interface**, which answers the internet over plain HTTP around Caddy and its TLS. The recommendation, taken as written. The timing is part of the ruling: binding loopback before a route exists leaves the app unreachable.

The 8181 static origin stays its own upstream and its own origin (`FJS-D345`). Caddy fronts it by host like any other route. **Adjudication in tension** (§ IV): *ergonomics vs. strictness*, resolved by cost. A reachable raw port quietly undoes every certificate this paper delivers. **§ V's ninth question**: *an app answers only through Caddy.* `packages/outpost/test/verify-docker.mjs` asserts that the published port refuses a connection from off the machine (`ingress.portRefusesOffLoopback`, which fails with the all-interfaces bind put back). **Enforced.** The bind is per app, keyed on the `/deploy` naming `hosts`: an app with no hostname keeps its port on every interface, which is this ruling's *not before* applied app by app. Where it lives: `packages/outpost/src/docker.js`. **Amended by [`FJS-D930`](#fjs-d930)**: the no-hostname clause is gone — every published port binds loopback, and raw-port exposure is a declaration on `App`.

### <a id="fjs-d564"></a>2026-09-30 · `FJS-D564` — Caddy runs on every fleet machine as a host service. Outpost installs it at enrollment and owns its configuration through Caddy's admin API on `localhost:2019`: it pushes a route (hostname → upstream) on deploy and removes it on teardown.

Asked in [`IDEAS/fleet-ingress.md`](IDEAS/fleet-ingress.md) D1. **A: installed by enrollment** (`installScript()` in `providers/compute/enrollment.ts`) was picked over **B: a container Outpost manages**. B puts a layer between Outpost and the one process it must configure, and a Docker restart takes the ingress down with it. The recommendation, taken as written. There is no config template and no reload, which is the part of CapRover's nginx customization this replaces. Kamal 2's `kamal-proxy` is the nearest prior shape.

**The routes' origin is basecamp's `Domain` and `AppServer` rows; Caddy's live config is derived from them.** Phase 1 owed an answer to one question: what restores the routes when Caddy restarts on its own. **Answered in the build: Caddy's `--resume`** — the deb's `caddy-api` unit, which reloads the config its admin API last autosaved — over Outpost pushing the full set when it starts, which would need Outpost to keep a copy of routes it otherwise never holds. No adjudication in tension. **§ V's ninth question**: *a deployed app answers over HTTPS by its hostname.* `verify-docker.mjs` asserts it against a real Caddy (`ingress.answersOverHttpsByName`), and again after `docker restart` of Caddy (`ingress.survivesACaddyRestart`, which fails with `--resume` removed). **Enforced.** Where it lives: `packages/outpost/` and `providers/compute/enrollment.ts`.

Asked in [`IDEAS/cloudflare-edge.md`](IDEAS/cloudflare-edge.md) D6. **Per record, as stated** was picked over **a global flag**, which would be a second origin for a value `Domain.proxied` already holds (default `false`, the external-dns default). The recommendation, taken as written.

No adjudication in tension. **§ V's ninth question**: *the proxied bit in Cloudflare matches the row.* A record flipped by hand in Cloudflare's dashboard is drift, reported by the drift read once it carries that kind. Until then **unenforced**. What a flip does to the origin certificate is `IDEAS/fleet-ingress.md` D4, not this ruling. Where it lives: `Domain.proxied` in `packages/basecamp/db/schema.lite`.

### <a id="fjs-d562"></a>2026-09-30 · `FJS-D562` — `EdgeConnector`'s writes take libdns's shape: `appendRecords` · `setRecords` · `deleteRecords` beside the existing `records` read. `setRecords` makes each given (name, type) set match its input and touches nothing else. The planned per-record `upsertRecord` / `deleteRecord` are not built.

Asked in [`IDEAS/cloudflare-edge.md`](IDEAS/cloudflare-edge.md) D5. **libdns's shape** (the interface Caddy's DNS providers share) was picked over **a per-record upsert and delete**, which makes a record with several values (two A records at one name) a loop in the service, and which carried legacy's bug of matching the first record by type and name. The recommendation, taken as written. libdns's `getRecords` is the connector's existing `records` read, which keeps its name.

**The connector enforces `FJS-D560`'s mark, because the mark is the connector's.** `setRecords` and `deleteRecords` refuse to change a set that holds an unmarked record, so no caller can skip the check by forgetting it. **Adjudication in tension** (§ IV): *familiarity vs. precision*. The shape and the words are stolen whole because both fit. **§ V's ninth question**: *a write touches only the (name, type) sets it names, and never an unmarked record.* **Enforced** by `api/test/edge.test.ts` § *the writes*, against the Cloudflare stand-in (`providers/edge/cloudflare-sink.ts`): an unmarked MX beside a set CNAME survives, a set or delete naming a foreign set is refused with no request sent, and a batch the vendor refuses applies none of itself. Where it lives: `packages/basecamp/api/src/providers/edge/index.ts`.

### <a id="fjs-d561"></a>2026-09-30 · `FJS-D561` — A `Domain` is a CNAME to its App's INGRESS RECORD, and basecamp owns both. There is one ingress record per App, named from the App's id in the workspace's ingress zone, holding the `ipAddress` of every server with a running placement. The ingress zone is a typed pair of columns on `Workspace`, not a key in `settings`.

Asked in [`IDEAS/cloudflare-edge.md`](IDEAS/cloudflare-edge.md) D4. **A CNAME to an ingress record** was picked over **an A record per placement IP on every `Domain`**. Per-placement A records are round-robin DNS with no health check, and every placement change would rewrite every domain on the app. The recommendation, taken as written. This is the consensus shape: external-dns publishes an ingress address and never a pod IP, and Vercel, Render and Fly hand the customer a CNAME. Cloudflare flattens a CNAME at the apex, so an apex `Domain` needs nothing extra.

**Per App, not per server or group.** The paper offered "per server or group". A CNAME names ONE target, so a per-server record serves only a single-server app. Basecamp has no group noun, and this ruling does not coin one. `AppServer` already answers *where does this app run*, so the ingress record is derived from it and never edited by hand. **The name comes from the App's id rather than its name**, so a rename rewrites nothing. That matters for a customer whose zone basecamp cannot reach, who types the CNAME by hand.

**The cost is named**: across two servers this is still round-robin with no health check. It sits in one record instead of every domain, so a dead placement is one rewrite. **It is inert until `IDEAS/fleet-ingress.md` Phase 1 ships.** A CNAME to a machine that cannot route by Host header reaches nothing, so the build waits on Caddy.

No adjudication in tension. **§ V's ninth question**: *the ingress record's addresses are the running placements' addresses.* **Enforced**: `edge.records` reports a mismatch as `stale`, `api/test/edge.test.ts` § *sync* grades it, and `verify:dns` shows one after a release moves machines and gone after a sync. With no ingress zone set, `sync` refuses with a 409 saying so. **A running placement had no producer** — `AppServer.status` was written `unknown` and never moved, so the ruling named nothing. Heard as code against doctrine and the code was fixed: the deploy job marks the placement a release landed on `running` (`markRunning`), and `servingAddresses` in `core/runtime.ts` is the one read of it — `running` and on an `online` server, the executor's rule. Where it lives: `Workspace`, `Domain` and `AppServer` in `packages/basecamp/db/schema.lite`.

### <a id="fjs-d560"></a>2026-09-30 · `FJS-D560` — `Domain` rows are intent and basecamp pushes them to the edge. Every record basecamp writes carries a MARK, and basecamp changes only marked records. An unmarked record at a `Domain`'s name is a conflict, refused and reported; an admin's explicit `adopt(domainId)` is the one way to take it over.

Asked in [`IDEAS/cloudflare-edge.md`](IDEAS/cloudflare-edge.md) D3, together with its owed sub-question. **Intent plus a mark** was picked over **owning the whole zone**, which deletes a customer's MX and SendGrid records, and over **read-only**, which leaves `Domain` a note nobody acts on. For an unmarked record at a `Domain`'s name, **refuse** was picked over **adopt silently** (octoDNS). This matches external-dns and Cloudflare Tunnel. Both recommendations, taken as written.

On Cloudflare the mark is the per-record `comment`, `basecamp:domain:<id>`. It exists on every plan, and the list call filters on `comment.startswith`, so *basecamp's records* is one query. Tags are Pro and up. A vendor with no comment field falls back to a TXT registry, so **the spelling of the mark is the connector's, never the service's**. This is the way compute marks a machine it made, so no new noun is coined. No mode switch is added. If one is ever argued for, it uses external-dns's names: `sync` · `upsert-only` · `create-only`.

**Adjudication in tension** (§ IV): *ergonomics vs. strictness*, resolved by what a mistake destroys. Overwriting an unmarked record can take down a customer's mail, so it is a refusal and not a warning. **§ V's ninth question**: *basecamp never changes a record it did not mark.* `FJS-D562` puts the refusal in the connector, and its stand-in test is the artefact. Deleting the comment by hand in Cloudflare turns the record into a conflict, which drift then shows. Where it lives: `packages/basecamp/api/src/providers/edge/` and `services/edge/edge.service.ts`.

Asked in [`IDEAS/cloudflare-edge.md`](IDEAS/cloudflare-edge.md) D2. **Adding it with a check** was picked over **a compute-only enum for `Server`**, which restates three values and makes two vendor lists to keep in step. The recommendation, taken as written.

Its cost is named rather than hidden: the next vendor that sells no machines has to join `Server`'s check, and a forgotten one is silent. Where it lives: `enum ProviderKind` and `model Server` in `packages/basecamp/db/schema.lite`.

### <a id="fjs-d558"></a>2026-09-30 · `FJS-D558` — A Cloudflare token is a WORKSPACE account, the compute pattern: a `Secret` of kind `provider_key` with `providerKind: cloudflare`, registered as the conduit target `provider:cloudflare:<secretId>`. `edge` leaves the install-wide `BasecampProviders` container.

Asked in [`IDEAS/cloudflare-edge.md`](IDEAS/cloudflare-edge.md) D1. **Per workspace** was picked over **one install-wide `providers.edge.api_token`**, which is `FJS-1020` again: whichever workspace registered last has its token used for everyone. The recommendation, taken as written.

Connect asks for an account-owned token (`cfat_`), which outlives the person who minted it. One target per account also covers maid.tech's token per client with no change to conduit. Where it lives: `packages/basecamp/api/src/providers/edge/` and `providers/compute/accounts.ts`.

### <a id="fjs-d557"></a>2026-09-30 · `FJS-D557` — How the Basecamp → Outpost command channel is encrypted — Pin a self-signed certificate at enrollment. The machine makes it, sends its PEM in the enroll exchange, `Server.outpostCert` keeps it, and the conduit target carries it as `pinned_cert`. A machine with no pin gets no target, and a target with no pin is no executor.

Asked in [`IDEAS/fleet-ingress.md`](IDEAS/fleet-ingress.md) D2, for `FJS-1603`. **B** was picked over **A** (Caddy fronts 8180 with an ACME certificate for the machine's own name. This needs a hostname per machine and makes the edge adapter a precondition for a secure deploy) and **C** (seal the secret values to a machine key. Headers, logs and every other body stay in the clear).

The paper's recommendation, taken as written. Enrollment is already the one trusted moment, a machine may have only an IP, and B depends on nothing else in the paper. Four smaller calls came with it, all as recommended:

- **Conduit owns the pin** (Invariant 4). `TargetDescriptor.pinned_cert` is refused at register() unless the protocol is `http` and the address is `https`, and the SQLite store round-trips it.
- **Only enrollment sets the pin.** A heartbeat that reports a non-`https` URL, or comes from a row with no certificate, registers nothing and takes away any target already held. Re-enrolling is how a pin changes.
- **Dev takes the same path.** `outpost-dev.ts` makes its own certificate and enrolls with it, with no loopback exemption on the command port.
- **`BASECAMP_URL` must be `https`, loopback aside.** The install script refuses any other, and so do `cloudInit` and `installCommand`. The enroll answer carries the machine's key.

**The mechanism is not the one the paper named.** In Bun 1.4.2 a `checkServerIdentity` callback never runs under `rejectUnauthorized: false`, so a fingerprint callback alone accepts every certificate. The pin is `tls: { ca: <pem> }`, which in Bun replaces the public roots rather than adding to them. A fingerprint callback beside it stands in for the hostname check, so the certificate names no address. **Adjudication in tension** (§ IV): *ergonomics vs. strictness*, for dev. It is strict because an exemption for loopback is the one path a downgrade could use. **§ V's ninth question**: *a command reaches only the machine that enrolled, and never in the clear.* `packages/conduit/conduit.test.ts` § pinned_cert shows the pinned server reached, another certificate refused, and the unpinned control refused. `api/test/compute.test.ts` shows the target pinned and then removed when the machine reports `http`. `verify:outpost` sends a release through the pinned target to a real Outpost, before and after re-enrolling. `verify-docker.mjs` asserts plain HTTP gets no answer on 8180. **Unenforced**: nothing would notice a future raw `fetch` to an Outpost that goes around conduit.
