### <a id="fjs-d1127"></a>2026-10-16 · `FJS-D1127` — Q4 — The third ingress: a subscription the app dials and holds open (Mattermost's WebSocket). Whose is it — A Target of kind `broker` (`FJS-D235`). The paper first refused this as *where we publish*; `transports/broker.ts` says the opposite — *dial out, then receive; nothing is sent over it* — and already owns the dial, an unbounded reconnect, `health()` for readiness and a handler per frame. What it lacks is Mattermost's framing: it reads `{id, type: 'message', body}` and acks, where Mattermost sends `authentication_challenge` after open and then `{event, data, broadcast, seq}` with no ack. So the connector supplies the frame codec and the post-open handshake, and each frame reaches `conduit.accept()` → Dialect → Receiver `apply` → litestone as system.

Asked in [`IDEAS/mirror-apps.md`](IDEAS/mirror-apps.md) § Open questions. **A** was picked over **B** (a Receiver with a transport other than HTTP: the app dials, the Dialect still verifies and parses each frame. The dial loop would have no owner, and would re-grow what `broker.ts` has), **C** (a long-running job (`app.jobs`) holds the socket and hands each frame to `conduit.receive()`. 0.4 proved caravan can — but it is a second place holding a socket open, beside the one conduit already keeps).

The paper's recommendation, taken as written: one owner for every socket the app holds open, and caravan appears only where a one-shot belongs: the REST backfill after a reconnect gap, dispatched `unique`.

The nine, answered before the build. Origin: one — `transports/broker.ts` is the dial, and the framing moves from a constant in it to a value the connector supplies. Concept: none — a Mattermost socket is a `broker` target, the kind `FJS-D235` already named; the paper's second noun for Q4 is not spent. Complexity: the problem's — a Provider that pushes over a socket it defines the frames of. Predictability: a held socket is every held socket; `health()` reads the same for a Kafka bridge and for Mattermost. Derived: the frame codec from the connector, the handshake from the credential, the dedupe key from the frame's `seq` through the Dialect. Owner, and it existed: conduit's broker transport, which the paper's first reading of `FJS-D235` missed — *where we publish* was the opposite of what the file says, found by reading the file. Boundary: typed — a codec answers a frame or `null`, a handshake runs after `open` and before the first frame is believed. Failure: an unbounded reconnect, as today, with `health().connected` the half an operator reads; a frame the codec refuses is dropped and counted, never buffered. Silence: `health()` under `app.registerReadiness`; what fails when the sync stops is `last_received_at` against what Mattermost says it sent, and until Phase 2.3's test it is `none`. Caravan's 0.4 probe stands for the one-shot backfill, dispatched `unique`, never for the socket.

### <a id="fjs-d1089"></a>2026-10-16 · `FJS-D1089` — How does a row name a self-hosted counterparty — its address and its token, sometimes on a private network — without a stored credential going where a stranger says — Two halves, neither a new option. *The token is the row's own*: `address_from: 'request'` admits `bearer`, `api_key` and `signed` when `auth.per_caller: true`, and such a send states `grant`, refused by name (`invalid_request`, nothing sent) without it — the credential and the address are read off the same row, so the writer of the address holds the token, and `withCache` keyed on the grant keeps two rows in one tenant from sharing one cached token (`FJS-2232` per row). The register refusal stays for a process credential. *A private address is never a row's*: the public grade stays before every attempt, so a self-hosted instance behind a public name (the common case) is reached and one on a LAN or a tailnet is the operator's to declare as a fixed-address target per install, or waits for Outpost vantage, as `FJS-D1018` ruled. `allowPrivate` stays a test receiver's switch. Cost: a per-row LAN instance has no spelling until vantage; a `getFor` that ignores `grant` answers a tenant's token for every row's address, which conduit cannot see and the hazard names.

Asked in [`IDEAS/owed-rulings.md`](IDEAS/owed-rulings.md) § Open questions. **A** was picked over **B** (A's credential half, plus an operator allow-list of private origins on the target, `destinations.origins: ['http://plausible.lan:8000']`: a row address on a listed origin is admitted ungraded, every other private address refused. Cost: the address is written twice (row and config) and a new client instance is a redeploy; it is `FJS-D1018`'s rejected **B**/**C** with per-origin granularity, and an allowed name that re-resolves somewhere worse is not caught), **C** (grade a fixed address too: `put()` runs `assertPublicUrl` on every `http` address unless `destinations.allowPrivate`, so a target registered per row is caught. Cost: every localhost dev target, `unix` socket and LAN PBX needs the flag, the operator's declaration is graded like a stranger's, and conduit cannot tell a `put()` at boot from env from one at runtime from a row, so the hole closes only by closing the legitimate case with it), **D** (rule the status quo: a fixed-address target per row is the spelling, documented. Rejected by the row itself — it is the hole).

The paper's recommendation, taken as written: the credential half is derived from `FJS-D848`'s seam rather than restated (the grant is already *which login*, and a row is a login), and the address half is `FJS-D1018`'s own answer applied to conduit, so the two rulings say one thing: a row names where, public only, and the credential that goes there is the row's own. Six months out it is one sentence; B is two places for one address, C grades the operator. Adjudications: *ergonomics vs. strictness* — the register refusal stays where the cost is a token leaving to a stranger's address and lifts exactly where the row owns the token; *paved road vs. the workaround* — the per-row fixed target was the workaround, and A is the road it measured. Artefact: the suite's case where two rows in one tenant each land their own token at their own address, and a send with no grant sends nothing; the `getFor`-ignores-`grant` hazard is `none`, written as such.

Both picks through the question tool, the recommended ones: A, and *refuse a send with no grant* over *allow it and leave the keying to the resolver*. The nine, answered before the code. **Origin:** none new — whose credential is `who.grant` (`FJS-D848`), and which address is reachable is `assertPublicUrl` (`FJS-1578`). **Concept:** no noun and no option; `per_caller` and `grant` exist. **Complexity:** the problem's — a row holds an address and a token, and the two must have one writer. **Predictability:** a per-caller target spends the caller's credential whether its address is fixed or per send, and a request-addressed target grades every address the same way. **Derived:** the credential is derived from the send's grant rather than declared on the target. **Owner:** `assertRequestAddressed` admits, `secretFor` resolves, `assertPublicUrl` grades, and the grant refusal sits in `attempt()` beside the address grade — one place grades a request-addressed send. **Boundary:** `TargetAuth.per_caller` and `ConduitRequest.grant`, typed; two refusals by name. **Failure:** a process credential beside `address_from` is still a `put()` throw; a missing grant is `invalid_request`, non-retryable, nothing sent; a private address is refused as before. **Silence:** the suite holds two rows in one tenant landing their own tokens at their own addresses, and a send with no grant sending nothing (`conduit.test.ts` § FJS-1667); a `getFor` that ignores `grant` is `none`. Tier: Register here; Map in conduit's `README.md`, `CLAUDE.md` and `types.ts`. Closes `FJS-2923`.

*Lives in:* `packages/conduit/src/conduit.ts` (`assertRequestAddressed`) · `packages/conduit/src/transports/http.ts` (`attempt`, the grant refusal) · `packages/conduit/src/types.ts` (`address_from`, `destinations`) · `packages/conduit/conduit.test.ts` § with the row's own credential.

### <a id="fjs-d1087"></a>2026-10-15 · `FJS-D1087` — Junction receives its own webhook scheme through a SUBSCRIPTION: the row this app holds to verify a far app's deliveries, at `POST {apiPrefix}/webhooks/subscriptions/{id}`, with one `receive` the app writes; the record-unapplied → receive → mark order is restated in junction beside conduit's `accept()`.

Asked in [`IDEAS/inbound-integrations.md`](IDEAS/inbound-integrations.md) § Order step 3 (*A, in junction*), through the question tool; both picks were the recommended ones. **The noun** — *subscription* over *no word* (`accept()` / `accepted()`, honoring the paper's *takes no noun* literally and reading oddly) and *inbound* (an adjective as a noun). A subscriber is the far side of our registration (`FJS-D193`); a subscription is our side of theirs, and the two sentences teach each other. Amends the paper's § The noun, which said junction's half takes none: it takes this one, and the register gains no row for it, because it is the webhooks plugin's own word the way *registration* is. **The order** — junction's own ~40 lines over one fixed dialect, over lifting conduit's `accept()` into junction and having conduit import it, which would end `receive.ts` being junction-free to save a restatement.

The nine, answered after the build. It is one new origin, named: the applied-not-seen order (`FJS-1805`) is written in `conduit/src/receive.ts` and in `junction/src/plugins/webhooks/index.ts`, and what keeps them from drifting is that verify, rotation (`verifyRequest({ secrets })`) and the nonce memory are toolbelt's, the outcome words (`applied · ignored · parked · duplicate`) and the three wire answers (`200 { received, outcome }`, `401 { error: 'not verified' }`, `500 { error: 'not applied' }`) are the same on both, and each suite holds the throw-once-then-retry case. One word added. The complexity is the problem's — Graph calls the row a subscription, Svix an endpoint secret — and nothing is added past the row, one route and one handler. Predictable: the route answers what conduit's does, the row lives in the webhook store beside the registrations, the path is fixed like the other eight. Derived, not restated: `path` is read from `apiPrefix` the way `app.get` reads it, the secret is minted on this side so the row is whole before anything is registered anywhere, and the dedupe key is the body's `id` — the SIGNED one, since `X-Webhook-Id` is outside the canonical string. One owner, and it already existed: the plugin that signs the scheme reads it. The boundary is `ReceiveHandler` → `ReceiveOutcome`; a `receive` answering any other word is a 500 by name. Failure is proportional: a forgery, a stale clock, a replayed nonce and an unknown id are one 401 sentence with the reason in the log and never the body; a throw leaves the receipt unapplied and answers 500 so the sender's retry gets a clean run; a verified body that is not the envelope is 200 ignored, because a 4xx retries for a day; with no `receive` the route is not mounted, so a subscription with nothing behind it is a 404 and not a 500 per delivery. What says so: `junction/test/webhooks.test.ts` § receiving, eleven cases, one of them a second junction app delivering over a real socket. Unenforced: a custom `IWebhookStore` lacking the seven receiving methods compiles only through `as never`.

Adjudications: batteries vs. smallness — the receiving end rides inside the webhooks battery, not a package; paved road vs. the workaround — the README's *verify by hand with `verifyRequest`* block was the workaround and is gone. Tier: Register here; Map in junction's `README.md` § Webhooks, `CLAUDE.md` and `docs/internals.md`. Not built: management routes and REPL commands for subscriptions, and a rotation verb — `secrets` is a list so a rotation is two valid keys, but nothing yet turns one. Resilience does not cross and the route mints no principal (`FJS-D177`); a counterparty becoming a caller stays `createApp({ credentials })` (`FJS-D475`). Closes `IDEAS/inbound-integrations.md` § Order.

### <a id="fjs-d1075"></a>2026-10-15 · `FJS-D1075` — A resolver's answer says when it expires: `get()` and `getFor()` answer `string | { value, expires_at }`, and `withCache` holds an answer until its `expires_at` or the cache's `ttl_ms`, whichever is first.

Asked in [`IDEAS/third-party-credentials.md`](IDEAS/third-party-credentials.md) § Open questions (*what does the resolver return once expiry matters*), through the question tool. Picked over the paper's **A** (the per-caller interface alone — 3CX and `conduit-oidc` are both client-credentials on `get()`, measured), **B** (a `refresh()` on the object — minting into conduit, where auth mints and conduit spends), and an object on every answer (fifteen resolvers and three built-ins change for one optional field an env var never has).

The TTL was the restatement. `withCache(mint, { ttl_ms: FCM_TOKEN_TTL_MS })` is a hand copy of the provider's lifetime: 3CX ships `expires_in` as 3600 or 60 depending on build and the reference guessed the unit, and `conduit-oidc` measured a one-second token handed out at 1.2s. Five callers — maidtech's Jobber, serpgrid's Google, ELA's Microsoft Graph and 3CX, `conduit-oidc` — each hand-built an expiry check, a refused set and an in-flight map beside `withCache`, because the cache could not see the expiry; all three are the cache's once it can. A past `expires_at` is used for the send that asked and not kept; a non-finite one is `auth_failed` by name, never read as forever. `valueOf()` is the one place either shape becomes a string.

What stays the app's: the cross-process refresh lock — a compare-and-set on the app's own row, as maidtech and ELA write it, since conduit has no row — and marking a grant lost. Deferred, each with its trigger: an `oauth` `TargetAuth` kind until the scope derivation (§ Sequencing step 4; `FJS-D891` refuses a variant per scheme), a `reconnect_required` error kind until a caller branches on it rather than reading the row (a resolver that throws already puts its words on `auth_failed`, `FJS-2723`), a skew before expiry until a vendor's quota counts the refused call (the 401 remints and replays once). Amends `FJS-D891`'s clause *the `withCache` TTL over a `get()` that mints is its expiry*: the answer carries the number, and `ttl_ms: Infinity` says the cache defers to it. Closes `FJS-2245`.

*Lives in:* `packages/conduit/src/types.ts` (`Material`) · `packages/conduit/src/credentials.ts` (`valueOf`, `withCache`) · `packages/conduit/src/transports/base.ts` · `packages/conduit/src/receive.ts` · `packages/conduit/conduit.test.ts` § credential resolvers.

### <a id="fjs-d899"></a>2026-10-15 · `FJS-D899` — What a conduit Receiver holds, and whose each field is — Split by owner: a connector exports the **Dialect** (`verify · parse · dedupeKey`, pure functions of a delivery and a credential, the clock passed in), the app declares the **Receiver** (`provider · path · dialect · credential · owner · apply`), and conduit owns the route, the order (credential → verify → parse → owner → receipt → apply → mark) and what a duplicate means: an APPLIED receipt, never a seen one. Receipts live in conduit's own store beside its targets. A handshake, a batched delivery and a subscription's lifecycle events stay out until a second app asks.

Asked in [`IDEAS/owed-rulings.md`](IDEAS/owed-rulings.md) § Open questions, found fixing `FJS-1804`. **C** was picked over **A** (one record carrying all seven steps, written by the connector — which puts the app's tenancy and domain into a vendor package) and **B** (`FJS-D681`'s four fields, `path · verify · window · dedupe`, with the rest left to the app — which the measured dialects do not fit, Quo's key being a row the path names and Standard Webhooks' dedupe key a header, and which leaves the record-then-apply order `FJS-1805` found wrong to every app). A second pick, through the question tool: the receipt row lives in conduit's store (`conduit_receipts`, the memory store's map) rather than in a litestone model the app declares, so an app with no litestone receives too and no schema moves; the cost is that a receipt is not in the audit trail or Studio.

The paper's recommendation, taken as written: each field lands with the party that knows it — a vendor knows its signature, only the app knows its tenants — and conduit owns the one thing nine hand-built receivers got wrong or copied. `credential` is a ref through the installed `CredentialResolver` for the ordinary one-key relationship, or a function choosing the key for one delivery before the body is believed. `owner` is optional and found AFTER verify. `apply` answers `applied`, `ignored` or `parked`; the first two mark the receipt and the third leaves it for a retry. A refusal is one sentence, 401, with the reason in the log and never the body. Resilience does not cross and a receiver never mints a principal (`FJS-D177`); a partner signing with FrontierJS's own scheme and becoming a caller stays junction's door (`FJS-D475`). Amends `FJS-D681`'s record text: *path, signature check, freshness window, dedupe key* is the dialect's half plus the path. Where it lives: `packages/conduit/src/receive.ts`, `receive.test.ts`, `example/api/src/app.ts`'s two receivers, `verify:pay` and `verify:stripe`.

### <a id="fjs-d949"></a>2026-10-13 · `FJS-D949` — What does 1.0 mean here — The numbers are wrong: litestone and auth move to the train's `0.x`, their `1.x` releases are deprecated on npm, and 1.0 is defined as the first release whose surface diff is graded.

Asked in [`IDEAS/version-compatibility.md`](IDEAS/version-compatibility.md) § Open questions. **A** was picked over **B** (The description is wrong for those two: litestone and auth are stable and keep `1.x`, and the README says which packages are pre-alpha), **C** (1.0 means nothing beyond *published*, stated in each README).

The paper's recommendation, taken as written: the repo is pre-alpha and nothing has a compatibility promise, so a `1.x` on npm promises something nobody is keeping. Pre-alpha nobody depends on the number, so the renumbering is free, and tying 1.0 to a graded diff gives the number something that checks it. B splits one framework's maturity by package, and C leaves a semver reader misled.

### <a id="fjs-d948"></a>2026-10-13 · `FJS-D948` — Does this workspace release as one train or twenty packages — One train: one version for every published package, bumped in lockstep, and every internal peer pinned to the train's number.

Asked in [`IDEAS/version-compatibility.md`](IDEAS/version-compatibility.md) § Open questions. **A** was picked over **B** (Twenty packages: independent semver, each bump graded by a diff of `exports.snapshot.md` (`fli ws:compat`)).

The paper's recommendation, taken as written: then B for a package once a third party depends on it alone. A matrix of size one needs nothing built, and pre-alpha nobody outside depends on any single number. B builds the matrix before anyone needs it.

### <a id="fjs-d941"></a>2026-10-13 · `FJS-D941` — A signer may name which answers are its scheme's own credential refusal, and conduit forgets and replays once on them as on a 401.

APNs refuses an expired provider token with a 403 whose body names it. Conduit
reads every 403 as the credential accepted, which must stay true for S3's
`AccessDenied` and a Cloudflare 403. So the stale token stayed cached and every
push failed until its TTL ran out (`FJS-2721`). The owner picked **a predicate
on the signer** over **`refusal: ['forbidden']`**, which would remint on every
403 and spend Apple's rate-limited token updates on `TopicDisallowed` too, and
over **a declarative body match in the descriptor**, which would be a
substring grammar inside JSON.

`Signer.refused?(answer: { status, headers, body }) => boolean` is consulted for
a non-2xx answer the 401 rule did not already call refused. A true is
forgotten through `invalidate` and replayed once, exactly as a 401 is, POST
included. A throw is a no. It lives on the signer because only the scheme can
read its body, and a function cannot ride a JSON descriptor. A `bearer` or
`api_key` target keeps the 401 rule alone.

*Lives in:* `packages/conduit/src/types.ts` (`Signer`, `RefusedAnswer`) · `packages/conduit/src/transports/http.ts` (`refusedCredential`) · `conduit-connectors/packages/conduit-push/src/apns.ts` (`apnsJwtSigner`).

### <a id="fjs-d940"></a>2026-10-13 · `FJS-D940` — An `api_key` target names where its key travels, a header or a URL parameter, and conduit keeps a URL-carried key out of everything it hands back.

Google's legacy Geocoding takes its key only as `?key=`. A signer could write
headers and the body but never the URL, so the one way through was the caller
writing the secret into `req.query`, which every observer and log is handed
(`FJS-2727`). The owner picked **`query` on `api_key`** over **a `query` slot
on `SignOutput`**. With the slot, every `?key=` vendor would have to write a
signer, and conduit would have to track which parameters to redact. With
`query`, conduit knows the parameter's name. `FJS-D891` is not overturned: this
is a field on an existing type, and *the key goes in the URL* is not one
vendor's scheme.

`{ type: 'api_key', ref, query: 'key' }` takes the place of `header`, exactly
one of the two. The key goes on the URL that is fetched and nowhere else. The
URL a redirect is judged from stays keyless, and a caller's parameter of the
same name is displaced. A connection failure's message and `raw`, which Bun
builds from the URL, and an echoed `Location` are scrubbed of the key. `put()`
refuses both names or neither, and refuses `query` on a protocol whose URL the
http transport does not build.

*Lives in:* `packages/conduit/src/types.ts` (`api_key`) · `packages/conduit/src/transports/http.ts` (`dispatch`'s `wire`, `scrubber`) · `packages/conduit/src/conduit.ts` (`assertApiKey`) · `conduit-connectors/packages/conduit-google-maps/src/index.ts` (`googleMapsGeocodingTarget`).

### <a id="fjs-d913"></a>2026-10-13 · `FJS-D913` — How does Studio get `@frontierjs/css` and its fonts without a CDN, given litestone depends on toolbelt alone — Vendor a generated copy of `frontier.min.css` (~88 KB) at `src/tools/studio.css`, text-imported and served by Studio at its own path; a `packages/css` build step writes it and a litestone test fails when the copy differs from `packages/css/dist`. Fonts drop to the system stack (Inter and JetBrains Mono stay first in the list for machines that have them). No dependency edge, works in a compiled binary, costs one generated file.

Asked in [`IDEAS/owed-rulings.md`](IDEAS/owed-rulings.md) § Open questions. **A** was picked over **B** (Studio resolves `@frontierjs/css` at runtime when it is installed (optional peer) and serves `dist/frontier.min.css` from it, keeping the CDN link as the fallback. No copy to drift, but a data-only app has no css installed, so the offline case this row is about still renders unstyled, and a compiled binary cannot resolve it), **C** (Leave the CDN and record it: Studio already works unstyled (`studio.html` header), and `--host` on an offline machine is the rare case. Smallest change; the row closes as a documented limit).

The paper's recommendation, taken as written: it is the only option that fixes the offline case without a dependency edge; the drift is checked by a test rather than by memory, and dropping web fonts for the system stack removes the second CDN call with no asset to carry.

### <a id="fjs-d939"></a>2026-10-13 · `FJS-D939` — A conduit target declares the further origins its counterparty answers on, and a send names an absolute address on one of them.

One provider is often several hosts. OIDC discovery answers absolute endpoints,
and Google's sit on three origins. Under one target per origin, `conduit-oidc`
refused a foreign endpoint and the app registered a second target for a host it
only learned at runtime (`FJS-2730`). The owner picked **`origins` on the
target**. The rejected options: **`origins` for `auth: 'none'` only**, which
leaves google-maps' shared key on two targets, and **ruling the status quo**,
which would cost Google OIDC three bound sends.

`TargetDescriptor.origins` is a list of bare origins. `ConduitRequest.address`
is admitted on any target when its origin is the target's own or one it
declares, and is refused by name otherwise, before anything is sent. The
credential goes to every declared origin. That is why the list is a declaration
and never something a send says. `put()` refuses `origins` beside `address_from`
(which takes any URL, graded per send), beside `pinned_cert` (one certificate),
on a protocol other than http, and on an entry that is not an origin. One
declaration covers every origin, so this keeps `FJS-D933`'s *one place declares
auth*.

*Lives in:* `packages/conduit/src/types.ts` (`origins`) · `packages/conduit/src/conduit.ts` (`assertOrigins`) · `packages/conduit/src/transports/http.ts` (`declaresOrigin`) · `conduit-connectors/packages/conduit-oidc/src/index.ts`.

### <a id="fjs-d936"></a>2026-10-13 · `FJS-D936` — What happens to `driver jsonl` — Retire the format as a logging driver. The audit trail moves to its SQLite form; `drivers/jsonl.js`, `jsonl-index.js`, the jsonl half of `retention.js` and `driver logger`/`driver trail` stay in the tree, each flagged NOT IN USE UNTIL FURTHER NOTICE, and no schema declares them. Basecamp, `example` and the prototypes redeclare their audit database (pre-alpha: the old trail files are deleted, not migrated). One engine; the trail gains gates, indexes and migrations, and runs in the browser. Retention becomes a `DELETE` plus incremental vacuum rather than a file rewrite.

Asked in [`IDEAS/litestone-scope.md`](IDEAS/litestone-scope.md) § Open questions. **C** was picked over **A** (Keep both drivers, and move `jsonl` behind the engine seam `#sql-engine` already gives `bun:sqlite` and wasm (`FJS-D305`). The core learns *an engine answering a subset of verbs* generically, in place of the 77 references to `jsonl` it has now. Weeks of work, and two engines stay), **B** (Retire `driver jsonl` as general model storage, and keep the format only as the logger's private storage, inside the audit-trail code. Removes the request-log use (only `packages/litestone/example` declares one); the `logger` branches stay), **D** (Move `jsonl` and `logger` together into an audit battery package (the first question's **A**, for this one area). - **Recommend C, after one measurement** — it is the one-level-simpler version: one storage engine, and FJS-D180's lock and the compaction machinery stop being litestone's to keep correct. The measurement that could overturn it is write cost: a `create()` on a logged model with the trail as a SQLite insert in a second database, against the jsonl append, interleaved A/B in `bench/audit-bench.mjs`. If the SQLite trail costs much more on the hot path, **B** is the fallback. - **Measured 2026-10-08: the SQLite trail is cheaper.** `bun run bench audit-trail-ab` (§ 13): a `create()` on a logged model, trail write flushed and settled inside the timing, 500 per batch, 12 interleaved rounds. Four runs: jsonl append 152–163 µs/op, SQLite insert 109–121 µs/op, a ratio of 0.67–0.74; the hot path before the deferred write is the same for both, 47–53 µs. Taken on a loaded machine (load 1.7–3.4), so the absolute numbers are soft and the ratio held across every run. The measurement that could overturn **C** does not, and **B** is not needed as a fallback).

C with one amendment by the owner: nothing written for jsonl is deleted. The SQLite trail measured cheaper (0.67–0.74) and is one engine, so it is the only trail an app declares; the jsonl code is parked, flagged NOT IN USE UNTIL FURTHER NOTICE, rather than removed. The 2026-10-08 hold on this question is lifted by this ruling.

### <a id="fjs-d934"></a>2026-10-12 · `FJS-D934` — Conduit's http `stream()` is the response body as it arrives: one chunk per event of a `text/event-stream` body, and the bytes of any other.

`FJS-D585` kept http `stream()` at `not_implemented` until an app needed it.
Three did at once. `conduit-anthropic` and `conduit-openai` each owned a `fetch`
that re-resolved the credential, re-set the headers and re-graded the status,
which cost them the breaker, the concurrency cap, the observers and the retry
ladder (`FJS-2728`). ELA buffered 3CX recordings of up to 64 MB under a raised
`max_response_bytes` (`FJS-2579`). One `stream()` serves both cases, and the
`content-type` decides the chunk, which extends D585's rule: a body is decoded
only when its type says what it is. An SSE body yields `{ event, data, id }` as
`@frontierjs/toolbelt/sse` reads it. Any other body yields a `Uint8Array` per
read, with no `max_response_bytes` cap. A request option for the shape was
rejected, because it would be a second way to say what the response already
says.

A stream opens through `send()`'s own `attempt()`, with the retries, the one
remint and `Retry-After`. A failure before the first byte throws the
`ConduitError` that `send()` answers, with the status on `ConduitStreamError.meta`,
so a connector's `translate()` handles both paths. The per-attempt timeout
covers the wait for headers, and the caller's `signal` bounds the body.
`conduit.stream()` now admits through `resilience` on every protocol and holds
the slot until the stream ends, because an open stream is a request the target
is still serving. A failure after the open is `stream_error` and not
`indeterminate`: the 2xx says the request was applied. Each chunk carries the
response's `meta`. That is the only place a raw route finds the `content-type`
it has to pass on.

The decision rules ran before the code. **Paved road vs. the workaround**
decided it: two connectors had written the same owned `fetch`.

*Lives in:* `packages/conduit/src/transports/http.ts` (`stream`, `exchange`) · `packages/conduit/src/conduit.ts` (`stream`) · `packages/conduit/stream.test.ts`.

### <a id="fjs-d933"></a>2026-10-12 · `FJS-D933` — HTTP Basic is conduit's one built-in signer, and a protocol that spends two credentials registers one target per credential.

`FJS-D891` stands: a vendor's scheme is a `signed` target and gets no `TargetAuth`
variant. Basic is not one vendor's scheme. Four connectors had each written it,
and the copies disagreed: twilio sent the secret as given, shipping added the
colon a key-only login needs, oidc form-encoded both halves first, and serpgrid
answered the whole `Basic …` value from its resolver under `api_key`
(`FJS-2233`). The owner picked **a built-in signer** over **a `basic` variant**
(which overturns D891) and over **an exported signer the app installs**
(every app has to remember the line). `basic` is always installed, and a connector's
signer may not take the name.

OIDC's token endpoint spends the client's Basic, and userinfo spends the user's
Bearer. The `oidc-client-basic` signer decided per request by method and by an
existing `authorization` header (`FJS-2729`). The owner picked **one target per
credential** over **per-route `auth`**, which would have been a second place that
declares auth. `oidcClientTarget` signs everything it carries and `oidcPublicTarget` carries
no auth. The same shape answers `FJS-2722`'s mint-through-a-second-target.

*Lives in:* `packages/conduit/src/signers.ts` · `packages/conduit/signers.test.ts` · `conduit-connectors/packages/conduit-oidc/src/index.ts` (`oidcClientTarget`, `oidcPublicTarget`, `assertSpends`).

### <a id="fjs-d932"></a>2026-10-12 · `FJS-D932` — Where a site-kit build finds the images to make responsive — In the built HTML: a postbuild step rewrites every local raster `<img>` in the prerendered pages.

Asked in [`IDEAS/site-kit-images.md`](IDEAS/site-kit-images.md) § Open questions.
Picked by the owner in session as **A** over **B** (the `Image` block emits a
`srcset` from a manifest the build writes, so every block rendering a photo
must use it, which is the Astro and enhanced-img model) and **C** (legacy
ksite's regex scan of source plus a component that rebuilds the variant
filenames).

The rendered `<img>` is the one place every image ends up: a markdown line, a
frontmatter list, a kit block or a client's own block. On the Luminous Heart
port that is all 208 tags on 23 pages, and none of its photos are set as CSS
backgrounds. B misses any block that writes its own `<img>`, and nothing would
report it. C's two halves agree only through a filename convention, which is
how legacy wrote two images with the same name to one file.

What A gives up, accepted with it: `sizes` is derived from the rendered `width`
unless a block states its own, dev serves the originals, and an image added in
the browser after load is not reached. The last does not affect a site-kit
page, which ships no app script, but it applies to any app the step serves once
it moves into Sierra.

Work: `FJS-2737`.
*Lives in:* `packages/site-kit/config/images.js` · `packages/site-kit/test/images.mjs`.

### <a id="fjs-d926"></a>2026-10-12 · `FJS-D926` — Which codec and which formats a site-kit build's responsive images use — `Bun.Image`, WebP only, on every host.

Asked in [`IDEAS/site-kit-images.md`](IDEAS/site-kit-images.md) § Open questions.
Picked by the owner in session as **A** over **B** (sharp as site-kit's
transformer, adding AVIF for eager images, as legacy ksite does) and **C**
(`Bun.Image`, adding AVIF wherever the build host can encode it).

Measured on the Luminous Heart photos: WebP at 480/1080/1920 is 94–97% smaller
than the source, and AVIF is a further 21–30% smaller than WebP, so resizing is
nearly the whole saving. `Bun.Image` refuses AVIF encoding on Linux x64 because
it relies on the OS codec, and `FJS-D311` does not mention this. C would make
`dist/` depend on which machine built it. B adds a native dependency to win the
last fraction.

**B reopens on one measurement**: the LCP difference AVIF makes on a real
client's hero. The step receives its transformer under `FJS-D311`'s seam, so
adopting B later means passing sharp in, with no change to the step.

Work: `FJS-2737`.
*Lives in:* `IDEAS/site-kit-images.md` (unbuilt).

### <a id="fjs-d892"></a>2026-10-10 · `FJS-D892` — AWS Signature V4 has one owner, and it is `@frontierjs/toolbelt`.

Litestone's `File` columns sign S3 requests today (`src/storage/sigv4.js`), and
`conduit-s3` (`FJS-D889`) signs the same requests. Conduit peers on junction, so
litestone may never import a conduit connector (Invariant 1). Two copies of one
signing scheme is the drift `toolbelt/signature` was created to end, so the
scheme goes below the dependency graph (`FJS-D26`). Litestone and `conduit-s3`
both read it.

The signer is WebCrypto, which the browser build of litestone already has
(`FJS-D305`). **The signing-key cache stays with the caller**: a cache is state,
and toolbelt exports pure functions (`FJS-D111`).

Work: `FJS-2543`.
*Lives in:* `packages/toolbelt/src/` (to move) · `packages/litestone/src/storage/sigv4.js` (to become a caller).

### <a id="fjs-d891"></a>2026-10-10 · `FJS-D891` — A vendor's authentication reaches conduit through ONE signer seam, never through a new `TargetAuth` variant per scheme.

`TargetAuth` holds `bearer`, `api_key`, `hmac` and `none`. The next connectors
need five more schemes:

- Basic auth (Twilio)
- a secret in the request body (Turnstile)
- an ES256 JWT minted hourly (APNs)
- an OAuth service-account token (FCM, Google)
- SigV4 (S3)

A variant for each means five edits to conduit core, each made for one vendor and
versioned on that vendor's schedule. That is `FJS-D153`'s first cost again,
landing inside the package the ruling kept vendor-free.

**Through the seam, a connector supplies the function that turns the resolved
credential and the serialized request into what goes on the wire.** Conduit
keeps `serialize()`, because the bytes signed must be the bytes sent
(`FJS-D153`), and the resolver keeps the secret out of every log. Two questions
are decided when the seam is built, not here: whether the four existing variants
move onto it as built-in signers, and how a minted credential states when it
expires.

Built under `FJS-2542`.
*Lives in:* `packages/conduit/src/types.ts` (`signed`, `Signer`) · `packages/conduit/src/transports/base.ts` (`authorize`) · `packages/conduit/signers.test.ts`.

**Built as one variant, `{ type: 'signed', signer, ref }`,** naming a function in
`ConduitOptions.signers` — a name, because a descriptor is stored as JSON. The
two questions it left, answered when built: **the four existing types stay**,
since no connector needs them moved; **a minted credential's expiry is the
resolver's**, the `withCache` TTL over a `get()` that mints, which `invalidate`
already forgets on a 401 — conduit gains no credential lifetime.

### <a id="fjs-d890"></a>2026-10-10 · `FJS-D890` — What an official connector contains: a target builder, payload types, an error mapping onto `ConduitErrorKind`, a sink and a drive, always. Add a webhook verifier where the vendor sends webhooks, and a fixture where a conforming server exists.

Asked in [`IDEAS/conduit-connectors.md`](IDEAS/conduit-connectors.md) § The order.
The list is read off the eight connectors already written in app code, not
designed ahead of them. Stripe and Telnyx carry all six pieces. DigitalOcean and
Hetzner carry four, because a compute vendor sends no webhook.

**It binds `@frontierjs/conduit-*`**, the connectors this project maintains. A
third-party connector (`@kobami/conduit-*`) may follow it, and nothing grades it
against the contract. A connector is TypeScript, like conduit.

It also answers the three questions `FJS-D153` left to a second connector:

- **Sink or fixture: both.** The sink owns chaos: a duplicate delivery, a lost
  response, a moved clock, each mapped onto `ConduitErrorKind`. That is most of
  what a connector is for. The fixture checks the sink, because one drive runs
  against both.
- **Return or install: return.** The builder returns a `TargetDescriptor` and
  installs nothing, which is what `stripeTarget()` already does. The app's
  conduit config owns installation.
- **Function or hook: a pure function** from raw body, headers and secret to the
  event or a refusal, called from a raw route over `ctx.$raw.rawBody`. A hook
  wrapping it is added once two apps write the same wrapper.

The contract is graded by `fli check`'s `connector-contract`: each `packages/conduit-*` holds a sink, a drive and `@frontierjs/conduit` as a peer. The rest of the list is a judgement no rule makes.
*Lives in:* this ruling · the first extraction, conduit-stripe in the sibling conduit-connectors checkout.

### <a id="fjs-d889"></a>2026-10-10 · `FJS-D889` — A connector may own a PROTOCOL, and is then named for the protocol: `conduit-s3`, `conduit-oidc`, `conduit-openai`.

Asked in [`IDEAS/conduit-connectors.md`](IDEAS/conduit-connectors.md) § The open
question the ruling does not cover. `FJS-D153` names connectors after vendors and
assumes one vendor per connector. But five storage vendors speak S3, and every
identity provider that publishes a discovery document speaks OIDC. Five
near-copies of one connector diverge by the third.

**The rule: a connector may own a protocol that more than one server implements,
and it is named for the protocol.** Conformance is measured, not claimed: the
connector's drive passes against at least two implementations. So a protocol
connector always ships a fixture beside its sink, such as MinIO for S3, a local
OIDC provider, or Ollama for the OpenAI chat shape. **A vendor's extension to the
protocol belongs to the app** until a second implementation shares it, so the
connector does not grow a flag per vendor (R2's `region: 'auto'`, path-style
addressing).

*Lives in:* this ruling · `IDEAS/conduit-connectors.md` § The order.

### <a id="fjs-d767"></a>2026-10-09 · `FJS-D767` — Is `unknown` allowed to ship — Yes, with a warning: `unknown` ships and is printed in the release output beside the bump.

Asked in [`IDEAS/version-compatibility.md`](IDEAS/version-compatibility.md) § Open questions. **B** was picked over **A** (No: as `release:check`, `unknown` counts as a contract and refuses a minor bump under `--strict`).

The paper's recommendation, taken as written: strictness follows cost (§ IV *ergonomics vs. strictness*). A wrong verdict on a package is fixed by the next publish, while a database cannot be half-migrated. Level 1, the export surface, never answers `unknown`, so the warning only appears for the levels that cannot be decided.

### <a id="fjs-d766"></a>2026-10-09 · `FJS-D766` — Should the peer ranges be generated rather than written — Generated at publish: each internal peer is written from the sibling's workspace version at pack time (the train's number under a train), and `exports.snapshot.md` records the result.

Asked in [`IDEAS/version-compatibility.md`](IDEAS/version-compatibility.md) § Open questions. **B** was picked over **A** (Written by hand, as today: a floor typed once).

The paper's recommendation, taken as written: a peer range is a fact about which sibling version a package was built and tested against, so it is derived. It holds under either answer to the train question, and the `snapshots` phase already shows the range moving.

### <a id="fjs-d738"></a>2026-10-09 · `FJS-D738` — Is `FJS-D297`'s severability test worth promoting out of one ruling — A ruling of its own about packaging, holding § *The test*'s five outcomes and citing `FJS-D297` as where it came from.

Asked in [`IDEAS/map-packages.md`](IDEAS/map-packages.md) § Open questions. **A** was picked over **B** (one sentence in `PHILOSOPHY.md` § IV, *batteries vs. smallness*: nothing that is the default is severable), **C** (this file stays its index).

The paper's recommendation, taken as written: the five-outcome table names precedents (`warden`, `foundry`, `chronos`), which § VII keeps out of a guiding document, and C is what § VII forbids. A ruling is the register an assessment may cite, and § IV may cite the ruling in turn.

### <a id="fjs-d635"></a>2026-10-08 · `FJS-D635` — What is litestone's edge — The batteries stay in litestone behind a seam. Nothing under `src/core/` imports them, a test fails if anything does, and each one leaves the main entry for its own subpath (`./storage`, `./replicate`, `./transform`). Studio's server leaves `cli.js` for its own file, and its saved queries leave the app's database. A new `.lite` word, `$` method or `src/` directory names the axis it serves, or it is a battery.

Asked in [`IDEAS/litestone-scope.md`](IDEAS/litestone-scope.md) § Open questions. **B** was picked over **A** (Each battery moves to its own package. The core's package exports only the four axes), **C** (Admit them into the core and widen the edge to name them).

The paper's recommendation, taken as written: § 1 measured all four as already outside the core, so B costs about a day and no core surgery. It writes the edge down and gives it a failing test (§ V's ninth question), and A stays open as a later move with nothing to untangle first. C makes "done" unreachable, which is the question this paper set out to answer.

**The edge: litestone owns what is true about a row in a database** — its shape, who may read and write it, what moves it may make, and how its shape changes. Object storage, moving data between machines, ETL, and showing data to a person are batteries. Work over time is caravan's, and invariants spanning rows stay in application code (`FJS-D168`). A new `.lite` word, `$` method or `src/` directory names the axis it serves, or it is a battery. `driver jsonl` is the one area this does not settle; it is its own question in the same paper.

*Lives in:* `IDEAS/litestone-scope.md` § 1 · `packages/litestone/src/index.js` (the subpaths) · `packages/litestone/test/edge.test.ts`.

### <a id="fjs-d549"></a>2026-10-05 · `FJS-D549` — Does FJS-D533 stand now that an app relies on nesting — A declared subset that includes nesting: block maps and sequences at any depth, `|` and `>` scalars, and flow collections, with anchors, aliases, merge keys and tags refused by name. It's one toolbelt kit with no dependency, as A intended, and it holds everything ksite writes. - **Recommend C.** D533's reason was the part of YAML that caused `FJS-821`, and C still refuses that part. The nesting D533 gave up is something a real client site depends on. A leaves ksite's content split across two formats, which is a cost every client site cut from the template would pay.

Asked in [`IDEAS/toolbelt-admissions.md`](IDEAS/toolbelt-admissions.md) § Open questions. **C** was picked over **A** (D533 stands. The kit is the flat subset, it refuses what it does not read, and a site keeps nested content in a JS module. ksite's port already does this for five files, so `content/` stops being all Markdown), **B** (full YAML (D533's option B). The parser stays sierra's, mesa reads what sierra reads, and the `FJS-821` mitigation stays with js-yaml).

D533's reason was the part of YAML that caused FJS-821, and C still refuses that part. The nesting D533 gave up is something a real client site depends on, and A would leave ksite's content split across two formats, a cost every client site cut from the template would pay.

### <a id="fjs-d554"></a>2026-09-29 · `FJS-D554` — The browser drive an app imports is `@frontierjs/mesa/drive`: the driver half of mesa's harness, published; the spec runner stays in `test/browser/` and is not.

Asked in [`FJS-1580`](ISSUES_ARCHIVE.md#fjs-1580). **A** was picked over **B** (a new leaf package, `@frontierjs/drive`), **C** (`@frontierjs/testing/browser`) and **D** (a toolbelt kit).

Mesa is the leaf, so every package's drive and every app's may import it. litestone's browser-client drive already did, by relative path. C sits above junction, so mesa, ui and css could not use it, which leaves two harnesses for good. D spends toolbelt's license: `FJS-D26` admits it below the graph because every export is pure, and a kit that spawns processes and installs exit handlers makes that "pure, except". B is the same code under a clearer name, plus a package and a noun. It is the rename to reach for if app-level helpers (an authenticator, server preflight, a report) outgrow a substrate subpath.

The driver is mesa-neutral but for one line: a console warning starting `[Mesa]` counts as a page error. A page mesa did not render never writes one, so that needs no option, and an option nobody passes is complexity the problem did not have. One option was added, `profile`, a directory kept across close and relaunch, because an offline app's drive cannot be measured without it. Lives in `packages/mesa/src/drive.js`. The copies still to fold onto it are `FJS-1588`.

Asked in [`IDEAS/toolbelt-admissions.md`](IDEAS/toolbelt-admissions.md) § Open questions. **A** was picked over **B** (full YAML is the meaning; the parser stays sierra's, and mesa's hand-rolled reader is the defect to close rather than the shape to standardize).

The paper's recommendation, taken as written: a frontmatter block is configuration written by hand into a route file, and anchors, aliases and merge keys are the part of YAML that produced `FJS-821` in the first place, so dropping them removes the mitigation along with the feature. **B is the honest answer if an app is found relying on nesting**, which nothing in this repo does — every `.md` and `.mesa` frontmatter here is flat.

### <a id="fjs-d339"></a>2026-09-20 · `FJS-D339` — Where does the token HMAC live — A `@frontierjs/toolbelt` kit (WebCrypto only; `/signature` already has a private `hmacHex`).

Asked in [`IDEAS/bearer-access.md`](IDEAS/bearer-access.md) § Open questions. **A** was picked over **B** (`bearerClaim` lives in auth, beside the API keys it resembles), **C** (junction owns it and auth's API keys move onto it).
